exp.0:3:
Paul says that he always gives thanks to God for the believers in Corinth. The reason is the grace of God, that is, his favor and undeserved gift, which they received through Jesus Christ. The word "always" and the phrase "given you" are the parts of the verse to note here: "always" means at all times, and "given you" means that God has bestowed this grace on them.

Paul writes from Ephesus, according to most scholars, to a church with many problems: divisions, pride, and disorder. Even so, he begins with thanksgiving, not with rebuke. He looks first at what God has done for them, and later in the letter he corrects what is wrong.

Today we can imitate Paul: before criticizing someone in the church, the family, or the workplace, let us ask God to show us the grace already at work in that person, and give thanks for it. This softens the heart to speak the truth in love.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that the message about Christ, that is, what Paul proclaimed to them, was established and made firm in the lives of the Corinthians. "Testimony" is the proclamation or truth about Jesus, and "confirmed" means made sure, proven. It refers to what God did among them, giving evidence that the gospel was real.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with many problems and divisions, as the letter will show. Even so, he begins by giving thanks for what God has already done in them. He reminds them that their spiritual gifts and riches do not come from themselves, but from God's grace in Christ.

For today: before correcting or criticizing others, let us learn to recognize and be thankful for what God is doing in your life. And let us examine whether the truth of Christ is taking firm root in ours.
exp.0:7:
He says that God himself will keep on strengthening and sustaining the believers in Corinth until the end of their lives or until Christ returns. The purpose is that they will be blameless, meaning without any valid charge against them, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, the day of his return and of judgment.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, a community rich in spiritual gifts but also marked by divisions and serious failings. Before correcting them, he reminds them of what God has done in them. His confidence rests not in their own strength but in the faithfulness of God, as the next verse says.

For today: if you feel weak or fall short, remember that your steadiness rests on God, not on your own perfection. Trust that he holds you up, and respond with a life of obedience and unity with other believers.
exp.0:12:
Paul asks three questions to show how absurd it is to divide into groups. "Is Christ divided?" means that Christ is one and is not split among factions. He then asks whether Paul was crucified for them, or whether they were baptized in Paul's name. The answer to all of these is no.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. People from the household of Chloe told him there were quarrels, since some said they belonged to Paul, others to Apollos, others to Cephas (Peter), or to Christ. Paul reminds them that only Christ died for them and that baptism is in his name.

For today: before we defend a leader, a group, or a way of thinking, let us remember that our primary loyalty is to Christ. We can value those who teach us, but without separating ourselves from other believers because of them.
exp.0:13:
Paul says he thanks God that he baptized very few people in Corinth: only Crispus and Gaius.

Paul is writing to a church divided into groups that identified with different leaders: Paul, Apollos, Cephas (Peter), or Christ. He reminds them that Christ alone was crucified for them. He gives thanks that, since he baptized so few, no one can say they were baptized in his name. He is not downplaying baptism; he is correcting pride and factionalism.

For today: value the leaders God has given you, but do not place your identity in them. Let your main loyalty be to Christ, and seek unity with other believers.
exp.0:15:
Paul says that he also baptized the household of Stephanas. Then he admits that he does not remember whether he baptized anyone else. The phrase "the household" refers to those of his house.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided because some followed one leader and others followed another. He makes clear that he did not want to form a group of his own. So, by correcting himself and acknowledging that he did not remember everything, he shows that baptizing was not the center of his calling. His priority was to preach the gospel of the cross of Christ.

Today, we can value the leaders God gives us without placing them in the place of Christ. May our unity be based on Jesus and his cross, not on people, styles or names.
exp.0:17:
It says that the message of the cross, that is, the news that Jesus died and rose again for us, seems like foolishness to those who are walking the road to destruction. But for those who are being saved, it is the power of God. The word "foolishness" means lack of sense, and "power" means strength or might.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who were divided and took pride in following different teachers and in their human wisdom. He reminds them that their task was to preach the gospel with simplicity, so that nothing would take away the strength of Christ's cross. He will later show that God works differently from how the world thinks.

For today: do not be ashamed of a simple message. If someone mocks your faith, remember that the cross does not need human decorations to transform lives. Trust in the power of God and share your faith with humility and love.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that the world, with all its human wisdom, did not come to know God. Although God had revealed himself in his creation and his work, people did not recognize him through their own reasoning. So God chose to save those who believe through the preaching of the message, which to the eyes of the world seems foolish. The word "pleased" means that it was his good will. "Foolishness" means something that makes no sense.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city that admired eloquence and learning. There were divisions among the believers, and some boasted of being wise. Paul reminds them that salvation does not depend on human cleverness, but on the message of Christ crucified.

For today: you do not need to be brilliant or to have all the answers to draw near to God. Trust the simple gospel, and share it with humility, without being ashamed that some see it as foolish.
exp.0:21:
This verse says that the Jews asked for signs, that is, miracles or visible proofs from God, and that the Greeks looked for wisdom, meaning reasoning and philosophy that would convince them. Each group wanted God on its own terms.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and took pride in its human wisdom. He reminds them that the message of Christ crucified did not fit what either Jews or Greeks expected. To some it was a stumbling block, to others foolishness, but to those called by God it is power and wisdom. The exact details of each kind of seeking are understood in several ways, but the central idea is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we demand from God proofs or explanations made to our own measure. Let us instead trust in Christ, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.0:22:
Paul says that he and his companions proclaim Christ crucified. For the Jews this is a stumblingblock, that is, something that makes them stumble or takes offense. For the Gentiles, meaning the non-Jews, it is foolishness, a meaningless nonsense.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and greatly admired human wisdom. The Jews asked for miraculous signs, and the Greeks looked for brilliant philosophy. A Messiah who died on a cross fit neither of these. But Paul goes on to say that, for those who are called, Christ is the power and wisdom of God.

For today: do not be ashamed of a simple message that others do not understand. Trust that the cross has power, and share Christ with humility, without dressing him up to please everyone.
exp.0:24:
It says that what seems to men to be the "foolishness" of God is wiser than all human wisdom. And what seems to be the "weakness" of God is stronger than human strength. "Foolish" means senseless or absurd; "weak" means frail. Paul does not say that God is really foolish or weak, but that this is how the world sees him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and proud of its wisdom. He reminds them that the message of Christ crucified seemed ridiculous to the Greeks and offensive to the Jews. Yet in that cross God showed his wisdom and his power to save.

For today: do not be ashamed if your faith seems foolish or weak to others. Trust that God works in ways we do not always understand. When you feel small or without resources, remember that God can do something great through you.
exp.0:27:
It says that God chose what the world considers base, that is, of little value or low standing, and what the world despises. He also chose what is not, meaning what the world regards as counting for nothing at all. With this, God brings to nothing what the world believes is important.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community divided and proud of its wisdom and its favorite leaders. He asks them to look at who they were when God called them: few wise, powerful, or of noble birth. In this way he shows them that salvation comes from God and not from human merit, so that no one may boast before him.

For today: if you feel like nobody special, remember that God does not look at you for your status or your achievements. Serve with humility and, if anything good comes out of your life, give God the glory.
exp.0:29:
This verse says that believers belong to God by being united with Christ Jesus. God himself made Christ to be wisdom for us, righteousness (being declared right before God), sanctification (being set apart for God and transformed), and redemption (being rescued, like someone who pays a ransom).

Paul writes to a church in Corinth that was divided and boasted in human wisdom and in favorite leaders. He reminds them that God chose humble people, so that no one may boast. Everything they have comes from Christ, not from themselves.

For today: when you feel proud of your achievements, or small because of your failures, remember that your worth before God does not depend on you but on Christ. Thank him today for what he has already done for you.
exp.1:3:
Paul says that when he announced the gospel to the Corinthians, he did not use fine speeches or arguments designed to impress. Instead, his message rested on a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that is, on clear evidence that God himself was at work.

Paul writes to a church in Corinth, a city that admired eloquence and human wisdom. Some there prided themselves on being good speakers or on following certain teachers. Paul reminds them that he arrived weak and fearful, so that their faith would rest on the power of God and not on human skill. Interpreters debate how that power was shown, but the text points to the work of the Spirit.

Today, do not trust that someone can be won over by good words alone, nor expect to win others that way. Share Christ with simplicity and pray that the Spirit will touch hearts.
exp.1:5:
Paul says that he does teach wisdom, but to those who are "mature," that is, to believers who are spiritually grown in the faith. The word "but" in this verse introduces a contrast. That wisdom does not come from this present age (this era or the present world) nor from its rulers and leaders, who come to nothing, meaning they pass away and lose their power.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and fascinated by brilliant speeches. He has just said that his preaching did not rely on persuasive words, but on the power of the Spirit. Now he clarifies that the gospel is not ignorance: it has a deep wisdom, but that wisdom comes from God. Some understand "mature" as mature believers; others understand it as all who are in Christ.

For today: do not measure your faith by what impresses the world. Seek to grow in maturity, asking the Spirit to teach you God's wisdom in his Word.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that God revealed his secret wisdom to us through the Holy Spirit. The reason is that the Spirit searches all things, even the deepest things of God. "But" is the word the verse uses to connect this thought to the one before it; "searches" means to investigate thoroughly, to know completely.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church that boasted in human wisdom. He reminds them that the rulers of this world did not understand the message of the cross. What God prepared is not discovered by intelligence alone; God himself makes it known.

For today: before you read the Bible or make important decisions, ask the Holy Spirit to give you understanding. Do not depend only on your own cleverness; come with humility, expecting that God will show you his truth.
exp.1:12:
Paul says that he and his companions speak about what God has given them, but they do not use elegant words or the wisdom that the world teaches. They speak with the words that the Holy Spirit teaches. The phrase "comparing spiritual things with spiritual" can be understood in several ways: joining spiritual truths with spiritual words, or explaining spiritual things to people who have the Spirit.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who greatly admired eloquent speech and human wisdom, and for that reason they were divided. He reminds them that his message does not depend on brilliant speeches, but on what the Holy Spirit reveals about Christ.

For today: when speaking about God with others, do not try to impress. Pray, ask for the Spirit's guidance, and explain the Bible with simple and sincere words.
exp.2:0:
Paul tells the believers in Corinth that he could not treat them as spiritual people, meaning mature in the faith, but had to treat them as people who are still ruled by their desires and human attitudes. He calls them infants in Christ: they are believers, but still immature.

Paul, who founded the church in Corinth, writes to them because there was jealousy, quarreling, and division among them. Some lined up behind different leaders. He uses the image of milk and solid food to show that their behavior revealed little spiritual growth.

Today we can ask ourselves: do my attitudes reflect growth? Jealousy and arguments show that we need to mature. One practical step is to read the Bible regularly, pray, and seek peace with anyone we are at odds with.
exp.2:8:
The explanation says that Paul and the other teachers are God's fellow workers, meaning collaborators or co-workers who serve alongside Him. It also calls believers a cultivated field and a building. Everything belongs to God: the workers labor, but the field and the house are His.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided because some lined up behind one leader and others behind another. To correct them, he reminds them that servants like himself and Apollos are not the most important. God is the one who gives the growth, and each worker will answer to Him for his work.

Today, if you serve in your church, do it with humility and without competing. Do not compare yourself to others or think you are indispensable. Work faithfully, knowing that the fruit comes from God and that His work is what counts.
exp.2:10:
Paul says there is only one possible foundation for life and for the church: Jesus Christ. No one can lay a different one. A foundation is the firm base on which a house is built. It is a base that God has already laid, not one invented by people.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who were divided and gathered around different leaders. He reminds them that teachers are only God's fellow workers. Paul laid the foundation when he proclaimed Christ to them, and others keep building on top of it. What matters is that each person takes care in how they build.

For today: examine what you are building your life, your family and your service on. If you rely on reputation, success, or some leader, return to Christ and let Him be the foundation of your daily decisions.
exp.2:11:
Paul says that someone can build on the foundation, which is Jesus Christ, using very different materials. Some are valuable and durable: gold, silver, and precious stones. Others are fragile and burn easily: wood, hay (dry grass), and stubble (straw or dry remains).

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided by rivalries between its leaders. He had founded the community, and other teachers continued teaching afterward. He reminds them that everyone works for God and that each person will answer for how they build. Christians have understood the fire and the reward in various ways, but all agree that God will evaluate the work.

For today: before you serve, teach, or counsel others, ask yourself whether you are doing it with truth, love, and humility, or out of pride and appearance. Build with what lasts.
exp.2:14:
It says that if a person's work is burned by the fire of testing, that work is lost and the person receives no reward. But that person will still be saved, though only just, like someone who escapes a fire.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided by followers of different leaders. He reminds them that the foundation is Jesus Christ, and that teachers and workers only build on him. God will test the quality of each work with fire. Interpreters debate exactly what that fire is, but the clear point is that God judges the service, not the salvation.

For today: serve God with pure motives and with faithfulness, not seeking fame or applause. What you do out of love for Christ and to build up others is what remains.
exp.2:15:
Do you not know that you yourselves are God's temple, and that God's Spirit dwells in you? Here "you" is plural: Paul is speaking to the whole community, and God's Spirit dwells in the midst of it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which is divided by rivalries between leaders. Earlier he spoke of workers who build on the foundation, which is Christ, and of how God will test each work. Now he reminds them that the church itself is God's holy building. For this reason he warns against anyone who would harm it with divisions or pride. Some also apply the principle to each individual body, but in this passage the emphasis is on the community.

For today: take care of the unity of your church. Before you criticize or divide, ask yourself whether your words build up or damage the place where God lives.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that no one should deceive himself. If someone in the church thinks they are wise by the standards of this age (that is, this present time or this world), they should become humble and free of pride, so that they can truly become wise.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided by rivalries and by admiration for certain teachers. He has just told them that they are God's temple, and that dividing the community harms it. For this reason he warns them against intellectual pride. The verses that follow explain that human wisdom, apart from God, is foolishness before Him.

For today: before arguing or boasting about what I know, I can ask God for humility, listen patiently to others, and recognize that I need to learn from Him.
exp.2:18:
What it says: Paul states that what the world calls wisdom is, in God's eyes, foolishness, meaning something of no true value. He quotes Scripture (Job 5:13) to show that God catches the wise in their own cleverness, that is, in their own clever schemes.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided over following different leaders and boasting in human wisdom. He reminds them that they are God's temple and that they must set aside intellectual pride. Being simple-hearted here does not mean being ignorant, but depending humbly on God.

For today: Before making an important decision, pray and ask God for guidance, even when you have good arguments. Be humble in listening to the Bible and to other believers, and do not boast in what you know.
exp.3:13:
Paul says that he is not writing these things to make you feel bad or to leave you in shame. His purpose is to correct you and advise you with affection, the way a father does with children he loves.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, a church he himself founded. They were dealing with problems of pride and division. Earlier, Paul had described with irony how the apostles suffer and are looked down on, while some Corinthians felt very important. Now he makes clear that his hard words come from love, not from a wish to humiliate them.

For today: when you need to correct someone, do it with love and with the desire to help them grow, not to put them down. And when someone corrects you, remember that honest correction can be a sign of care.
exp.3:18:
Paul says he will come to visit the Corinthians soon, if the Lord allows it. When he arrives, he will not be concerned with what those who are puffed up with pride say in words. He wants to find out whether they have real power, meaning the actual working of God in their lives.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided. Some, full of pride, criticized Paul and thought he would not come back. That is why he sent Timothy to remind them of how he taught. The verses that follow say that the kingdom of God is not a matter of words, but of power.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed only by someone who speaks beautifully. Look at whether a person's life, including your own, shows humility, love, and true fruit.
exp.3:19:
It says that the kingdom of God, that is, God's rule and work among his people, is not shown by fine speeches, but by power. In the verse, the word for this is simply power: the real strength of God that changes lives. It also speaks of people who are puffed up and swollen with pride.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some boasted about their eloquence and looked down on his authority, thinking he would not come back. Paul tells them that he will come, if the Lord wills, and that he will not be concerned with their impressive words, but with whether there is truly the power of God in their lives.

For today: it is not enough to talk about faith, to know Christian phrases, or to sound convinced. Ask yourself whether your life shows the power of God in your character, your love, your patience, and your obedience.
exp.3:20:
Paul asks the believers in Corinth a question: do they want him to come with a rod, that is, with firm correction, or with love and a spirit of gentleness and humility in how he treats them? The rod is an instrument of discipline, like the one a father or a shepherd would use.

Paul writes to them as a spiritual father, since he founded that church. Some in Corinth were proud and talked a great deal, and some even questioned his authority. He tells them that what matters is not fine-sounding words but the power of God seen in a life. The choice is left to them: their attitude will determine how he deals with them.

For today: when someone corrects us, or when we have to correct someone, let us remember that humility and love open doors. And if we are corrected, let us listen with simplicity, before a harsher correction becomes necessary.
exp.4:5:
It is not good that the Corinthians take pride in themselves. Their boasting is presuming to be above others. Paul reminds them of something they already know: a little yeast makes the whole batch of dough rise.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. They were tolerating a man who was living in serious immorality, and yet they felt proud. Paul uses leaven as an image: sin that is not confronted can affect the whole community. Some understand the handing over to Satan as expelling the man from the church, although its exact scope is debated.

Today we can ask whether we are ignoring some sin, in ourselves or in our community, while we boast about how good we are. With humility and love, it is wise to face it, always seeking the restoration of the person and the purity of the church.
exp.4:11:
Paul asks: what have I to do with judging those outside the church? That is, it is not his place or the church's place to correct outsiders. Instead, he asks the Corinthians whether they themselves should not judge, that is, evaluate and correct, those who are inside the community of faith. "Judge" here means to discern and act with discipline, not to condemn with contempt.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a brother who was living in serious immorality (this has been the subject since verse 1). They were even proud of it. Paul makes clear that he is not asking them to isolate themselves from the world, but not to give shelter or close fellowship to someone who calls himself a Christian and lives in sin without repenting. His goal is to protect the church and, according to other passages, also to help the person return to God.

For today: instead of criticizing those who do not believe, care with humility and love for the life of your own community. If a brother is going astray, speak with him in private, with the aim of restoring him, and leave the final judgment of others to God.
exp.4:12:
Paul says that God himself will judge the people who are outside the church. But the church has a responsibility to remove the wicked person, meaning the one who calls himself a brother and lives in serious sin without repenting. To put away means to take out or separate.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church that tolerated a man living in serious sexual immorality (5:1). He does not ask them to judge the world, but to protect the purity and witness of the community. Many understand that the goal of this discipline is also that the person will feel the weight of his sin and be restored; the letter later mentions something similar (2 Corinthians 2:5-8), although not everyone agrees that it is the same case.

For today: instead of criticizing those who do not believe, examine your own life and the life of your church. If you must correct a brother, do it with humility, prayer, and a desire to see him restored, not with pride or rejection.
exp.5:0:
Paul asks a question that sounds like a rebuke: how does a believer who has a problem with another believer dare to take it before judges who do not know God, instead of settling it among the brothers?

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which had many divisions and disorders. Some brothers were suing each other in civil courts, and this damaged the church's witness before the city. The following verses explain that believers will take part in God's judgment, so they should be able to settle small matters. Some debate how far this applies today, especially in serious cases or crimes.

For today: if you have a conflict with another believer, first seek to talk it through with humility and ask wise leaders in your church for help, before making it public.
exp.5:2:
Paul reminds the believers in Corinth that they will judge angels.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had many problems. Some brothers and sisters were taking one another to court before unbelieving judges. Paul is ashamed of this and wants them to settle their disputes within the church. It is not known in detail how or when they will judge angels; interpreters understand this in different ways.

Today, when you have a conflict with another believer, seek first to resolve it with humility, prayer, and the help of mature brothers and sisters, before turning to lawsuits that harm the church's witness.
exp.5:6:
Paul tells the believers in Corinth that it is already a defeat for them to have lawsuits between brothers and sisters. He asks why they do not prefer to bear the wrong, that is, the harm or offense, and why they do not prefer to be cheated, meaning to be deceived or to have something taken from them unjustly.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and problems. Some brothers and sisters were suing one another before unbelieving judges. Paul says this to shame them, because the church should have been able to settle its conflicts with wisdom. Then he reminds them that they themselves were also doing harm.

For today: before entering a dispute with another believer, ask yourself whether you can forgive or give something up. If that is not possible, seek the help of mature brothers and sisters who can guide you in peace.
exp.5:7:
Paul says that instead of putting up with an offense, the Corinthians themselves are going around doing harm and taking what does not belong to them, and the worst part is that they do it to their own brothers and sisters in the faith.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided. Some believers were taking one another to court before judges who did not know God. Paul is saddened because this damages the church's witness. So he reminds them that they themselves are causing the very harm they should be willing to suffer.

For today: before you get into a fight with another believer, stop and pray. Seek first to speak with humility and to be reconciled, even if it costs you something. Caring for the unity and the witness of Christ is worth more than winning an argument.
exp.5:10:
Paul reminds the believers in Corinth that some of them used to live in those sins. But something changed: they were washed (cleansed from their guilt), sanctified (set apart for God), and justified (declared righteous before Him). All of this happened through Jesus and through the Spirit of God.

Paul writes to a church with many problems of conduct and division. He has just said that those who practice wrongdoing will not inherit the kingdom of God. Now he reminds them that their past no longer defines them, and that their new life must show in how they live, especially in how they use their bodies.

For today: if your past shames you, remember that in Christ God has cleansed you and given you a new identity. Live from that grace, not from your old story, and ask the Spirit to help you walk in it.
exp.5:18:
He says that the body of each believer is a temple of the Holy Spirit, that is, a place where God himself lives. That Spirit is given by God; we do not earn him. That is why Paul concludes that you are not your own.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city with a great deal of sexual freedom, where some believers thought that what they did with their bodies did not matter. He reminds them that the body belongs to the Lord and is joined to him. The next verse adds that they were bought at a price, which Christian tradition understands as the sacrifice of Christ.

For today: before deciding how to use your body, whether in your relationships, your habits, or your rest, ask yourself whether that honors God, who lives in you and cares for you.
exp.6:9:
Paul now turns to those who are already married. He gives a clear command: the wife must not separate from her husband. Paul's own words are not his personal opinion alone, since Jesus had already taught about marriage.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. Earlier he spoke about the unmarried and the widows; now he moves on to married couples. The verses that follow explain that if a separation does happen, reconciliation should be sought. Many scholars think this reflects what Jesus taught in the Gospels.

For today: if your marriage is going through difficulties, do not give up quickly. Seek honest conversation, forgiveness, and help from the church or a wise counselor, and ask God to heal the relationship.
exp.6:13:
It says that when a believer is married to someone who does not believe, that marriage is not something defiled. The unbelieving spouse is made holy, meaning they are joined in some way to what is holy through their relationship with the believer. For that reason the children are not unclean (impure, set apart from God), but holy (set apart, close to God). Here "unbelieving" simply means one who does not believe.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage. Some believers feared that staying married to an unbeliever would spiritually defile them. Paul tells them not to separate. Scholars discuss how far this holiness reaches: the verse does not say that the spouse is automatically saved.

For today: if you live with someone who does not share your faith, do not see them as a burden. Love with patience, be steadfast, and pray for that person, trusting that God can work through your life.
exp.6:15:
This verse asks: how do you know, wife, whether you will bring your husband to salvation? And the same question is put to the husband about his wife.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage. He speaks of couples where only one of them believes in Christ. He has just said that if the unbeliever chooses to leave, the believer should let them go, because God has called us to live in peace. Interpreters debate whether this verse offers hope that the spouse will be converted, or whether it instead warns that no one can be sure of this and so a person should not hold back by force someone who wants to leave. Both readings are possible.

If you live with someone who does not believe, live with love, patience, and peace. Do not press or despair: salvation is the work of God, and your good witness can be a seed.
exp.6:18:
It says that being circumcised or not being circumcised is not what matters most before God. What truly counts is obeying what God commands. Circumcision was the physical sign of belonging to the people of Israel. The phrase "keeping" means carrying out with care, and "commandments" refers to God's instructions.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were both Jews and non-Jews who believed in Jesus. There were questions about whether they should change their condition when they became Christians. Paul answers that each person can live out their calling to God in the situation they were already in. What is essential is obedience, not cultural or religious identity. How this relates to the law of Moses he explains in his other letters.

For today: do not let your background, your culture, or your customs make you feel superior or inferior. Instead, ask yourself each day: am I obeying God in what He asks of me now?
exp.6:21:
Here the explanation says that whoever was called by the Lord while a slave is, in truth, a freedman, that is, someone whom his master has given freedom; now he belongs to the Lord as a free person. And whoever was called while free is a servant of Christ, since he belongs to Him. Being called refers to being invited by God to believe.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about how to live the faith in concrete situations. He teaches them that their social condition does not limit their worth before God. Even so, in the preceding verse he advises taking the opportunity to become free if it presents itself. Paul does not approve of slavery; he speaks to people who were living within it.

For today: your work or your social position does not define who you are. If Christ has called you, you are free and valuable; live with that dignity and treat everyone with that same respect.
exp.6:24:
Paul speaks about the unmarried, that is, people who have never married. He says he has no direct command from the Lord about them, meaning Jesus left no specific teaching on this subject. For that reason he gives his opinion, his honest judgment. He can be trusted in his advice because God showed him mercy and made him faithful.

Paul is responding to questions the Corinthians had written to him about marriage and remaining single. He distinguishes between what Jesus taught and his own counsel as an apostle. According to the verses that follow, he advises with an eye to the present distress, a difficult situation that scholars explain in various ways.

Today we can learn to give and receive advice with humility, without presenting our opinions as commands from God. And when deciding whether to marry or not, it is wise to pray, ask for wisdom, and serve the Lord faithfully in whatever stage of life we are in.
exp.6:28:
Paul tells the brothers that the time is short. For this reason, even those who are married should live as though they had none. He does not command leaving marriage, but not making marriage the center of life.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and being single. He speaks of a present distress (v. 26), though the text does not fully make clear what it was; some think of persecution or scarcity. "The time is short" may also point to the imminent return of Christ. His intention is pastoral: to guard their devotion to the Lord.

For today: love your family and your work, but remember that nothing in this life is the last word. Today, put God first and let Him order your other loves.
exp.7:0:
Paul says that, concerning meat offered to idols, believers have a certain knowledge. But he warns that knowledge puffs up, that is, fills a person with pride, while love builds up others, that is, strengthens and constructs them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city where a great deal of meat was sold after it had been used in pagan temples. Some believers felt superior because they knew that idols are nothing, and did not think about fellow believers with a more fragile conscience. Paul responds to questions the church had put to him.

For today: before you show what you know in a debate or on social media, ask yourself whether your words help others grow or only make you look good. Use what you know to serve with humility and to care for someone who is still learning.
exp.7:3:
This verse speaks about meat that was offered to idols. Paul says that the idol is nothing: it has no real power and is not a true god. There is only one God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of pagan temples. The believers were debating whether they could eat meat that had passed through those temples. Paul starts from what many already knew, but first he warned that knowledge without love puffs up. Later he will ask them to take care of brothers and sisters with a weak conscience.

For today: being clear that only God deserves our trust frees us from fear of superstitions and false powers. But that certainty must be joined with love, taking care that what I do in freedom does not wound another person's faith.
exp.7:5:
This verse says that, for Christians, there is one God, the Father. From Him come all things, and we live for Him. It also says that there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist, and through whom we too have life.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted whether they could eat meat that had been offered to idols. Paul reminds them that idols are nothing compared to the one true God. But he also asks them to be careful, because not everyone has that same knowledge, and a weak conscience can be harmed.

Today we can remember that only God deserves first place in our hearts. And at the same time, we can lovingly care for those who are growing in faith, avoiding anything that we see as freedom from causing them to stumble.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that not all believers have the same knowledge. Some, even until now, still think of the idol when they eat meat that was offered to idols. The explanatory notes on the wording have been left out because they refer to words that do not appear in the verse you are reading.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, who lived surrounded by pagan temples. He had just said that idols are nothing and that there is only one God. But here he clarifies that not everyone has taken this in equally, and for that reason he asks for love and care toward those who are still struggling with their conscience.

Today, even if something is not sin for you, another brother or sister may feel hurt or confused by it. Before using your freedom, ask yourself whether it helps or causes someone else to stumble. Love with patience those who are growing in faith.
exp.7:11:
Paul says that when someone causes a brother or sister with a weaker faith to act against what their conscience allows, that person is sinning against the brother or sister. Wounding their weak conscience means hurting or harming the conscience of someone who is still unsure in their faith. And since that person belongs to Christ, wounding them is sinning against Christ himself.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city where meat that had been offered to idols was sold. Some believers, who had more knowledge, knew that idols are nothing and ate without any problem. But others, who came out of paganism, felt that eating was worshiping the idol. Paul asks them that their knowledge not make them insensitive.

For today: before using my freedom in something doubtful, I can ask myself how it will affect the one who is watching me and is still growing in faith. Loving my brother or sister is worth more than being right or exercising my right.
exp.8:1:
Paul says that other people may not recognize him as an apostle, but the believers in Corinth should. A "seal" was a mark that guaranteed something was genuine, like a signature. "Apostleship" is the work of an apostle, a sent one of Christ. For Paul, the church in Corinth is the proof of his calling.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some of them doubted his authority. He had preached there and a church had been born. So he reminds them that their own faith is evidence that God sent him. With this he begins to defend his right to receive support for his work, although he had chosen not to use it.

For today: God often shows his work in changed lives. When someone points something out to you, do not defend yourself with empty words; let your testimony and your love speak. And remember that whoever serves faithfully leaves marks on others.
exp.8:4:
Paul asks whether he and Barnabas do not have the right to bring along a believing wife, as the other apostles, the Lord's brothers, and Cephas (Peter) do.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to defend his apostleship, since some were questioning it. He shows that he has the same rights as other leaders, including the right to be supported by the church. This text suggests that Peter and others were married, although we do not know in detail how their wives traveled. Paul does not insist on these rights; he mentions them to explain why he gives them up for the sake of the gospel.

Today we can learn to use our freedom with humility. Having a right does not always mean we must demand it. Before doing so, it is good to ask ourselves what will help others come to know Christ most.
exp.8:9:
Paul asks whether the law about not muzzling the ox was said only for the animals. He answers that it was also written for us, that is, for people. "Plow" means preparing the ground, and "thresh" means separating the grain from the straw. Those who do this work do it in the hope of receiving a share of the harvest.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and defends his right, as an apostle, to receive support from them. He uses the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 25:4) to show that the one who works deserves to live from his work. However, he immediately says that he did not use that right, so as not to hinder the gospel.

Today, we can generously support those who serve us spiritually, such as pastors or missionaries. We can also work by serving others with hope, trusting that God sees our effort.
exp.8:17:
Paul asks what his reward is, and answers: that when he preaches the gospel, he offers it free of charge, so that he does not make full use of the right he has as a preacher.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends the way he serves. Earlier he explained that those who work for the gospel have the right to be supported by the church. But he chose not to charge, so that nothing would get in the way of the message. His joy was in preaching without placing obstacles in anyone's path. Then he says that he became a servant to all in order to win more people.

Today, we might ask ourselves whether there is something we have the right to do or demand, but which could hinder others from drawing near to Christ. Sometimes love means letting go of a right for someone else's good. Serve generously and expect nothing in return.
exp.9:2:
It says that all the Israelites, the ancestors of the Jews, ate the same spiritual food in the desert. Paul is referring to the manna that God gave them from heaven each day. He calls it "spiritual" because it came from God and not from the earth, and perhaps also because it pointed to something greater.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who felt secure because they had been baptized and took part in the Lord's Supper. He reminds them that Israel also received great blessings from God, and yet many fell into sin and were judged. It is a warning not to become complacent.

For today: receiving blessings from God and taking part in the life of the church is not enough. We need sincere and constant obedience. Be thankful for what God gives you, but guard your heart so that you truly follow him.
exp.9:4:
It says that although all the Israelites received the same blessings from God in the wilderness, God was not pleased with most of them. The verse says they were overthrown in the wilderness, meaning they fell and died there.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, a city full of immorality and idolatry. He reminds them of what happened to Israel after leaving Egypt (Numbers 14). They had received the manna, the water from the rock, and God's guidance, yet they still rebelled. Paul uses this as a warning so the Corinthians would not become complacent simply because they had received blessings.

For today: having received God's blessings, or being part of a church life, does not replace sincere obedience. Today you can ask yourself with humility: "Am I trusting God, or just enjoying what He gives me?"
exp.9:5:
These things happened to Israel in the desert as examples for us, to keep us from craving evil things the way they did.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a city full of sexual immorality and idolatry. He reminds them that God rescued Israel and provided for them, and yet many of them fell in the wilderness. Paul uses that story to warn the Corinthians that spiritual privileges do not protect anyone who becomes careless.

For today: do not assume you are secure just because you know God. Examine which desires are gaining ground in your heart, and learn from the mistakes recorded in Scripture so that you turn quickly away from whatever pulls you away from God.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that the temptation we face is common to all human beings; no one experiences something completely unique. God is faithful: he will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear. Along with the temptation, he provides a way out, a way of escape, so that we can endure it. Enduring means bearing up without giving in.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of idolatry and immorality. He has just recalled how Israel fell in the desert, and he warns that whoever thinks they stand firm must be careful. This verse encourages: falling is not inevitable. Right after this, he asks them to flee from idolatry.

For today: when temptation comes, do not think there is no remedy. Ask God for help and look for the concrete way out: move away from the place, end a conversation, or tell a trusted friend.
exp.9:14:
He says that Paul speaks to the Corinthians as to people with good judgment. He wants them to be seen as sensible and discerning. He asks them not to accept his words without thinking, but to examine what he says and judge for themselves whether it is true. The word "judge" means to weigh carefully and consider with attention.

Paul, the apostle, writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of pagan temples. He has just warned them to flee from idolatry. Now he is going to give them an argument about the Lord's Supper and its fellowship with Christ. That is why he appeals to their reasoning before explaining why they cannot mix the Lord's table with pagan rites.

Today, God invites us to think, not only to obey. Compare what you hear with the Bible, calmly and in prayer, and your faith will be firm and reasoned.
exp.9:16:
It says that, since there is one loaf on the Lord's table, all of us who take part in it, though we are many, form one body.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and was tempted to join in feasts held in honor of idols. He reminds them that the Lord's Supper is a communion with Christ and also among brothers and sisters. For this reason one cannot share the Lord's table and the table of idols at the same time. Christians have understood in various ways what happens exactly at the Supper, but all of them see here a real union.

Today, when you take part in the Supper, remember that you do not come alone. Before taking it, try to make peace with some brother or sister, and treat them with the affection of someone who shares the same bread.
exp.9:19:
Paul says that when pagans offer sacrifices to their idols, they are actually offering them to demons and not to God. For this reason he does not want believers to have fellowship, that is, to join together or share in common, with demons.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, surrounded by pagan temples and festivals. Some believers were attending banquets held in idol temples. Paul had already said that an idol is nothing in itself, but he warns that behind this worship stand spiritual realities opposed to God. He compares this with Israel, where eating from the sacrifice joined the person to the altar.

For today: examine which practices or environments lead you to divide your loyalty. If something pulls you away from Christ, even if it seems harmless, be honest and choose to remain faithful to Him.
exp.9:21:
It says that we should not make God angry by stirring up jealousy. The word "provoke" means to make someone become upset, and "jealousy" refers to the jealousy of one who demands exclusive loyalty. "Are we stronger than he?" is a rhetorical question: the answer is no. No one can challenge God and come out ahead.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city where there were many temples and festivals with idols. Some believed they could take part in those religious meals and also in the Lord's Supper. Paul warns them that one cannot share the table of God and the table of demons. He also recalls how Israel provoked God in the wilderness (vv. 1-12), although some scholars debate how closely this connects to the phrase.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something in my life that competes with God for my loyalty? It is wise to be honest with him and to turn away from it.
exp.9:23:
What it says: This verse asks us not to live thinking only about what suits us. Instead, we should also care for the good of the other person, that is, of our neighbor.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who were debating whether they could eat meat that had been offered to idols. Paul says they have freedom, but that freedom is not the only thing that matters. What counts is whether something builds up, that is, whether it helps others grow in faith and does not make them stumble. The following verses show that, in most cases, eating was fine without any problem.

For today: Before using your freedom in something, ask yourself: "Does this help the people around me, or could it confuse or hurt them?" Choose love over your own comfort.
exp.9:28:
Paul makes clear that when he speaks of "conscience," he means the conscience of the other person, not of the one who is eating. If someone warns you that this meat was offered to an idol, you must take care of that person's conscience. Then Paul asks: "why is my liberty judged by another man's conscience?" This sentence is difficult: some believe it is an objection from Paul himself, and others think it is the words of an opponent. It can be understood in several ways.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city where meat was sold after pagan sacrifices. There was division over whether eating it was sin. Paul defends liberty, but limits it with love.

For today: before using your freedom in something debatable, think about who is watching you and how it will affect them. Yielding out of love for a brother also glorifies God.
exp.9:30:
Paul says that everything we do, even the most ordinary things like eating or drinking, should be done to honor God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who were debating whether it was right to eat meat that had been offered to idols. He reminds them that they have freedom, but that this freedom must care for others. That is why, in the next verse, he asks them not to be a stumbling block to Jews, Gentiles, or the church, seeking the good of many so that they may be saved.

For today: before deciding what to watch, what to say, or how to spend your time, ask yourself whether it honors God and helps the people around you. Even everyday life can be a form of worship.
exp.9:32:
Paul says that in everything he tries to please everyone, that is, to be considerate of others. He does not seek what is good for himself, but what helps many, so that they may be saved.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were disagreements about eating meat that had been offered to idols. He teaches them that, even though they have freedom, they must not cause Jews, Gentiles, or the church to stumble. He presents himself as an example, since he gives up his rights for the good of others. In the next chapter, he invites them to imitate him as he imitates Christ.

Today, before you use your freedom in something debatable, ask yourself: "Does this help others draw near to God, or does it push them away?" Choose what builds up, even when it costs you something.
exp.10:7:
It says that the first man, Adam, was not formed from a woman, but that the first woman, Eve, was formed from the man. Paul refers to the account in Genesis 2, where God forms the woman from Adam's rib.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a church with many disorders. In this passage he corrects practices in worship, such as covering the head. He uses the order of creation as an argument. Scholars disagree about what exact custom of the time was in view and how to apply it today. Paul himself balances this in verses 11 and 12: neither is independent of the other, and everything comes from God.

Today we can remember that men and women need each other. Let us honor others in the church with respect and humility, and seek the common good before our own comfort.
exp.10:11:
The explanation says that woman came from man, since Eve was formed from Adam, and that now man is born through woman. Neither is superior in origin, because both depend on each other. And the word that appears in the verse as "but" means "but": the source of everything is God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was disorder in the worship meetings. Earlier he spoke about the order of creation and the customs about covering the head. Here he balances his argument: no one should feel superior. Scholars discuss the exact meaning of the word for authority and of the phrase about angels, so it is wise to be humble when interpreting them.

Today we can treat people of the other sex with respect and gratitude, knowing that we need one another. In the family and in the church, let us recognize that every gift and every person comes from God, and let us serve one another with humility.
exp.10:14:
It says that for a woman, letting her hair grow long is a glory and something to be honored, because her hair was given to her as a covering. Letting the hair grow long means leaving it uncut. Something fitting is worthy of respect. Something improper is shameful.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about order in worship. He uses the customs of his time and the way things naturally are as part of his argument. Scholars debate whether the "covering" refers to a cloth or only to the hair itself, and what local customs Corinth had. This is not entirely clear.

For today, take care to show respect and order when you worship, and do not turn cultural customs into a cause for quarrel. Ask yourself how you can honor God and others with humility and simplicity.
exp.10:16:
Paul says that what he is about to mention now is not a reason for praise. The idea is that when the Corinthians come together, those gatherings do not make them better, but worse.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and disorder. Earlier he had spoken about customs in worship, and in verse 2 he had commended them. Now he changes his tone, because he is going to correct what was happening at the Lord's Supper: the divisions and the unfair treatment among brothers and sisters (verses 18 to 22).

For today: gathering together as a church is not enough; how we treat one another matters. Before going to a service, we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking unity, humility, and respect for others, and not just fulfilling the duty of attending.
exp.10:17:
He says that Paul hears that when the Corinthians gather as a church, there are divisions among them, that is, splits or factions between them. He says that he partly believes it: he does not accept every rumor outright, but he recognizes that there is some truth to it. The word "hear" indicates that reports reached him from other people.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and begins to correct problems in their meetings. Earlier he has said that their gatherings harm them instead of helping them. Later he shows that the divisions even affected the Lord's Supper, since some ate without waiting for or sharing with others. Scholars debate the exact details of these groups, but the text makes the conflict clear.

For today: before we gather to worship, it is good to examine our hearts. If there is pride, resentment, or contempt toward someone, let us seek reconciliation so that our unity is real.
exp.10:21:
Paul asks the Corinthians several sharp questions. He says to them: if what you want is to eat and drink to your own liking, do you not have houses for that? If you do it at the gathering, you are looking down on the church and shaming those who have nothing. To look down on someone is to treat them as unimportant. In the end he says that he cannot praise them for this.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. At those gatherings a meal was shared together with the Lord's Supper. The better-off ate and drank without waiting for the others, and the poor were left hungry. Paul corrects this because it contradicts the meaning of the Supper, as he explains right after.

For today: when we gather together as a church, we should think of others and not only of ourselves. We can ask ourselves whom we are leaving out and how we might share with those who have less, so that no one feels ashamed.
exp.10:27:
Before taking part in the Lord's Supper, the explanation says, each person should examine themselves honestly. "Examine" means to test oneself or look carefully at one's own heart. After that self-examination, the person may eat the bread and drink from the cup.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided. When they gathered for the meal, some looked down on the poorer members and behaved without respect for what that moment represents. Paul reminds them that the Supper proclaims the death of Christ. For that reason he calls them to take part with seriousness, not with carelessness or selfishness.

Before communion, take a moment to pray. Ask forgiveness if you have wronged someone, seek reconciliation, and take part with gratitude, remembering what Christ did for you.
exp.10:28:
The explanation says that whoever takes part in the Lord's Supper in an unworthy manner, that is, without respect or seriousness, brings judgment on himself. Here "judgment" means correction or punishment, not necessarily eternal condemnation. Not recognizing what the bread means is the sense of the phrase about not discerning the Lord's body: the sacrifice of Christ and, according to many, the church as his body.

Paul writes to the Corinthians because in their communal meals some were getting drunk while others went hungry, looking down on the poorer members. The Supper had become selfish. Interpreters explain in various ways the sickness and death he mentions afterward, but he sees them as God's discipline.

Before taking part in the Supper, stop and examine your heart: confess whatever is wrong, ask forgiveness, and make peace with anyone you have offended. Then eat and drink with gratitude and respect toward Christ and toward your brothers and sisters.
exp.10:30:
It says that if each person examined themselves honestly before God, they would not have to be judged.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth because, when they celebrated the Lord's Supper, there were divisions, selfishness, and a lack of respect among them. Some ate and drank without thinking about others. Paul tells them that this attitude had consequences, and he invites them to examine themselves. The verses that follow explain that the Lord's correction aims to keep them from being condemned along with the world.

Before you pray, take part in the Lord's Supper, or spend time together as a church, take a moment to ask yourself honestly: is there something I should confess, or someone I should treat better? Correcting yourself in time is a sign of humility and of trust in God's grace.
exp.11:11:
The verse says the human body is one, yet it has many parts. Although the parts are many, all of them form one body. Paul says that Christ is the same way, meaning Christ and his church, which he calls his body.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and argued about who had the most important spiritual gifts. Earlier he listed gifts such as miracles, prophecy, and tongues, and he said that all of them come from the same Spirit. With the picture of the body, he teaches them that diversity does not break unity.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or look down on them for being different. Ask God how you can serve with what he has given you, and value what others contribute in your church.
exp.11:14:
This verse imagines the foot feeling less important and saying, "Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body." Paul answers with a question: does thinking this way make it stop being part of the body? The answer is no.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, a church marked by divisions and rivalry over spiritual gifts. Some felt superior, and others perhaps felt inferior. Paul uses the image of the body to explain that all believers form one body by the same Spirit, and that each one is necessary.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or think that your service is worth little. If you belong to Christ, you are part of his body. Do with joy what God has given you, without envy and without contempt.
exp.11:15:
This verse imagines the ear feeling less important than the eye and reasons that, because it is not an eye, it no longer belongs to the body. Paul responds with a question: does feeling that way mean it stops being part of the body? The answer is no.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and comparisons between those who had more visible gifts and those with less showy ones. He uses the image of the human body to explain that the church is one body with many members. What makes someone belong is not their function or talent, but that God placed them there.

For today: if you feel unimportant because your service is quiet or different from others', remember that you belong to the church by God's will. Do not compare yourself; serve with joy where He has placed you.
exp.11:16:
It says that a body cannot be just one organ. If everything were an eye, there would be no hearing; if everything were hearing, there would be no sense of smell. The word translated as sense of smell is the sense of smelling. Paul uses questions to make us think: a body like that would not work.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and some considered themselves more important because of their spiritual gifts. He compares the church to a human body, where each member is different but necessary. The verses that follow say that God placed each member as he wanted.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or think that your service is worth little. Ask God how you can serve with what he has given you, and value those who have gifts different from yours. All of them are needed.
exp.11:25:
It says that in the church we are all as closely joined as the parts of a body. If one part suffers, all of them feel that pain together. If one part is honored, meaning recognized or praised, all of them rejoice together.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and rivalry over spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the body to show that every believer is necessary, and that God gave greater honor to those who seemed less important, so that there would be no division and everyone would care for one another.

Today we can practice this with a simple step: go to a brother or sister who is suffering and support them with prayer and your presence. And when someone in the church receives an achievement or a blessing, celebrate it wholeheartedly, without envy.
exp.11:27:
He says God himself placed different people with different tasks within the church. He mentions apostles (those sent out with authority), prophets (those who speak a message from God), teachers, workers of miracles, gifts of healings, helps (serving those in need), governments (leading and organizing), and various kinds of tongues.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church with divisions and with pride in the most visible gifts. Earlier he compared the church to a body, where all the members need one another. The verses that follow ask whether everyone has the same gift, and the expected answer is no.

Today: discover what your place is in your church and serve others with that gift, without envying or looking down on the gifts of others. Both the one who teaches and the one who helps are valuable to God.
exp.12:1:
Paul says that a person can have very great gifts: prophecy, which means speaking on behalf of God; understanding all mysteries, that is, truths of God that were once hidden; having a great deal of knowledge; and a faith able to move mountains. But without love, which here means love, the person is nothing.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride about spiritual gifts, especially speaking in tongues. He does not look down on the gifts, but he shows them that without love they lose their value. This idea continues what he said in the previous verse about tongues.

For today: before you serve, teach, or defend the truth, ask yourself whether you are doing it with love. Today, treat one specific person with patience and kindness, even if it costs you something.
exp.13:4:
Paul says he would like everyone to speak in tongues, but he would prefer that they prophesy. In his view, the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets what was said. The reason is that in this way the whole church receives edification, that is, help to grow in faith.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church that valued spectacular gifts very much and had disorder in its meetings. He does not despise tongues, since he wants them to be spoken, but he corrects the focus. What matters is that everyone understands and is strengthened. Some scholars understand "prophesy" as speaking a message from God to encourage and guide; others see it in a somewhat different way.

For today: before you speak, sing, or serve in the church, ask yourself whether what you are doing helps others understand and grow, not only whether it makes you feel good.
exp.13:5:
Paul tells the brothers in Corinth: if I came to you speaking in tongues, what good would that do you? It would only benefit you if I spoke to you with something you can understand. He mentions four forms: revelation (something God makes known), knowledge (understanding), prophesying (a word from God), and doctrine (teaching).

Paul writes to a church that was very divided and enthusiastic about spiritual gifts. Some valued speaking in tongues in the meetings a great deal, even though no one understood it. Paul does not despise that gift, but he insists that what matters is that the church be built up. He sets himself up as an example.

For today: before speaking, singing, or serving in the church, ask yourself whether what you are doing helps others understand and grow in faith, not just whether it makes you look good.
exp.13:6:
Paul says that even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp (a stringed instrument similar to a guitar), need clear and distinct sounds. If they only make noise without rhythm or distinct notes, no one can recognize the tune.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued speaking in tongues very highly in their gatherings, but without anyone understanding it. He uses this example to show that a confusing message helps no one. He prefers what builds up the whole church.

For today: when you teach, pray aloud, or serve in your church, try to speak with clarity and simplicity, so that others understand and are encouraged in their faith.
exp.13:19:
Paul asks the brothers not to be like children in their way of thinking and understanding. Instead, they should be like children in malice, that is, innocent and without any desire to harm others.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which placed great value on speaking in tongues, even though no one understood what was being said. He corrects this disorder with care: what matters is that everyone understands and is built up. That is why he says he would rather speak a few clear words than many that no one can understand.

For today: Seek to grow in understanding of the Bible and think with maturity before following trends or emotions. At the same time, guard your heart: do not hold on to resentment or wrong intentions, and live with simplicity and innocence.
exp.13:20:
The verse says that in the Law, meaning the Scriptures of the Old Testament, God announced that he would speak to his people through other tongues and through foreign lips. Even so, the people would not listen to him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued speaking in tongues too highly during the gatherings. He quotes Isaiah 28:11-12, where God warned a hardened people that they would hear foreign languages, and even then they would not believe. Paul wants the Corinthians to think with maturity: what matters is that everyone understands and is built up.

For today: before you speak, pray, or sing in church, ask yourself whether others will be able to understand and receive help. Let your way of serving always seek the good of others, not merely to impress.
exp.13:21:
The explanation says that tongues are a sign, but not for believers; they are for those who do not believe. Prophecy, that is, the word of God spoken to guide and encourage, is for believers. "Unbelievers" here means those who do not believe, and "believers" means those who do.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to correct the disorder in their gatherings. He quotes Isaiah, where God speaks to a people who will not listen. Scholars explain the "sign" in different ways: as a warning, or as a sign that this people was not listening. What is clear is that Paul wants everything in the church to be understood and to build people up.

For today: when you serve in the church, try to speak so that others can understand you and go away strengthened. Let your aim be to help others, not to draw attention to yourself.
exp.13:22:
This verse says that if the whole church comes together in one place and everyone speaks in tongues at the same time, and people come in who do not know what is going on in the church, or who do not yet believe, they will think the believers are out of their minds. It is a question that expects the answer yes.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had a great deal of disorder in its meetings. He valued the spiritual gifts, but he wanted everything to help build up everyone. So he compares speaking in tongues, which without interpretation cannot be understood, with prophecy, which speaks clearly and reaches the heart. Scholars debate exactly what speaking in tongues was like in Corinth.

For today: when we gather, let us think of the person who comes for the first time. Let us make sure that what we do or say is clear, orderly, and useful, so that others can understand and find God.
exp.13:23:
This verse says that if, during the gathering, everyone prophesies (that is, speaks words from God that teach and encourage) and someone comes in who does not believe or who does not understand these things, that person feels convinced and examined by what they hear.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to bring order to their gatherings. They valued speaking in tongues very highly, even without interpretation. Paul explains that if no one understands, a visitor will think they are out of their minds. By contrast, a clear message reaches the heart and uncovers it.

For today: when the church gathers, let us make sure that everything is said clearly and with love, so that any visitor can understand and meet with God.
exp.13:27:
It says that if someone has the gift of speaking in tongues and there is no one to interpret what he says, he should keep quiet during the church meeting. He may speak in private, alone, between himself and God.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly and each person wanted to show off his gifts. Paul asks them for order and that everything serve for building up, that is, for strengthening everyone. A message that no one understands does not help the congregation.

For today: before you speak or take part in church, ask yourself whether what you are about to do will help others grow. Your love for God can also be expressed in silence and in personal prayer.
exp.13:28:
It says that in the church gathering two or three prophets should speak, that is, people who communicate what God shows them to help others. The others present should examine carefully what was said to see whether it is true and in line with God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had disorderly meetings, with many people speaking at the same time. He asks for order so that everyone may learn and be encouraged. Some understand that the rest are the other prophets, and others think it is the whole congregation. The text leaves this open.

Today, let us not accept every message just because it sounds spiritual. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, with humility and prayer, and let us do it with respect, seeking the good of everyone in the church.
exp.13:29:
It says that if, while a prophet is speaking in the meeting, God shows something to another person who is seated, the one who was speaking first should stop and be quiet.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly and many wanted to speak at the same time. He seeks order so that everyone receives encouragement and teaching. The prophets speak in turns, and the others weigh what is said. Scholars understand in different ways how this "revelation" worked, but the purpose of building up everyone is clear.

Today we can practice listening well and making room for others. Even when we have something valuable to say, in the church and in small groups it is wise to speak with humility, without monopolizing the conversation, so that everyone is encouraged.
exp.13:32:
It says that God is not a God of disorder or confusion, but of peace. Here "disorder" is understood as confusion or commotion. It adds that this is so in all the churches of the saints, that is, of the believers.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whose meetings were disorderly: several people spoke at once, using gifts such as prophecy and tongues. He asks them to speak in turns, so that everyone may learn and be encouraged. The sentence that follows about women has been interpreted in various ways among Christians, so it is wise to read it carefully and in its context.

For today: when you take part in your church, or in a group, try to listen and wait for your turn. Seek to speak in a way that builds up others and does not create confusion. Order, rightly understood, is a way of loving.
exp.13:34:
It says that if women want to learn something, they should ask their husbands at home.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to correct the disorder in their meetings (14:26-40). Before this, he speaks of weighing prophecies calmly. Many believe that here he is correcting questions or interruptions that were disrupting that moment. Others understand it as a general rule for worship. In 11:5 he mentions women who pray and prophesy, and for this reason Christians interpret this passage in different ways.

For today: seek to have everything in your church done with order, respect, and a desire to learn. Ask questions with humility, listen well, and create spaces where everyone can learn without disrupting others.
exp.13:39:
It says that everything done in the church meeting should be done in a fitting and orderly way.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth. In that congregation there was confusion in the meetings: several people spoke at the same time, especially with gifts such as prophecy and tongues. Paul has just encouraged them to use those gifts, and now he closes the chapter with this balance: spiritual freedom, but with order, so that everyone is built up and it is clear that God is not the author of confusion (v. 33).

For today: before taking part in your church, whether by singing, teaching, or praying, ask yourself whether what you are about to do will help others understand and grow. Serving with preparation and respect is also a way of showing love.
exp.14:8:
Paul says that he considers himself the least of the apostles. He states that he is unworthy to be called an apostle, and the reason is clear: he once persecuted the church of God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians when he recalls that the risen Jesus appeared to many witnesses. He was the last to see him. He mentions his violent past against believers to show that his calling is not due to his own merits. He then adds that everything he is comes from the grace of God.

For today: you do not have to hide your past mistakes or live buried in them. You can acknowledge them with humility and trust that the grace of God transforms you and enables you to serve others.
exp.14:9:
Paul says that what he is today, an apostle, is due to the grace of God, that is, to his undeserved favor. That grace was not without result: Paul worked harder than the other apostles. But he immediately clarifies that it was not by his own strength, but by the grace of God working with him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who doubted the resurrection. Earlier he reminded them that the risen Christ appeared to him, even though he had persecuted the church.
