He calls himself the least by humility and because of that past. Here he defends his calling, and then he will remind them that all the apostles preached the same message.

For today: do not live crushed by your past or proud of your achievements. Put your effort into what God has given you, and give thanks, because even the strength to serve comes from Him.
exp.14:11:
Paul asks a confronting question. He says that he and the other apostles proclaim that Christ rose from the dead. Then why do some in Corinth claim that the dead do not rise?

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, a church he himself founded. Some of them denied the resurrection of the dead, and scholars are not sure exactly what their reasoning was. Paul reminds them that the message they believed is the same one all the apostles preach. For that reason, denying the general resurrection contradicts the center of their faith.

For today: check whether your hope rests on what Christ has already done. His resurrection gives meaning to your faith and steadiness in the face of pain and death. Reflect on it, and share it with someone who is suffering.
exp.14:12:
This verse says that the resurrection of Christ and the resurrection of the dead are bound together. If it were impossible for the dead to rise, then Christ would not have risen either. "Resurrection of the dead" means that the dead come back to life with a body raised up by God.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul answers them with logic: they believed that Christ rose, because that is what they were taught. But denying all resurrection would leave that message without any basis. For Paul, the resurrection of Jesus is the center of the gospel.

For today: our hope is not just a pleasant idea, but rests on a fact. Because Christ rose, we can face the loss of loved ones and our own death with a firm hope, and not with despair.
exp.14:15:
What it says: Paul repeats a logical argument. If it is true that the dead never rise, then Christ was not raised either, because his resurrection would be an impossible exception. The two things are bound together: the resurrection of Christ and the resurrection of believers.

Context: Paul is writing to the church in Corinth. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead (v. 12). Paul shows them where that idea leads: if there is no resurrection, the preaching, the faith, and the forgiveness of sins are left without foundation. He does not doubt that Christ was raised; he only exposes the absurdity of denying the resurrection.

For today: Our hope is not just a pleasant idea, but rests on a fact: Christ lives. When you face loss, fear, or grief, lean on that certainty. You can pray: "Lord, strengthen my faith in your resurrection and in the promise that we too will live."
exp.14:17:
It says that, if Christ was not raised, the believers who have already died have also perished. "Fallen asleep" is a gentle way of saying they died, and "perished" means they would have no salvation or hope after death. Without resurrection, their faith in Christ would have led them to nothing.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul shows them that denying this has serious consequences: if the dead do not rise, then Christ did not rise either, and the whole gospel falls apart. He then makes clear that Christ did rise, and that his resurrection is the guarantee of ours.

For today: when you say goodbye to a loved one who trusted in Christ, or when you think about your own death, rest on the resurrection of Jesus. Your hope is not a pleasant idea but a fact you can lean on, one that gives you comfort and encouragement to live.
exp.14:20:
This verse says that death came into the world through one man, and that the resurrection of the dead also comes through one man. The phrase "since" in the verse expresses the same reasoning as the original. The first man is Adam, and the second is Christ, as the following verses explain.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, where some were saying that there was no resurrection of the dead. Paul answers them that if Christ was not raised, faith is empty. Here he shows that Christ's resurrection is the beginning and the guarantee of the resurrection of those who believe in him.

For today: if you face the loss of a loved one or the fear of death, remember that death does not have the final word. You can rest in the hope that Christ, who overcame death, will also give life to his own.
exp.14:24:
It says that Christ must reign until all his enemies are placed under his feet. The phrase "must" is a stand-in for what is necessary or required. Placing enemies under the feet was an image of complete victory.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection of the dead. He lays out the order of events: Christ was raised first, then those who belong to him will be raised, and at the end Christ will hand the kingdom over to the Father. Paul uses words from Psalm 110:1 to show that Christ's victory is certain, and that the last enemy to be defeated will be death.

For today: when evil or fear seem stronger, remember that Christ reigns and his final victory is assured. You can live with hope and keep doing good without losing heart.
exp.14:25:
What the verse says: Paul affirms that death is the last enemy that Christ will destroy. "Destroyed" means annulled, with its power taken away. "Last" means final. Death does not have the final word; God does.

Context: Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. He explains that Christ rose and that his reign advances until it overcomes everything that opposes God. Death appears at the end of that list, as the hardest enemy. How and when all of this will happen in detail, the Bible does not fully explain.

For today: If you are grieving or afraid of death, this verse invites you to wait with confidence. You can mourn your loved ones without losing hope, because your faith rests on a Christ who has already won and who will complete his work.
exp.14:35:
He says that when someone sows a seed, that seed does not come to life unless it first dies.

The apostle Paul is answering those who doubted the resurrection and asked how the dead would be raised and with what kind of body they would come. Paul uses an example from the field that everyone knew. The buried seed seems to come to an end, but from it a new plant grows. With this image he shows that death is not necessarily the end, and that God gives life in ways that surprise us.

For today: when you go through losses or painful endings, remember that God can bring life out of what seems to be nothing. Trust in his power and wait with patience, knowing that he keeps his promises.
exp.14:37:
It says that God is the one who gives form to the body of the plant that grows from the seed, just as he chose to. Each kind of seed receives the body that belongs to it.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some there doubted the resurrection of the dead. Paul uses the example of the planted seed: what dies in the ground comes up different, with a new body. In this way he helps us understand that the risen body will have continuity with the present one, but will also be transformed by God. The exact details of what it will be like, the Bible does not fully explain.

Today we can trust that God takes care of what we do not understand. If you are going through a loss or a season that seems like an ending, you can entrust it to God, for he knows how to make new life grow.
exp.14:38:
The explanation says that not every physical body is the same. Here "flesh" means the kind of body or living matter. Human beings have one kind of body, animals another, fish another, and birds another. Each creature has the body that belongs to its kind.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. He answers the question of how the dead rise and with what kind of body. He uses the example of the seed and the variety of creation to show that God can give each thing the body he chooses. So a risen body does not have to be identical to the present one.

For today: when it is hard to believe God's promises, look at creation. If he made bodies so different from one another, you can trust that he will also keep his promise of new life in Christ.
exp.14:39:
Paul says there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, and that each kind has its own glory, that is, its own splendor or beauty. They are not the same, but both have value.

The apostle Paul responds to those in Corinth who were asking how the dead can be raised and with what kind of body they will come. He uses examples from creation: seeds, animals, birds, and heavenly bodies. His point is that God makes bodies that are very different according to his purpose. If the Creator makes so much variety, he can give the believer a risen body suited to the new life. Scholars discuss exactly what the heavenly bodies are, but the central argument is clear.

For today: do not be afraid of what you do not understand about the resurrection. Trust the God who made a world so varied. And if today you suffer because of your weak or sick body, remember that God has a glory prepared for you.
exp.14:42:
It says that the human body, when it dies and is buried, is like a seed that is sown. It is laid in dishonour (dishonour, weakness before death) and in weakness (lack of strength). But God will raise it in glory (honour and splendour) and in power (strength and vigour). Our raised body will be very different from the present one.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. To explain it he uses the image of the seed: what is buried does not look the same as what sprouts. Earlier he spoke of corruption and incorruption, and later he will speak of the spiritual body. Exactly what that body will be like, the Bible does not fully describe.

For today: if you are tired, sick, or in mourning, remember that weakness is not the last word. You can entrust to God your frailty and your loved ones who died in faith, with a firm hope.
exp.14:43:
It says that our present body is like a seed that is buried, and that God will raise it up as a new body. "Natural" here does not mean wild animal, but a body made for life in this world, with hunger, sleep, and weakness. "Spiritual" does not mean invisible, but a renewed body guided by the Spirit of God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. He uses the image of sowing to show that what dies does not disappear, but that God transforms it. It is believed that he describes a real body, yet glorious, although exactly what it will be like is a mystery.

For today: if your body is tired, sick, or limited, do not lose hope. Care for it with gratitude and serve God with it, knowing that God is preparing something much better.
exp.14:44:
This verse compares two men: Adam and Christ. Paul quotes Genesis 2:7, saying that Adam was made a living soul, that is, a being with natural life, who breathes and depends on what God gave him. Christ, the last Adam, is a quickening spirit, that is, someone who gives life to others.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. He explains that the present body is natural and fragile, but the risen body will be transformed by the power of Christ. Just as we inherit a weak life from Adam, we receive a new life from Christ.

For today: if you are tired or limited, remember that your frailty is not the end. Trust in Christ, who gives life, and live with hope.
exp.14:45:
It says that God's order is first the natural and then the spiritual. The word "natural" here does not speak of beasts, but of what has ordinary life, with a soul, as every human being has in this world. "Spiritual" refers to the risen body, renewed by God's Spirit.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection of the body. He explains that just as we all receive from Adam a frail and earthly life, those who believe receive from Christ, the last Adam, a risen and heavenly life. First comes what we are now; then, what God promises.

For today: if your body or your strength grows weak, do not lose hope. This life is the beginning, not the end. Live with patience and confidence in the promise of Christ.
exp.15:4:
Paul tells the Corinthians that he will come to visit them after passing through Macedonia. That region lay to the north of Greece, and his travel route went through there.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth from Ephesus, near the end of the letter. He has already spoken to them about the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, and now he explains his travel plans. He wants them to know that he will not visit in a hurry, but desires to stay with them for a while, if the Lord permits.

For today: Make your plans with order and sincerity, but with humility, leaving room for God's will. Planning well is not a lack of faith; just remember that He has the final word.
exp.15:6:
Paul says he does not want to visit the Corinthians only in passing, a quick stop with no time to talk. He hopes to stay with them for a good while, if the Lord permit, that is, if God allows it or sees it as good.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, which had problems and needed close attention. He plans to pass first through Macedonia and then reach Corinth, perhaps to spend the winter there. A brief visit would not be enough to help them grow and work through their differences.

For today: make your plans with seriousness and with care for people, but with a heart ready to depend on God. Give quality time to those you love and serve, and remember that the future is in the Lord's hands.
exp.15:7:
Paul says that he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost. The word "but" is used here to show a contrast, and "Ephesus" is the city of Ephesus. Pentecost was the Jewish feast celebrated fifty days after the Passover, and Christians later remembered it for the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Paul writes from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, and he explains his travel plans. He wants to visit them unhurriedly, not just in passing. But first he stays in Ephesus because there he has a great opportunity to preach, although there are also many opponents, as the following verse says.

For today: sometimes God asks us to remain where we are, even when there are difficulties, because there is work to be done there. Before you move, ask God whether your present place is still your door of service.
exp.15:9:
The explanation says that if Timothy comes to Corinth, the believers should make sure he is at ease and without fear among them. Paul explains the reason: Timothy works in the work of the Lord, just as he himself does.

Paul writes from Ephesus, where he faces much opposition, but also a great opportunity to preach. He plans to send Timothy, a younger co-worker, to a church marked by divisions and tensions. For this reason he asks that Timothy be received well and that no one look down on him, as the following verse says.

Today we can encourage and support those who serve in the church, especially the younger or less experienced ones. A kind word, a respectful manner, and a prayer for them give them confidence to serve without fear.
exp.15:11:
Paul says that he strongly encouraged Apollos to visit the Corinthians together with other brothers. But Apollos did not want to go for now. Paul says that he will come when he has a good opportunity.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, and some preferred Apollos while others preferred Paul. That is why it is remarkable that Paul speaks of Apollos with respect. We do not know for certain why Apollos did not go; the text only says it was his decision, and Paul does not pressure him or criticize him.

For today: we can work with other believers without controlling them. Let us respect that each servant of God has his own time and his own way of serving, and trust that God guides each one.
exp.15:17:
Paul says that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus "refreshed" his spirit and that of the Corinthians, meaning they encouraged him, revived him, and gave him rest. For this reason he asks that such people be acknowledged, that is, that people like them be publicly valued and honored.

Paul writes from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, at the close of his letter. These three men visited him and made up, by their presence, what the Corinthians could not give him while they were far away. They probably carried the church's questions to Paul, though the letter does not state this with complete clarity.

Today we can notice those who serve without drawing attention and thank them. This week, tell someone in your church, in specific words, how their service has encouraged you.
exp.15:19:
All the brothers and sisters who are with Paul send greetings to the Corinthians. Then Paul asks them to greet one another with a holy kiss. This is a respectful and pure kiss, not a romantic one, as a sign of affection between brothers and sisters in the faith.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus, near the end, and closes with greetings from the churches and from friends such as Aquila and Priscilla. The Corinthians had divisions and arguments, so this greeting reminds them that they are one family. Kissing or embracing as a greeting was a common custom in that culture.

Today we do not have to copy the exact form, since every culture greets differently. What matters is expressing sincere affection: give a hug or a warm greeting to someone in your church, especially to someone you have been distant from, and seek peace with that person.
exp.15:22:
Paul says he wishes the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ to be with the believers in Corinth. "Grace" means the undeserved favor of God, his kindness that we cannot earn. It is a closing blessing, like a farewell full of affection.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, disorder, and difficult questions. Just before this verse, he takes the pen himself to sign with his own hand, and he gives a serious warning about loving Christ. Having corrected so much, Paul ends with grace and with love.

Today, before speaking with someone with whom you have tension, ask God that his grace accompany both of you. Correct with truth, but say goodbye with kindness.
exp.10:2:
This verse sets out an order of relationship: Christ is the head of every man, the man is the head of the woman, and God is the head of Christ. Paul says he wants his readers to understand this. The word "head" is understood in several ways: some see authority, others see origin or source.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its gatherings. He has just praised them for following his teachings, and now he introduces a subject about how men and women prayed and prophesied in public. Scholars debate the exact meaning of the customs of that time regarding covering the head.

For today: the verse reminds us that all relationships, even the closest, are lived under Christ. We can ask ourselves whether our conduct at home and in the church reflects humility, respect and service, like that of Christ toward the Father.
exp.6:37:
He says that the one who marries the virgin does well, but the one who chooses not to marry her does even better. "Does well" and "does even better" do not mean that marrying is a sin, but that not marrying is the more fitting choice in that situation.

Paul is speaking here, answering questions from the Corinthians about marriage and remaining single. He gives his advice with "the present distress" (v. 26) in mind, and makes clear that marrying is not a sin. Some scholars think the verse is about a father and his daughter; others think it is about a man and his fiancée. The text allows for both readings.

For today: when faced with decisions such as marrying or remaining single, avoid judging others. Seek what God shows you, decide with freedom and conviction, and serve the Lord wholeheartedly in either case.
exp.0:8:
God is faithful, that is, he keeps his promises. He himself has called us into fellowship with his Son, which means sharing a life of union and friendship with Jesus Christ, our Lord. The phrase "who has called you" in this verse refers to God, the one who makes the call, and the words "our Lord" point to Jesus Christ as the one we belong to.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He thanks them for the gifts they have received and reminds them that God will keep them strong until the end. But he will soon call their attention to their divisions and quarrels. First, he reminds them that all of them were called to the same thing: to be united with Christ.

For today: when there are tensions in your church or family, remember that God has called you together with others to live in Christ. Trust that he is faithful, and seek unity with humility and patience.
exp.2:16:
If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. The reason is that God's temple is holy, set apart for God. And Paul makes clear that this temple is you: the community of believers.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, divided by rivalries between leaders and by pride in human wisdom. He reminds them that, as a community, they are the place where the Spirit of God dwells. For this reason he warns with seriousness those who, through divisions or twisted teachings, harm the church. Interpreters debate how to understand "destroy," but all see here a grave warning.

For today: take care of the unity of your church. Before criticizing, gossiping, or dividing, remember that this community is holy to God.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that men and women need each other. In the Lord, that is, within the life and order that Christ establishes, neither one stands on their own apart from the other. The word "however" marks a correction to what has just been said.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its gatherings. He had been speaking about customs of covering the head when praying, and about the relationship between man and woman. Here he corrects any idea of superiority: he says they depend on one another. Some details of this passage, such as the part about the angels, are interpreted in several ways.

For today: in the home, the church, and the workplace, let us value the other sex as a gift from God, not as a rival or as someone inferior. Today you can thank a person of the other sex for something concrete they contribute to your life.
exp.12:4:
This verse continues describing what love is like, which here is called "love." "It is not rude" means that it does not act in ways that are disrespectful or offensive to others. "It is not self-seeking" means that it does not demand its own benefit first. "It is not easily angered" means that it does not get angry quickly. "It keeps no account of wrongs" means that it does not hold on to offenses or keep a running tally of how others have hurt us.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, pride, and disorder, even in the use of spiritual gifts. Before this passage, he says that even the most impressive gifts or the greatest sacrifices have no value without love. That is why he describes what this love looks like in daily life.

Today, when someone bothers you, before responding in anger, pause and pray. Try to think the best of that person and respond with calm, also seeking their good.
exp.15:1:
Each week, on the first day, every believer was to set aside something at home from whatever income they had. To "set aside" means to keep money back for a purpose, and "collections" are gatherings of offerings. This way, when Paul arrived, nothing would need to be gathered in a rush.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He was organizing help for the poor Christians in Jerusalem, and he had already given the same instruction to the churches in Galatia. Many understand "the first day of the week" as the day when Christians met together, although the text gives no further detail. Paul wanted order, and he wanted the Corinthians themselves to choose the people who would carry the gift.

For today: give with planning, not on impulse. Decide in prayer on a regular portion of what you receive, set it aside faithfully, and use it to help others.
exp.3:0:
Paul says that people should see us as servants of Christ, that is, helpers who obey their Lord. He also calls us stewards of the mysteries of God: managers entrusted with carefully sharing the divine truths that God has revealed, especially the gospel. The word "regard" means "consider" or "think of."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions because some were proudly following different teachers. He corrects that attitude by explaining that leaders are not celebrities or bosses, but servants and managers. That is why, in the next verse, what matters most is that they be faithful to the one who placed them in that work.

For today: if you serve God in something, whether teaching, helping, or leading, do not seek applause or compare ministries. Ask yourself whether you are being faithful with what God has entrusted to you, and do it with humility.
exp.12:9:
It says that "the perfect" will bring an end to what is now partial. "That which is in part" refers to gifts such as prophecy, tongues, and knowledge, which today give us only a limited view. "Passes away" means they will no longer be needed when the perfect comes.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were boasting about their spiritual gifts. He reminds them that love is more important and lasts forever. Christians have understood "the perfect" in different ways: the return of Christ, heaven, or the maturity of the church. The context, with "face to face," strongly points to the meeting with God at the end.

For today: be humble about what you know, because your knowledge is partial. Seek to love more than to show off, and trust that one day you will see everything clearly.
exp.13:2:
This verse says that the one who prophesies speaks to people for three purposes: building up, which means helping them grow and become stronger in faith; encouragement, which means cheering them on and urging them to live faithfully; and comfort, which means giving them consolation in their sorrows.

The phrase "speaks to people" simply means exactly that: speaking to other people.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued speaking in tongues very highly. He does not despise that gift, but he reminds them that if no one understands, the church receives no help. So he emphasizes prophecy, which is understood and serves everyone. Christians have understood prophecy in different ways, but here it is described by its practical fruit.

For today: before speaking with someone in the church, ask yourself whether your words will help them grow, encourage them, or comfort them. May your service be clear and useful to others.
exp.5:12:
It says that food and the stomach were made for each other, but both are temporary: God will bring them to an end. The body, however, is not intended for sexual immorality (sexual relations outside of marriage), but for the Lord, and the Lord cares for and takes an interest in the body. "Food" refers to what we eat, and "destroy" means that God will bring them to an end.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of immorality. Some used the saying "All things are lawful for me" to justify their behavior. Paul answers that being free does not mean doing anything at all. What seems natural, such as eating, cannot be compared with the use of the body in sexual matters, which belongs to the Lord. He also announces that God will raise up the bodies.

Today we can ask ourselves: "Am I using my body to honor Christ?" Before deciding anything, let us think about whether it is good for us and whether it enslaves us, and ask the Lord for help to live in purity.
exp.10:29:
According to the explanation, because of the wrong way the Lord's Supper was being shared, many in Corinth were sick and weak, and some had fallen asleep, a gentler way of saying they had died. The word "irreverently" describes a disrespectful manner, not the idea that someone is not perfect.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where at their shared meals some ate too much while others went hungry, looking down on the poor. Paul sees this as failing to recognize the body of the Lord, that is, not valuing what the Supper means or the community. He understands their sickness and death as a correction from the Lord, so that they would not be condemned with the world. He does not say that every illness is a punishment.

Today, before taking part in the Lord's Supper, examine your heart: ask for forgiveness, be reconciled with anyone you have offended, and treat your brothers and sisters with respect and love.
exp.13:17:
Paul says that he thanks God because he speaks in tongues more than all the Corinthians do. "Speaking in tongues" was a gift given by the Spirit to pray or praise in languages that the speaker had not learned.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some took pride in this gift and used it in gatherings without anyone understanding. He does not look down on tongues; he acknowledges that he also practices them, and a great deal. But he quickly makes clear that in the congregation what matters most is that everyone understands and is built up.

For today: give thanks for the gifts God has given you, but use them with humility and with others in mind. Before you speak or serve in your church, ask yourself: "Does this help others understand and grow in faith?"
exp.9:18:
Paul asks a question to clarify his point: is he saying that an idol is something real, or that food sacrificed to an idol has power in itself? The phrase "food sacrificed to an idol" refers to meat offered in pagan rites. The question expects a "no," but Paul will soon make clear that something more serious lies behind it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, surrounded by pagan temples. Earlier he spoke of communion at the Lord's Supper and of the example of Israel, where those who ate of the sacrifice shared in the altar. Now he avoids two errors: thinking that idols are real gods, and thinking that taking part in those feasts is harmless. He warns that behind those practices there are spiritual forces opposed to God.

Today, let us ask what things receive our loyalty and worship. Even if we have no statues, we must take care that our lives are not divided between Christ and other devotions.
exp.14:33:
Paul says: "Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning". He adds that some of them are ignorant of God, and he says this so that they will be ashamed. "Sober up as you ought" means to wake up fully and think clearly, the way a person does after drinking too much, and then to stop sinning.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul warns that this idea, together with bad company, was opening the door to living without restraint: "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die". His rebuke is strong, but he seeks to correct them with love.

For today: what we believe about the future affects how we live now. Think about who you associate with and which ideas you accept. Choose friendships and teachings that draw you closer to God, and live with the hope that Christ has risen.
exp.0:2:
This verse is a greeting. Paul wishes the believers "grace," which is the undeserved favor of God, and "peace," which is the calm and harmony that come from being at rest with Him. Both come from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. By naming them together as the source of these blessings, Paul places Jesus alongside the Father.

Paul writes, together with Sosthenes, to the church in Corinth. It was a community with many problems, such as divisions, which he will address in the letter. Even so, before correcting them, he greets them with affection and reminds them that they are sanctified in Christ. His wish for grace and peace shows that his dealings with them begin from love.

For today: before speaking with someone with whom you have a conflict, pray that they receive grace and peace from God, and try to offer both yourself in your words.
exp.14:28:
It says that some people are baptized "for the dead." Paul asks what they will do if the dead are not raised at all. He also asks why people are baptized for them. "At all" means "in any way."

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who doubted the resurrection. He uses this practice as an argument: if they themselves do it, they basically expect a resurrection. It is not known with certainty what that baptism consisted of; there are several interpretations, and Paul neither recommends it nor explains it. The following verses strengthen his point: he risks his life every day because he believes in the resurrection.

For today: examine why you do what you do in your faith. If Christ rose and we too will rise, then obedience, service, and even sacrifice make sense and carry hope.
exp.9:0:
Paul says he does not want the believers to be unaware of something important: the ancestors of Israel, "our forefathers," were all under the cloud that guided them, and all of them passed through the sea.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community marked by divisions and a great tolerance of sin. He reminds them of Israel's story in the Exodus. All of them received great blessings from God, but then many fell into idolatry and immorality, as he explains in the verses that follow. He says "our forefathers" because he sees the church as part of God's people.

Having received God's blessings is not the same as living in obedience. Do not rely on your spiritual past, your church, or your experiences. Ask God to keep you faithful and attentive today.
exp.15:15:
The explanation says that the believers of Corinth should submit to people such as the household of Stephanas, and to everyone who helps and works hard in God's service. Such people are those who serve with devotion.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. He has just mentioned that the household of Stephanas was among the first converts in Achaia, a region of Greece, and that they devoted themselves to serving the believers. Paul asks that they be valued, because their service had made up for what was lacking. Submitting here does not seem to mean blind obedience, but recognizing and supporting those who serve with love.

Today we can look to those who serve quietly in the church, thank them, support them, and, when possible, help alongside them.
exp.2:13:
It says that if what someone has built on the foundation survives the testing, that person will receive a reward. To "build upon" means to keep building on top of something already laid. To "survive" means to remain standing. God rewards work that proves firm and valuable.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, who were divided and boasted in their leaders. He laid the foundation, which is Jesus Christ, and others keep building on it. Paul reminds them that each worker will give an account, and that the fire of the Lord's day will test the quality of what has been done. Christians interpret in different ways what that reward will be, but all agree that God will judge with justice.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we do for God, in the church, at home, or at work, we do with love, truth, and humility, and not to show off, because that is what lasts.
exp.11:17:
God himself, the explanation says, placed each part of the body in its position, according to his design. "Members" means the parts of the body, such as the eye, the ear, or the hand. The word "arranged" means put in order and given a purpose. Nothing is there by chance.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and people who felt more important than others. He uses the image of the human body to speak about the church, which is the body of Christ. He wants to show that each believer has a place and a function given by God, and that variety is part of his plan.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or feel worthless because your service is little seen. If God put you where you are, your part matters. Ask him how to serve with what he has given you, and value others as well.
exp.6:0:
Paul begins to answer the questions the Corinthians had asked him in a letter. He says that it is good to abstain from sexual relations, meaning not having intimate relations, whether inside or outside of marriage. The phrase "for the matters you wrote about" points to the questions they had raised, and it is a way of saying he is now turning to those issues one by one.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, a city with much sexual immorality. Some scholars believe this phrase quotes what the Corinthians themselves thought, and others believe it is Paul's own view about remaining single. The verses that follow clarify that marriage is good and protects against immorality.

For today: whether you are single or married, live your situation as a calling from God, with purity and gratitude, without looking down on others for their choice.
exp.12:8:
It says that our knowledge and our prophecies are limited. "In part" means incompletely: we know something, but not everything. "We prophesy" refers to communicating messages on behalf of God. Even the spiritual gifts do not give us the complete picture.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some boasted about their spiritual gifts and neglected love. For this reason he shows that those gifts are temporary and partial, while love remains. Christians do not agree about when the "perfect" thing mentioned in the following verse will come; many think it is the return of Christ.

For today: let us be humble when we speak about what we know of God. Recognizing that we understand only in part helps us listen better, treat with patience those who think differently, and put love first.
exp.8:3:
Paul asks a rhetorical question: don't we have the right to eat and drink? In his verse, the idea is that of a right to food and drink. He means that, as an apostle, he has the right to receive food and drink, that is, support, from the churches he serves.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his apostleship, since some were questioning it. He reminds them that they themselves are the proof of his calling. Then he shows that other apostles receive support, but he and Barnabas have worked with their own hands. He does not demand his rights, although he has them.

Today we can learn to generously support those who serve in the church. We can also ask ourselves whether we are willing to set aside a legitimate right out of love for others and for the good of the gospel.
exp.10:1:
Paul commends the believers in Corinth because they remember him in everything and keep the traditions he passed on to them. The word "commend" means to recognize something good. "Traditions" refers to what was handed down to them, that is, what he taught them by word and by his example.

Paul writes this letter to a church with many problems and disagreements. Even so, he begins here with a sincere acknowledgment before correcting them. The verse just before this one says to imitate his example as he imitates Christ. Then, starting in verse 3, he addresses matters of order in worship. Some details of those topics are interpreted in different ways.

Today we can learn to encourage first and correct afterward. Before pointing out a fault, honestly recognize the good you see in someone.
exp.9:13:
It says we should stay completely away from idolatry. The word "flee" means running far away, not merely avoiding something or looking at it carefully. The phrase "my beloved" shows Paul's affection as he gives them this command. The word "therefore" shows that this follows from what came before: if God provides a way out in temptation, they should take it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a city full of temples and meals tied to idols. Earlier he reminded them how Israel fell in the wilderness. Then he speaks of the Lord's Supper, to show that a person cannot be united to Christ and also to idols.

For today: idolatry is not always statues. It is anything that takes the place of God in the heart, such as money, fame, or success. Ask yourself what is pulling you away from Him, and today make one concrete decision to turn away from it.
exp.0:4:
In Him you have been enriched in every way. The BSB words "in every way" name the whole range of what God has given. "Speech" is the ability to speak and express yourself, and "knowledge" is understanding. "Have been enriched" means you have received abundance, not because of your own merit, but because you are united to Jesus.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with remarkable gifts, but also with divisions and serious problems, which he addresses later in the letter. Before correcting them, he begins by thanking God for what He has already done in them. Some think that "speech" also points to spiritual gifts of speaking, but the text does not specify this.

For today: before criticizing others or yourself, acknowledge with gratitude what God has already given you in Christ. Use your words and your knowledge to serve and build up others, not to boast.
exp.13:18:
Paul says that when the church is gathered, he would rather speak just five coherent words that instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue. The word "coherent" means clear and understandable, so the point is that words people can follow matter more than many words they cannot. "Instruct" means to teach.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who valued speaking in tongues very highly. He himself speaks in tongues more than they do, and he is thankful for it, but he corrects them: in the meeting, what matters is that everyone is built up. Words that no one can follow do not help the congregation.

For today: before you speak, pray, or serve in the church, ask yourself whether what you say will help others understand and grow. Use clear and simple words, because loving others includes making sure they can follow you.
exp.0:11:
Paul says that in the church at Corinth people were splitting into factions. Some were saying, "I follow Paul," others, "I follow Apollos," others, "I follow Cephas" (that is, Peter), and still others, "I follow Christ." The phrase "What I mean is this" introduces the point he is about to make plainly.

Paul writes this letter to a church that he himself helped to start. Some people from the household of Chloe had told him there were quarrels among the believers. Before this verse he urges them to be united, and right after it he will remind them that Christ is not divided. Some think that the group saying "I follow Christ" also believed itself to be better than the others.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we admire a particular leader, pastor, or style of church so much that we look down on other believers. We can be thankful for what God does through different people, but remember that we all belong to Christ.
exp.11:18:
If all were one part of the body, such as only an eye or only a hand, there would be no complete body. Here "part" means one piece of the body. In your verse the question is, "where would the body be?"

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride over spiritual gifts. Some felt superior to others. Paul uses the image of the body to show that God placed each believer in the church with a place and a function, as he willed. Variety is not a problem; it is part of God's plan.

Today we can stop comparing ourselves with others in the church. If your gift seems small or less visible, it is still necessary. And if another person's gift is different from yours, thank God for that difference and seek to serve alongside that person.
exp.14:7:
The explanation says that the risen Christ appeared to Paul last of all, after the other witnesses. Paul describes himself as one of untimely birth, meaning someone who came along unexpectedly and at an unusual moment. The phrase "He appeared to me" means that Jesus showed himself to Paul personally.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to argue that Christ truly rose from the dead. He lists the witnesses: Peter, the twelve, more than five hundred people, James, and all the apostles. He includes himself at the end. Scholars debate why he uses such a harsh description of himself. Perhaps his critics used it against him, or perhaps he is speaking of his unworthiness because he had persecuted the church. It is not certain.

God can reach and use anyone, regardless of their past. If you feel unworthy or late, remember that Paul credited everything to God's grace. Acknowledge your failings with humility, but rest in the knowledge that grace sustains you and enables you to serve.
exp.8:21:
He says that Paul put himself on the level of the "weak," that is, those who were weak in faith or in conscience, in order to win them over. Here "weak" means weak, not thin. Then he sums up his method: he became all things to all people, adapting himself to each person, so that by all possible means he might save some.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth. He had been speaking about his freedom, and about how he gave up using his rights out of love for others. He adapted himself in customs and in dealings with people, without abandoning the law of Christ or betraying the gospel. He did all of it for the sake of the gospel, and right away he compares it to a race.

For today: before speaking about your faith, listen patiently and treat each person with respect, according to their situation and their struggles. You may yield in tastes and customs, but never in the truth of Christ.
exp.11:28:
Here Paul asks a series of questions whose obvious answer is "no." Not everyone in the church is an apostle, a prophet, or a teacher. The verse itself makes clear what teachers are and what it means to work miracles, so no extra word needs to be explained here.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who were divided and thought themselves superior because of the gifts they had. He reminds them that the church is a body with many parts, and that God himself distributed the gifts as he chose. For that reason no one should feel more important or less valuable. Then he leads them to love, the way of love described in chapter 13.

For today: instead of comparing yourself with others, be thankful for the place God gave you and serve with what you have. And value those who serve in other ways.
exp.9:6:
Do not be idolaters, as some of them were. The verse points to the meaning of "idolaters": people who give honor to something as if it were God. Paul quotes Exodus 32:6: "The people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry," describing the Israelites feasting and carousing beside the golden calf.

The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, who lived surrounded by pagan temples and festivals. He reminds them of what happened in the desert as a warning: Israel was rescued by God, yet still fell into sin. Scholars understand that "revelry" also includes immoral behavior, although the text says it only briefly.

For today: examine what things have taken the place of God in your heart, even when they seem like simple pleasures. Enjoying a meal or a celebration is not wrong, but do not let pleasure, money, or fame rule you.
exp.8:6:
He asks three questions from everyday life. Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? No one goes to war paying his own way. Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? The one who plants it has the right to enjoy its grapes. Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk? The shepherd has the right to share in the milk of the flock. These are three examples: the soldier, the farmer, and the shepherd.

Paul is speaking to the Corinthians to defend his right as an apostle to receive support from the church. Although he chose not to ask for payment and to work with his own hands, he wants to make it clear that those who serve in the gospel have the right to live from that service. He will then back this up with the law of Moses.

For today: let us give fair and generous support to those who teach and care for us spiritually, such as pastors and missionaries, and not assume that their work should be free.
exp.3:12:
When people speak falsely about Paul and the other apostles and damage their name, they answer with gentle words. The phrase "the scum of the earth" points to the dirt or sediment that settles at the bottom of a vessel, and "the refuse of the world" is what everyone throws away. That is how they were treated, and it is how they are still treated today.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who felt proud and wise. With irony and sorrow, he shows them the real life of an apostle: suffering and contempt. Then he makes clear that he does not write to shame them, but to correct them as a father corrects his beloved children.

For today: when someone insults you or looks down on you for following Christ, you do not have to repay evil with evil. You can respond with kindness and prayer, trusting that the worth of your life does not depend on the opinion of others.
exp.11:3:
It says that God gives different gifts to believers, but that all of them come from one and the same Spirit. "Different" means "varied" or "distinct," and the verse speaks of different kinds of gifts that are given out. The gifts are spiritual abilities that God gives by grace, not something earned.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with many problems of division and pride. Before this verse, he reminds them that they came from paganism and from mute idols, and that only the Spirit leads a person to confess Jesus as Lord. Now he wants them to understand that different gifts should not divide them, because they share a single origin. Then he links the Spirit with the Lord and with God, something many see as a reflection of the Trinity.

Today, instead of comparing yourself with others or envying their gifts, be thankful for the gift God gave you and use it to serve. And value the gifts of others as part of the same gift.
exp.11:8:
It says that the Holy Spirit gives to one person faith and to another gifts of healing. "Gifts of healing" means the ability to help the sick be healed, and the word is plural, perhaps because there are different kinds of healing. This faith is not the basic faith for salvation, but a special trust in God for difficult situations.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and proud of its spiritual gifts. He reminds them that all the gifts come from the one Spirit, are given for the good of everyone, and are not meant for showing off.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or look down on your gift or your brother's. Ask God how you can serve with what he has given you, and give thanks for what others bring to the church.
exp.7:2:
This verse says that the one who loves God is known by God. Loving God means having affection for him, and being "known by God" means that God recognizes that person as his own, in a close relationship. It does not only mean that God knows facts about that person, but that it is a relationship of affection.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was debating whether it was right to eat meat offered to idols. Some were boasting of having a great deal of knowledge. Paul reminds them that knowledge without love puffs up, and that what matters is loving God and loving others. Some scholars note that the text can also be understood as a warning against intellectual pride.

For today: instead of boasting about what you know of the Bible, seek to love God and to deal patiently with those who think differently. Knowledge helps, but love is what shows a real relationship with God.
exp.2:1:
Paul says he gave the Corinthians "milk" and not solid food. The BSB says "solid food" directly, so the explanation uses that phrase instead of the older word "meat." Milk represents the most basic teachings of the faith. Paul explains that they were not yet ready for something deeper, and that they were still not ready when he wrote the letter.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, whom he himself had brought to the Gospel. He calls them "babes in Christ" because there was jealousy, quarrels, and factions among them: some said they belonged to Paul and others to Apollos. He speaks to them firmly, but as a father who wants to see them grow.

For today: growing in faith is not measured by how much we know, but by how we live and how we treat others. Ask yourself whether there is envy or rivalry in your heart, and ask God for humility so that you may mature.
exp.13:36:
It says that if anyone thinks of himself as a prophet or as a person guided by the Spirit, he should recognize that what Paul writes is the Lord's command. The Berean wording "considers himself" carries the sense of how a person sees himself, and "recognize" means accept or admit.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where the gifts were being used in disorderly ways, especially in the gatherings. He firmly corrects those who considered themselves very spiritual and did not want to accept his instruction. The verses before this one about women have been understood in various ways, and Christians debate their scope. Even so, the point of this verse is the authority of apostolic teaching.

For today: true spirituality shows itself in humility. Whoever says he is guided by God must be willing to be corrected by Scripture.
exp.11:30:
It says that we should eagerly desire the greater gifts, the ones that are most useful for everyone. "But" is the plain meaning of the word, and "eagerly desire" means "pursue with determination." Paul adds that he is going to show them the most excellent way, something better than any gift.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over gifts, such as speaking in tongues. He reminds them that the church is one body with many members and that no one has all the gifts. With this verse he prepares chapter 13, where he speaks about love. Some understand "eagerly desire" as a command, others as a description of what they were already doing.

For today: use your gifts to serve others, not to stand out. Before asking what gift you have, ask how you can love someone better today.
exp.14:49:
Paul says that our present body, fragile and mortal ("flesh and blood"), is not made to live in God's eternal kingdom. "Nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable" means that what wears out and dies cannot possess what lasts forever.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. Earlier he spoke of Adam, the earthly man, and of Christ, the heavenly one. Here he makes clear that we need to be changed. Right after, he explains this "mystery": believers will be transformed when the final trumpet sounds.

For today: do not live as if this fragile life were all there is. Rest in the fact that God will give you a new body, and so invest your time and strength in what endures: loving, serving, and trusting in Christ.
exp.11:13:
This verse says that the body does not consist of just one part, but of many. It is very obvious: no one would say that a single hand is a complete body. The word "part" refers to a piece of the body, such as the hand, the foot, or the eye.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, a church with divisions and with people who thought they were more important because of their spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the body to explain that, although they are different, all of them belong to Christ through one and the same Spirit. The verses that follow continue with examples of the foot and the ear.

For today: do not compare yourself with others in your church. If your gift seems small, it is still necessary. And value those who serve differently from you, because God placed them there on purpose.
exp.2:3:
Here Paul says that some in Corinth were saying, "I follow Paul," and others, "I follow Apollos." Paul asks them whether this does not show that they are acting as mere men, that is, living according to their human nature and not according to the Spirit.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had split into groups around their favorite leaders. He had already rebuked them for jealousy and quarreling. His point is that these rivalries showed spiritual immaturity. Right away he reminds them that he and Apollos are only servants, and that God is the one who makes things grow.

For today: when we admire a pastor or teacher, let us remember that he is only a servant of God. Let us avoid boasting "my leader" in front of other believers, and seek unity around Christ.
exp.13:10:
If someone does not know what a language means, then the person speaking will be a foreigner to the listener, and the listener will be a foreigner to the speaker. The word "foreigner" here does not mean a savage, but someone whose language another person cannot understand. The phrase "the meaning of someone's language" refers to what is being said.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some took pride in speaking in tongues during the gatherings. He uses everyday examples to show that speaking in a way others cannot understand helps no one. His goal is that the congregation be built up, that is, strengthened in faith.

For today: when you teach, pray aloud, or share your faith, use simple words that others can understand. Avoid technical or religious language that leaves others out, because love seeks for the other person to understand.
exp.8:16:
Paul says that if he preaches the gospel voluntarily, he will receive a reward. But if his preaching is not voluntary, he is still entrusted with a responsibility. A responsibility here means a charge, like that of a steward who looks after what someone else has placed in his care. The phrase "not voluntary" does not speak of mistreatment, but of a calling he cannot set aside.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He explains that, although he had the right to receive support for preaching, he did not use that right. He did not want anyone to think he preached for money, or that anything would hinder the gospel. His motive was to serve, not to collect payment.

For today: serve God gladly, not only out of duty. Even when a task costs you something, remember that God has entrusted you with something valuable, and do your part with a willing and grateful heart.
exp.3:15:
Paul asks the Corinthians to imitate him. The word "imitate" means copying his way of living and serving Christ. "I urge you" is a loving appeal, not a cold command.

Paul writes to them as a spiritual father, because it was through his preaching of the gospel that they came to believe. The guardians who looked after children were the ones who guided them. The church in Corinth was divided and proud, and Paul corrects them tenderly, without wanting to shame them. Soon he will send Timothy to remind them of how he lives in Christ.

Today we can be thankful for the people who have given us a good example of faith and look closely at how they live. Our own conduct also teaches others, so it is wise to live with humility, love and perseverance, and not only to talk about it.
exp.11:12:
All believers, regardless of their background or position, were united into one body by the work of the Holy Spirit. "Baptized" here speaks of being immersed into or joined to that body. The list of pairs, "whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free," means that no difference of nationality or social standing separates anyone from this body. And the words "we were all given one Spirit to drink" show that every believer receives the same Spirit.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride over spiritual gifts. He reminds them that the gifts come from one Spirit and that the church is like a body with many members. Some debate whether the "baptism" refers to water or to the inner work of the Spirit; the text emphasizes above all the unity.

Today, do not look down on another believer because of their culture, their money, or their gifts, and do not feel inferior yourself. If the same Spirit lives in both of you, you are part of the same body. This week, look for a way to serve or reach out to someone in your church who is different from you.
exp.11:2:
He says that the Spirit of God never leads anyone to say "Jesus be cursed," and that no one can truly say "Jesus is Lord" without the help of the Holy Spirit. To be cursed means to be given over to condemnation. The phrase "I inform you" simply means "I want you to know."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community made up largely of people who once worshiped silent idols. They had questions about the spiritual gifts and how to recognize what comes from God. Paul first gives them a basic test: the true Spirit always exalts Jesus. Later he will speak about the variety of gifts and about unity.

For today: before we are impressed by an experience or a gift, let us ask whether it honors Jesus as Lord. And if today you can sincerely say that Jesus is Lord, give thanks that the Spirit is at work in you.
exp.12:6:
This verse describes what love is like. Your Bible says "love" here, so we speak of love in this verse. The idea of enduring means bearing up patiently under hard things, and the idea of holding firm means staying steady without giving up. Believing all things and hoping all things speak of trusting others and holding onto hope for them. Many understand this not to mean being naive, but to mean not being quick to suspect.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and boasted about its spiritual gifts. In this chapter he shows them that without love, the gifts are worth nothing. He describes how true love behaves, and then says that love remains, while the gifts are temporary.

For today: when someone lets you down, before reacting with anger or distrust, pray and choose to give them one more chance, with patience and hope, without giving up on telling the truth.
exp.6:39:
Paul says that a widow will be happier if she decides not to marry again. He makes clear that this is his judgment, not a command. The Berean Standard Bible renders the verse as "In my judgment, however, she is happier if she remains as she is," so the word "however" signals a contrast with what came before. He adds that he thinks he too has the Spirit of God, so that his opinion is taken seriously.

Paul is answering questions the Corinthians had asked him about marriage and singleness. He has just said that a widow is free to marry another believer. Now he gives his view: because of the difficulties of that time, and because a single person can serve the Lord with fewer distractions, he judges it better for her to remain alone. Some scholars debate how to understand the "distress" he mentions earlier in the chapter.

When you make decisions about your marital status, seek God's guidance and that of wise people, without pressure or comparisons. Both marrying and remaining single can be a good path, if it is lived for the Lord.
exp.9:10:
What happened to the Israelites in the wilderness took place as an example or warning. The word "examples" points to a pattern that we can learn from, and "warnings" are meant to correct us. Those stories were written down for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come, meaning we live in the time when what God had been doing across the ages is brought to completion.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who felt secure yet tolerated idolatry and immorality. He reminds them that Israel was delivered by God and yet fell through disobedience, testing God, and grumbling. Some understand "the fulfillment of the ages" as the era that began with Christ.

Today, do not read the Old Testament only as ancient history. Ask yourself what mistake of theirs you might repeat, such as complaining ungratefully or playing with temptation, and ask God for help to obey him.
exp.3:11:
They say that Paul and his companions worked hard with their own hands to support themselves. When people insulted them, they answered with a blessing. When they were persecuted, they endured it. "Working hard" means laboring with real effort, and "endure it" means they bore it without striking back.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some felt superior and boasted of their wisdom. With an ironic tone, he contrasts his humble life as an apostle with that pride. He does not aim to shame them but to correct them, like a father who loves his children. His way of living reflects the example of Christ.

Today, when someone speaks badly of you or treats you unfairly, you can choose to respond with a kind word or a prayer for that person, instead of returning the same treatment. It is hard, but it is a real way of becoming more like Jesus.
exp.14:4:
It says that the risen Jesus was first seen by Cephas, who is Peter (his name in Aramaic), and then by the group of disciples known as the Twelve. "Appeared" means that he truly let himself be seen. The word "appeared" in the verse above is the one this comment explains.

The apostle Paul is speaking, writing to the Christians in Corinth. Some of them doubted the resurrection of the dead. Paul reminds them of the essentials he himself received: Christ died, was buried, and rose again. He lists witnesses who saw him alive. That he mentions "the Twelve" even though Judas was no longer among them is a way of naming the group; some explain it this way, though the text gives no further detail.

Our faith rests on witnesses and on events, not only on ideas. If you have doubts, read the accounts of the resurrection calmly and speak to God with sincerity. And remember that Peter, who had denied Jesus, was among the first to see him: Christ seeks out those who have failed.
exp.15:2:
In this verse Paul tells the Corinthians that when he arrives, he will send letters with the people they recommend to carry their gift to Jerusalem. These are the ones the church chooses to deliver the money.

The word "gift" here refers to the generous help they are giving. The phrase "on my arrival" means the same as "when I come."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He has already explained how to set aside money each week. Now he clarifies who will carry the money: not he alone, but people recommended by the church itself. In this way trust was protected and any suspicion was avoided. Some think the letters were letters of introduction; the text gives no further details.

For today: if we handle money for a church or for a relief work, let us do it with order, clarity and accountability. Generosity is best cared for when everything is done with transparency.
exp.13:30:
Paul says that all who have the gift of prophecy may speak, but in turn, one at a time, without interrupting one another. The goal is twofold: that everyone may be instructed, and that everyone may be encouraged and strengthened. Here, to prophesy means to speak a message from God in order to build up others.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly, with many speaking at the same time. That is why he gives rules: only a few prophets speak, the others weigh what is said, and if someone receives a revelation, the one speaking gives way. The following verse clarifies that God is a God of peace, not of confusion.

For today: when you take part in your church or group, listen with patience, wait your turn, and seek for what you share to help others grow, not to draw attention to yourself.
exp.11:7:
It says that the Holy Spirit gives different gifts to different people. To one he gives the "message of wisdom," which is usually understood as the ability to give good counsel or to apply the truth of God wisely. To another he gives the "message of knowledge," that is, spiritual understanding and insight. Here "knowledge" means understanding, not modern science.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over spiritual gifts. He reminds them that all the gifts come from the same Spirit and are given for the common good, that is, for the benefit of everyone. Scholars debate exactly how these gifts operated, but the purpose is clear.

For today: do not boast about what God has given you, and do not envy what he has given to others. Ask God how you can use your gift to serve your church, and give thanks for the gifts of others.
exp.6:34:
Paul says that what he has explained he says for their own good. He does not want to restrict them or place a burden on them. What he seeks is what promotes proper decorum, that is, what is orderly and fitting, so that they can give undivided devotion to the Lord.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and remaining single. He had said that, because of the difficulties of that time, being single allowed a person to devote more of themselves to the Lord. Even so, he makes it clear that he is not imposing a rule: marrying or not is a free decision, and both are good.

For today: whatever our situation, let us ask ourselves which things distract us from God and how we can serve him with more attention and without anxiety.
exp.12:3:
Love is shown in how we treat other people. Being patient means enduring without giving up or taking revenge. Kind means gentle and good. Love does not envy, which means it does not become bitter over what others have. Love does not act improperly or foolishly. Love is not proud and does not boast.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, rivalries, and pride over spiritual gifts. Just before this verse, he says that even the most impressive gifts are worth nothing without love. Here he describes what love looks like in practice.

For today: when someone irritates you or things go better for them than for you, respond with patience and a kind word instead of envy or self-importance. Ask God to help you love in this way.
exp.10:31:
What he says: Paul explains that when the Lord judges us, he is disciplining us the way a loving father trains his children. "Disciplined" here means corrected and trained, not destroyed. The purpose is that believers will not be condemned along with the world that rejects God.

Context: Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some were abusing the Lord's Supper: they ate without waiting for others, and the poor were left humiliated. He says this brought consequences, such as sickness and even death among some. Interpreters debate whether all the illnesses there were caused by this, but Paul does see a discipline from God.

For today: When God corrects you through his Word or your conscience, do not see it as rejection, but as love. Examine yourself with humility, confess what is wrong, and treat your brothers and sisters with respect and consideration.
exp.15:23:
Paul closes his letter by saying that his love is with all of you, and he says it "in Christ Jesus," meaning a love that flows from your union with Christ. The phrase "in Christ Jesus" points to that union. The closing word "Amen" affirms the blessing and means "so be it."

Paul writes to a church full of divisions, pride, and moral problems, and he corrects them firmly throughout the letter. Before saying goodbye, he wants them to know that the correction does not come from rejection, but from affection.

Today, when we have to correct someone or say a hard truth, let us do it as Paul did: making it clear, in words and deeds, that we do it out of sincere love.
exp.15:0:
Paul is speaking to them about the offering being gathered for poor Christians, whom he calls "the saints." The word "collection" in the verse refers to a gift of money gathered from the people. He asks them to do what he has already directed the churches of Galatia to do.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth. The believers in Jerusalem were in need, and Paul was organizing help from churches in other regions. For that reason he gives practical instructions, so that everything will be ready before he arrives. The verses that follow show that he wanted order, not pressure at the last minute.

For today: giving with order and planning is a good way to practice generosity. Instead of waiting for an emergency to arise, we can set something aside regularly, according to what God allows us, to help whoever is in need.
exp.6:31:
He says that Paul wants believers to live free from worry and anxiety. The word rendered as "anguish" points to distress or restlessness. Paul notes that the unmarried person can give their attention to the work of the Lord, seeking how to please him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. He has just said that the present form of this world is passing away, meaning that everything present is temporary. He does not condemn marriage; he gives practical advice, since the married person naturally also seeks to please their spouse. Some scholars think that a difficult situation of that time also influenced his counsel.

Whatever your situation, ask yourself: "Do my concerns draw me closer to the Lord or pull me away from him?" Give him your cares today, and seek to serve him where you are.
exp.13:15:
Paul says that if someone praises God "in the spirit," meaning in a tongue others do not understand, the ordinary listener who is present (someone without that gift or that knowledge) will not be able to say "Amen" to the prayer of thanks. The reason is simple: that person does not know what was said.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the use of tongues in the gatherings was causing disorder. His concern is that everything should build up the others. He himself speaks in tongues, but he wants public prayer to be understood. Some scholars think the "uninstructed" person is a listener without the gift; others think he is simply a visitor or a new believer.

For today: when we pray or take part together in a group, let us do it so that everyone can understand and join in with their "Amen." Loving others includes being clear.
exp.14:21:
This verse compares two men: Adam and Christ. Because of Adam's disobedience, death came upon all human beings. Through Christ, who rose from the dead, new life comes. "Made alive" means that they receive life, that is, they are raised.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom denied the resurrection of the dead. He answers that Christ's resurrection is the beginning and the guarantee of ours. The verses that follow say that this happens "in order": first Christ, then those who belong to him when he comes. Some debate whether "all" means that everyone will be raised or that everyone who is in Christ will receive life. The context points strongly to those who belong to Christ.

For today: if your hope is in Christ, death does not have the last word. You can face grief, illness and fear with confidence, and live today as someone who belongs to the life God promised.
exp.8:0:
Paul asks four questions, and all of them expect a "yes" as the answer. He asks whether he is free, whether he is an apostle, whether he has seen Jesus our Lord, and whether the Corinthians are his workmanship in the Lord.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some doubted his authority as an apostle. Earlier he had spoken of giving up his freedom out of love for others, and now he defends his calling. His proof is the very existence of the church he helped to found. Scholars understand in different ways what he means by "I have seen Jesus," but many think of his encounter with the risen Christ on the road to Damascus.

Today, the fruit of a life given to God speaks louder than words. Serve faithfully, and let God show the results in people.
exp.2:12:
It says that the work of each person in God's service will be brought to light. "The Day" refers to the day of Christ's judgment, and the fire is an image of testing: it shows what quality each work has. The phrase "will be revealed with fire" and the words "the fire will prove the quality of each man's work" describe the same testing from two angles: the fire exposes what each person has built and shows its true quality.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided over following different leaders. He reminds them that teachers are God's co-workers, and that Jesus Christ is the only foundation. Each person must take care how they build on him. Christians do not agree on the details of this judgment, but Paul affirms that the believer's salvation is not at stake, but rather their reward.

Today, before we serve, let us ask ourselves with what motives and with what faithfulness we do it. Let us seek what endures: love, truth, and obedience to Christ, rather than applause or fame.
exp.14:46:
The first man, Adam, was made from the dust of the earth, which is why he is of the earth. The second man is Christ, whom Paul calls "the Lord," and his origin is from heaven. There is a difference between what we inherit from Adam and what we receive in Christ.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. He explains that the raised body will be different from the present one, because just as we have been like Adam, we will be like Christ. The contrast between the two was shown in the phrases "living being" and "life-giving spirit": Adam received life, but Christ gives life.

For today: although we live in fragile bodies, our hope does not end in the earth. You can face tiredness, sickness, or loss with confidence, because Christ will bring us into his heavenly likeness.
exp.6:11:
Paul is speaking about a believer who is married to someone who does not believe. In his verse the word "unbelieving" describes the wife's faith, and the verb "divorce" describes leaving her. If the unbelieving wife is willing to keep living with him, the believer must not divorce her.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage. Earlier he had cited a clear teaching of Jesus about not divorcing. Here he says "I say this, not the Lord," because Jesus had not addressed this particular case: mixed marriages of faith. This does not mean his word lacks authority, but that he is giving apostolic guidance for this new situation.

If your spouse does not share your faith, do not take that as a reason to abandon the home. Serve with patience, love, and a good example, and trust that God can work in your family.
exp.13:7:
If the trumpet sounds a muffled call, no one knows whether to advance, retreat, or get ready. A call that cannot be clearly heard leaves the soldiers unsure what to do, so no one prepares for the battle. In ancient times, the trumpet gave signals to soldiers, and those signals had to be clear for them to act.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were proud of speaking in tongues during the meetings, yet no one understood what they were saying. Paul uses the example of the trumpet to show that a message no one can follow helps no one. His goal is for the church to be built up.
