For today: when we teach, pray together, or share the Word, let us speak with clarity and simplicity. What matters is not sounding impressive, but helping others understand and obey God.
exp.9:22:
It says that although there are many things that are permitted to me, not all of them are good or helpful to me. "Permissible" means allowed. "Beneficial" means that it is good for me, that it is the best course. "Edifying" means that it builds up, that it strengthens one's own faith and the faith of others.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who lived surrounded by temples and by meat offered to idols. Just before, he warned them not to become involved in the worship of demons. Here he clarifies that, in matters where there is freedom, it is not enough to ask whether something is allowed, but whether it helps others. Then he adds that no one should seek only his own good, but the good of his neighbor.

For today: before doing something that is permitted, such as a form of entertainment or a way of spending your time, ask yourself whether it draws you closer to God and whether it strengthens those around you.
exp.6:27:
Saying that marriage is not a sin, whether for a man or for an unmarried woman, is the main point of this verse. Paul makes clear, however, that those who marry will face troubles in this life, meaning the difficulties and pressures that come with everyday living. An unmarried young woman is the one he has in mind when he speaks of a "virgin," and "those who marry" refers to the people he is addressing. At the end, Paul says, "I want to spare you this," meaning that he wishes to spare them those hardships.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage. He speaks of a "present distress," probably a time of pressure or suffering, and reminds them that "the time is short." He does not condemn marriage; he offers pastoral advice with real care. Some interpreters debate exactly which crisis he had in mind.

For today: if you are married or are thinking about marriage, do not see it as a sin or as the solution to everything. Prepare for its difficulties, and put God first.
exp.15:12:
It says we should be on the alert, stand firm in the faith, be people of courage, and be strong. "Be on the alert" means to stay awake and watchful. "Be men of courage" means to act bravely and with maturity; it is not limited to men, but refers to brave conduct.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with divisions and problems. As he ends his letter, he gives several brief and direct instructions. After speaking of his plans and of co-workers like Timothy and Apollos, he encourages them to remain faithful. In the next verse he adds that everything should be done in love, so the courage he asks for is not separate from love.

Today, this invites us not to be carried away by distraction or by fear. You can choose one concrete decision this week, such as praying with persistence or speaking the truth with respect, and do it with firmness and love.
exp.11:22:
Paul says that the parts of the body that seem less valuable or less presentable are the ones we treat with the greatest care and respect. "Less valuable" describes the first group; the second refers to the parts we consider less honorable, or that we prefer not to show openly; and the third is the special modesty and care we give to them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided, and where some boasted of their spiritual gifts and looked down on others. He uses the image of the human body to show that all believers are necessary, and that God himself chose to give greater honor to those who seemed to have less.

Today we can notice the people who go unnoticed in the church, such as those who clean, care for children, or help quietly. Let us do something concrete this week: thank them personally and treat them with special respect.
exp.11:9:
This verse continues the list of gifts that the Spirit gives. "The working of miracles" refers to supernatural acts of power; "prophecy" is speaking a message on behalf of God; "distinguishing between spirits" is the ability to tell what comes from God and what does not; "speaking in various tongues" refers to different kinds of tongues or languages; and "the interpretation of tongues" is explaining what was said in them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride over spiritual gifts. He reminds them that all of these gifts come from the same Spirit, who distributes them as he wills. The gifts are not prizes but gifts for the good of the whole body of Christ.

For today: instead of comparing yourself with others or boasting about what you know how to do, ask God how you can serve with what he has given you, and give thanks for what others contribute to your community.
exp.5:11:
Everything is permitted to me, the verse says, but not everything is good for me or for others. "Permissible" means allowed, and "beneficial" means that something does good. It also says that I will not be mastered by anything, meaning I will not become a slave to something or fall under its control.

The apostle Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, a city with a great deal of moral freedom. Some believed that, since they had been forgiven, everything was allowed to them. Many interpret that Paul is quoting one of their slogans and correcting it. He reminds them that they were washed and made holy, and that their bodies belong to the Lord.

For today: before doing something that is not sinful in itself, ask yourself whether it helps you grow or whether, little by little, it masters you, like a phone, food, work or a habit. Use your freedom to serve God.
exp.14:40:
It says that the sun, the moon, and the stars do not shine alike. Each one has its own splendor, that is, its own beauty and brightness. Even among the stars there are differences: one does not shine like another. "Differs" here means that each star is distinct, with its own brightness.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. To explain it, he uses examples from creation: there are many kinds of bodies and many kinds of splendor. So the risen body will be different from the present one, but it will still be real. Some think it also suggests differences among believers in the resurrection, but the text does not say so clearly.

Today, you can trust that God is the creator of variety and power. If He gives each star its own brightness, He can also give you a new body. So do not compare yourself with others; live grateful for how God made you.
exp.11:0:
Paul begins a new topic: spiritual gifts. He says he does not want the brothers and sisters to be uninformed about this. The phrase "I do not want you to be uninformed" points to his wish that they understand the matter clearly. Gifts are abilities or favors that the Spirit gives.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, a church with many strengths, but also with disorder and divisions. Before, they had lived in paganism, and so they could confuse what comes from the Spirit with other religious experiences. Paul wants to give them clarity and a good foundation, beginning by affirming that Jesus is Lord.

Today, we should not leave the subject of gifts to chance or to trends. We can study the Bible with humility, ask what it says about the Spirit, and use what God gives us to serve and strengthen the church, not to boast.
exp.8:23:
Paul asks the Corinthians whether they realize that in a race, all the runners compete, but only one receives the prize. So he urges us to run with such effort and discipline that we reach the goal. The Berean Standard Bible wording, "Run in such a way as to take the prize," gives the same charge.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, a city where athletic games were well known. He had been explaining that he adapted himself to different people in order to bring them the gospel. He uses the image of the race to show that his life of service has a clear purpose and calls for total commitment.

For today: the Christian life is not meant to be improvised or lived halfway. Think of one area, such as prayer, Bible reading, or serving others, and decide on one concrete habit for this week. Practice it with steady consistency, trusting in the grace of God.
exp.6:20:
Paul tells the one who was called by God while a slave: don't be troubled by it. But if you have the chance to become free, take hold of it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about the Christian life. He teaches that social status does not determine a person's worth before God: the slave is the Lord's freed person, and the free person is a slave of Christ. Some scholars debate whether the final phrase means "take the opportunity" (seize your freedom) or "remain in your condition as it is"; most prefer the first reading.

For today: your work or difficult situation does not define your worth before God. Live with peace and faithfulness where you are, but if an honest door opens to improve your situation, dare to take it.
exp.3:16:
Paul says that for this reason he has sent Timothy to them. He calls Timothy his beloved child and faithful in the Lord. Timothy will remind them of Paul's way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what Paul teaches everywhere in every church.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a divided and proud church. He founded it and regards himself as their spiritual father. Since he has urged them to imitate him, he sends them Timothy, a living example of that way of life. Some had become puffed up, thinking Paul would not come back to them.

Today we need humble and faithful examples who show us how to live out the gospel. Seek out someone like this to learn from, and try to be a simple and faithful example to others yourself.
exp.9:27:
If someone tells you, "This food was offered to idols," do not eat it. You refrain out of consideration for the person who told you and for their conscience. Remember that the earth and everything in it belongs to the Lord.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city where a lot of meat was sold after being used in pagan temples. He had already said that eating in itself is not sin, because everything belongs to the Lord. Here he explains that if someone presents that food as something religious, eating it could seem like supporting idolatry. Some understand that the warning comes from a weak believer; others, from an unbeliever. The text does not specify.

Today, before using your freedom, think about how it affects others. If something confuses the faith of someone close to you, give it up out of love, without losing your trust in God.
exp.6:14:
If the unbelieving spouse decides to leave and end the marriage, the believer may let them go. "Unbeliever" here means someone who does not believe. A believing brother or sister is not bound to that marriage in such a case. God has called you to live in peace.

The apostle Paul is answering questions from the Corinthians about marriage. Earlier he asked that a believer not abandon an unbelieving spouse if that spouse wants to stay. Here he speaks of the opposite case: when it is the unbeliever who leaves. Christians interpret differently whether this also allows a new marriage; the text does not say so clearly.

For today: work to keep your marriage with love and patience, but if the other person decides to leave, do not carry a guilt that is not yours. Seek God's peace and the counsel of a pastor.
exp.9:11:
The explanation says that a person who thinks they are standing firm in their faith should be careful not to fall. The phrase "should be careful" means "pay attention" or "watch out." To stand firm is to feel strong and steady on the path with God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. He reminds them how the people of Israel, although they had received great blessings from God, fell into idolatry, immorality, and complaining. Those stories were written as a warning for the church. Some Corinthians believed their knowledge made them immune to danger.

For today: do not trust in your past spiritual strength. Recognize your weak points, seek counsel from mature brothers and sisters, stay close to prayer and the Word, and flee quickly from whatever makes you stumble. Humility keeps us standing.
exp.2:21:
The explanation says that everything God has placed in the lives of believers is for their good: teachers such as Paul, Apollos and Cephas (this is Peter), the world, life, death, the present and the future. "Belong to you" means "of you," and "the future" refers to things yet to come. It does not mean we can possess everything, but that nothing is foreign to us or can separate us from God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided because some followed Paul, others followed Apollos, and others followed Cephas. He tells them not to boast in human leaders. They are not owners of the church; they are servants who help the church. The following verse explains it: you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

For today: value teachers and pastors as gifts from God, without competing or taking sides. And if you face change, loss or fear, remember that you belong to Christ.
exp.12:7:
This verse says that love never fails. The word "love" here means generous, self-giving love, the kind that seeks the good of others. By contrast, prophecies, tongues (speaking in languages one has not learned), and knowledge will come to an end. Where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some boasted about their spiritual gifts and caused divisions. He shows them that those gifts are partial and temporary, and that love is more important. Christians interpret in different ways when the gifts cease: some say it will be when Christ returns, others think of an earlier moment.

For today: before seeking to stand out for what you know or do, ask yourself whether you are using it to love others. Today, listen patiently to someone or help them without expecting anything in return.
exp.14:51:
It says the change will happen suddenly, "in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye," at the last trumpet. Then the dead will be raised with a body that does not perish, and believers who are still alive will also be changed. "The last trumpet" is the final trumpet call. "Imperishable" describes what does not decay or break down.

The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection. He explains a "mystery," that is, a truth that God reveals. Our present body cannot enter the kingdom of God as it is, so it needs to be transformed. Christians understand in different ways when and how this will happen, but all agree that God will do it.

For today: if in Christ death does not have the final word, we can face sickness, grief, and fear with hope. Today you can comfort someone with this promise and live trusting in God.
exp.15:10:
Paul says that no one should treat Timothy with contempt. The phrase "treat with contempt" means to think little of him or fail to give him proper honor. Instead, the Corinthians should send him on his way "in peace," that is, with good treatment and without conflict, so that he can return to Paul. Paul is expecting him along with the brothers who are traveling with him.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth from Ephesus. He has just said that Timothy does the Lord's work just as he does. Timothy was young, and Paul does not explain why he asks for this care; some think he feared Timothy would be treated with contempt because of his age or his character, but that is an interpretation.

For today: value and support those who serve God, regardless of their age or experience. A word of encouragement or a concrete help can strengthen them greatly.
exp.9:25:
He says that the whole earth belongs to God, and also everything that fills it. The word "fullness" means everything that fills the earth: the earth and all that is in it belong to the Lord.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city where a lot of meat sold in the market had first been offered to idols. Some wondered whether eating it was a sin. Paul quotes Psalm 24:1 to say that food does not belong to idols but to God. So in the market one may eat freely, without anxiety. Later he adds that one should look after the conscience of a brother who may be offended.

For today: receive with gratitude what God gives you, without fear or unnecessary guilt, but use your freedom with love, thinking about how your decisions affect those around you.
exp.6:4:
The explanation says that spouses should not deprive one another in the intimacy of marriage. They may step away only for a brief time, if both agree, in order to devote themselves to prayer. Afterward they should come together again. "Deprive" here means to withhold what is owed to the other. A "lack of self-control" is the weakness Paul warns about, and "tempt" means to put to the test.

The apostle Paul is answering questions the Corinthians had written to him about marriage. In a city full of immorality, some thought the most spiritual choice was to abstain completely. Paul corrects that: in marriage, each belongs to the other with mutual respect.

For today: speak honestly and decide together about your intimacy and your spiritual life, caring for each other without imposing your will or using silence as punishment.
exp.3:8:
He says that God has placed the apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners condemned to die. "It seems to me" expresses his own view. "Last" means at the very back. A "spectacle" is something everyone stares at, like a show in a theater. The apostles are watched by the whole world, by angels, and by people.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who felt proud, rich, and superior. With some irony, he shows them that his life as an apostle is very different: he suffers, he is despised, and he lives in humility. He probably alludes to Roman parades, where condemned prisoners walked at the end, although this is a common interpretation, not something the text states.

Today, let us not measure the value of a Christian life by success, applause, or comfort. Serving Christ can cost, and humility matters more than fame.
exp.15:16:
Paul says he is glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived. Their coming made up for the distance between Paul and the Corinthians. What was missing from the Corinthians, these three supplied: they did what the church could not do from where it was, which was to be with him and encourage him.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus, at the end of a letter to a church with many problems. Earlier he asked the church to respect Stephanas and his household, who had devoted themselves to serving the believers. We do not know in detail what help these three gave, but the next verse says they refreshed his spirit.

For today: notice the people who serve quietly, like those who visit, help, or encourage others. Thank them with specific words, and look for a simple way to serve this week yourself.
exp.6:2:
The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and the wife should do the same for her husband. Here "marital duty" refers to the affection and intimacy that belong to marriage. It is something owed, a duty of love.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. In a city with much sexual immorality, he makes clear that marriage is good. What stands out is that he treats both spouses equally: the duty is mutual, not only from one toward the other.

For today: instead of demanding, seek to serve each other with tenderness and respect. Speak honestly about your needs, and care for the other as you would care for yourself.
exp.10:33:
If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home before going to the meeting. In this way, when the church comes together, the gathering does not result in judgment, that is, in correction from God. "The remaining matters" means the other questions Paul will settle when he arrives, and "when I come" means when he visits them in person.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. They celebrated the Lord's Supper within a common meal, and some ate and drank without waiting for the others, while others were left hungry. This shamed the poor and showed a lack of love. Paul corrects them so that the Supper becomes a time of unity.

For today: when we gather together as a church, let us think of others before ourselves. We can arrive with patience, share what we have, and make sure that no one feels left out.
exp.15:20:
Paul says that this closing greeting is in his own hand. Up to this point, another person had probably written the letter while Paul dictated it, and now he takes up the pen and writes these words himself.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth from Ephesus. In his time it was common to dictate letters to a secretary. Paul would add a few lines in his own handwriting, perhaps to give authenticity and a personal touch. The text says nothing more here, so we cannot be certain of all his reasons. What follows are serious words of love for Christ and of grace.

For today: put a personal touch into how you care for others. A sincere message, a phone call, or a handwritten note can show that you truly care, and that your affection is not just a routine habit.
exp.3:17:
Paul says that some in Corinth had become arrogant, full of pride and thinking themselves important. They acted as if Paul were never going to return, and so they believed they would not have to answer to him. The word "quickly" that appears later means "soon."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and boasted of its wisdom and of its favorite leaders. He had sent Timothy to remind them of how to live in Christ. Some felt secure while he was far away and spoke with arrogance. Paul warns them that he will come, if the Lord wills, and that he will not be concerned with their speeches, but with whether there is real power of God in their lives.

For today: live with humility, as if we were always standing before the Lord, whether or not anyone sees us. Let us ask ourselves whether our faith shows in our character and not only in our words.
exp.3:14:
What it says: Paul explains that the Corinthians may have countless guardians in Christ, but they do not have many fathers. Those who guide and look after children were the ones who cared for and directed them; to "become a father" through the gospel means that Paul was the one who brought them into the life of faith.

Context: Paul writes to the Corinthians after describing the sufferings of the apostles. He clarifies that he does not want to shame them, but to correct them with affection, as a father would. He founded that church, and that is why he speaks to them with such tenderness and authority. He will ask them to imitate him and will send Timothy to remind them of his way of life.

For today: Thank those who guided you in the faith, and let them correct you with love. If you teach others, do it with family affection, not with pride or a desire for control.
exp.13:13:
Paul says that if someone prays in a tongue, their spirit prays, but their mind is left without benefit. A tongue is a language that nobody understands without interpretation. "Unfruitful" means it produces no benefit, neither for the one who prays nor for those who listen.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued speaking in tongues very highly during the gatherings. He corrects them with affection: the gifts must serve to build up everyone. For this reason he asks that whoever speaks in a tongue also ask for the gift of interpreting it. Some understand that he is speaking of private prayer, others of public worship.

For today: when you pray or sing, try to keep your heart and your mind present. In church, look for what is said to help everyone understand and to say "Amen."
exp.4:10:
Paul is clarifying what he meant in his earlier letter. He is not asking them to pull away from every sinner in the world, but from someone who claims to be a "brother" in the faith and yet lives in serious sin without repentance. "Associate with" means not mixing with or keeping close company with that person. Someone who is "sexually immoral" lives in sexual sin; someone who is "greedy" is driven by a desire for more and more; a "verbal abuser" is someone who insults or tears others down with words. "Do not even eat with" means not sharing a meal with him.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a man living openly in immorality. He wants the church to guard its purity and to correct its own members. God judges those outside the church. Many understand that the purpose of this discipline was that the person would be moved to change and be restored.

For today: if a fellow believer lives in sin and refuses to change, love him enough to speak to him with humility and truth, praying for his restoration, and do not treat with contempt those who do not believe.
exp.4:8:
Paul reminds the Corinthians that he had already written them an earlier letter, which has not been preserved, telling them not to associate with sexually immoral people, that is, with those who live in sexual sin. Here "associate with" means having close, personal contact with them.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a serious case of sexual immorality among its members. He speaks of Passover and leaven to show that tolerated sin spreads like yeast through the dough. He makes clear right away that he was not referring to people of the world, but to someone who calls himself a brother and lives in sin without repentance.

For today: the church must guard its purity with love and firmness, without judging harshly those who do not believe, but without approving sin among believers, always seeking their restoration.
exp.10:3:
The explanation says that a man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, meaning he brings shame or disgrace on it. To pray is to speak to God in public; to prophesy is to speak on God's behalf to encourage or teach. To dishonor something means to bring shame or disgrace upon it. The word "head" can refer to the physical head and also to Christ, who was mentioned earlier. Scholars debate this.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its gatherings. He responds to customs about how people should present themselves when worshiping. It is not known with certainty what covering was meant (a veil, a shawl, or a hairstyle), nor what exact custom in Corinth he had in mind. That is why interpreters differ. What is clear is that Paul seeks order and honor to God.

For today: when you worship, take care that the way you present yourself and behave honors God and does not distract or offend others, according to your culture and with a humble heart.
exp.14:31:
Paul says that if the dead are not raised, all his suffering is worth nothing. The phrase about fighting wild beasts at Ephesus means that he faced an extremely hard struggle. The words "for human motives" mean "in a merely human way," or "with merely human strength." The saying "let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" expresses living only for the pleasure of the moment.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, some of whom denied the resurrection. We do not know whether the "wild beasts" were real animals or hostile people; many believe it is a figure of speech. The final saying sounds like a popular proverb that also appears in Isaiah 22:13. Paul shows that, without the resurrection, faith and sacrifice lose their meaning.

For today: the hope of the resurrection gives us strength to persevere and to live with purpose, not only for today's pleasure. Ask yourself what decision you could make this week with eternity in mind.
exp.0:14:
Paul says he is thankful that he baptized only a few people in Corinth, so that no one could say they were baptized into his name, that is, as followers of Paul. The phrase "so that no one can say" means "so that no one could claim."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had split into groups. Some said they followed Paul, others Apollos or Peter. He reminds them that only Christ died for them and that baptism does not tie them to a human leader. He does not look down on baptism; he wants to correct their pride and their divisions.

For today: value those who teach you, but do not place your identity in a pastor, a ministry, or a group. Your primary loyalty is to Christ. Seek unity with other believers instead of competing with or comparing yourself to them.
exp.13:26:
This verse says that if anyone speaks in a foreign tongue (another language or speech that the others do not understand) in the meeting, only two, or at the most three people should speak, one at a time, and someone must interpret what is said. "At most" means no more than, and "in turn" means one after another.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whose meetings were disorderly, with many people speaking at once. He does not forbid speaking in tongues, but he asks for order so that everything serves to build up everyone. Christians have understood in different ways what these tongues were exactly.

For today: when we take part in the church, let us seek what helps others understand and grow, and not only what expresses ourselves. Order and respect are also a way of loving.
exp.6:30:
Here Paul says that those who use the things of this world, such as money, work, and possessions, should do so as if they were not dependent on them. They are to enjoy and handle these things without clinging to them. The reason is that this world in its present form is passing away.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. He says that the time is short, and for that reason he invites them to live with inner freedom. Scholars debate whether he is speaking of a present difficulty or of the nearness of Christ's return. In either case, his desire is that they live without anxiety.

For today: enjoy what God gives you, but do not let your possessions, your work, or your worries take the place of God in your heart.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that what Paul has just explained is his defense before those who question him. The word "defense" refers to his explanation or answer. The phrase "to those who scrutinize me" refers to those who test or judge him, perhaps with doubts or criticism.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some were doubting his authority as an apostle. He responds by reminding them that he saw Jesus and that the church itself, the fruit of his work, is proof of his calling. Then, in the verses that follow, he will defend his right to receive support for his service, though later he will explain that he chose not to use it.

For today: when someone questions your faith or your service, respond with calm and with facts, not with anger. A life that bears fruit speaks better than words. And it is good to give explanations with humility, without losing the desire to serve others.
exp.14:29:
Paul asks: "And why do we endanger ourselves every hour?" The phrase "endanger ourselves" here means "run into danger" or "put ourselves at risk." He is speaking of himself and the other apostles, who were under constant threat for preaching the gospel.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom denied the resurrection of the dead. He answers with a practical argument: if there is no resurrection, there is no point in risking one's life every day for Christ. His suffering makes sense only if the hope of the resurrection is true. Regarding the baptism "for the dead" mentioned in the previous verse, there are several interpretations, and it is not known with certainty what practice he had in mind.

For today: our hope in the resurrection gives value to what it costs to follow Jesus. Today you can forgive, serve, or be honest even when it costs you, trusting that nothing done for the Lord is lost.
exp.0:26:
It says that God chose what the world considers foolish and weak in order to shame those who think they are wise and strong. The word "foolish" describes something that lacks sense or understanding, and "weak" describes something without strength; "to shame" means to expose human pride.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a divided community that boasted of its wisdom and importance. He reminds them that, when they look at who they themselves were, few were powerful or noble. His message is that the cross seems like madness to the world, yet God uses it to save. In this way, no one can boast before Him.

Today we can remember that our worth does not depend on titles, money, or success. If God calls you, do not become discouraged because you feel insignificant; let Him work through your weakness, and give Him the credit.
exp.14:23:
This verse says that after the resurrection the end will come. Then Christ will hand over the kingdom to God the Father, after he has destroyed every dominion, authority, and power that opposes God.

The words "dominion, authority, and power" refer to forces that hold power. Some believe they refer to spiritual powers, others to human powers, or to both.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection. He explains the order of events: Christ was raised first, then those who belong to him will be raised when he comes, and at the end Christ will present his complete victory to the Father. Paul wants to give them hope and assurance.

For today: even when you see injustice or powers that seem to be in charge, history is not outside God's control. You can live with peace and faithfulness, trusting that Christ reigns and will bring everything to its fulfillment.
exp.14:52:
It says that our present body, which wears out, gets sick, and dies, will be changed into one that is not damaged and does not die. The word "must" means that this change is necessary. "Perishable" refers to what spoils or decays, and "imperishable" and "immortal" describe what cannot be destroyed or die. The picture of being "clothed" suggests that we will receive something new, like someone putting on different clothing.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. In this chapter he reminds them that Christ rose and that believers will also be raised and transformed when He returns. This verse explains why that change is needed.

For today: if your body gets tired or sick, do not lose hope. Serve God with what you have today, trusting that He is preparing something better.
exp.1:6:
Paul says that the message he proclaims is the wisdom of God, which had been kept hidden, like a secret. Here "mystery" does not mean something strange, but something God planned from the beginning and is now making known. "Destined" means that God decided it beforehand. "Before time began" points to the time before the world existed. And he did it "for our glory": to bring his people to share in his honor.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who greatly admired clever speech and human wisdom. He reminds them that the message of Christ crucified does not come from philosophers or rulers, but from God. For that reason their faith must rest on the power of God.

Today we can stop looking for security only in what sounds clever or popular. Ask God to show you his truth in his Word, and trust that his plan for you began with love long before you understood it.
exp.14:1:
This verse says that the gospel Paul preached to them is the same gospel through which they are saved, with one condition: that they hold firmly to the message he preached to them. To "hold firmly" means to keep, to hold tightly onto. To believe "in vain" means without foundation or without result, that is, that their faith was never real from the beginning.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. For that reason he reminds them of the basic message they received: Christ died, was buried, and rose again. Christians have understood the phrase "if you hold firmly" in several ways: as a call to persevere, or as a sign that the faith is genuine.

Today we can often return to the essentials of the gospel, by reading the Bible and remembering what Christ has done for us, so that our faith does not grow weak with doubts or with passing trends.
exp.10:15:
He says that if anyone is inclined to argue about this, Paul and his companions have no other practice, and neither do the churches of God. "Inclined to dispute" describes someone who looks for a quarrel or enjoys arguing. "Practice" here refers to the custom accepted in the churches.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church with many divisions. He has just spoken about how men and women should present themselves when praying and prophesying in the congregation. Scholars disagree about which exact custom is meant, since it concerned either the veil or the hair according to the culture of that time. With this verse he closes the topic and appeals to the common practice of the churches.

For today: when differences arise over matters of custom, let us seek order and unity among brothers and sisters, without turning every issue into a fight.
exp.5:5:
One brother takes another brother to court, and he does it in front of unbelievers, that is, people who do not follow Christ.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a church marked by many divisions. He is troubled because their legal disputes were being carried into the courts of non-believers. He tells them this is shameful, since there should be someone among them wise enough to settle these matters. Scholars debate which specific cases he had in mind, but the rebuke is clear.

For today: if you have a conflict with another believer, try first to resolve it with humility, through honest conversation, and with the help of mature leaders in the church. Take care that your witness is not harmed in front of those who do not believe.
exp.0:10:
Paul says that someone told him how the Corinthians are doing. "I have been informed" is the plain way to say it. The people who told him were from Chloe's household, probably members of her family or her group. The news is that there are quarrels among them, meaning fights and arguments among themselves.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and addresses them as "my brothers." He has just asked them to live united and to agree with one another. Now he explains why he says this: it is not a guess, but something he was told. About Chloe we know only this name; it is not known for certain who she was or where she lived. The following verses show that they were splitting into groups according to their favorite leaders.

When we see divisions in the church or in the family, it is good to speak with humility and clarity, as Paul did, and without gossip. Let us make sure that Christ, and not our own preferences, is the center of the unity.
exp.14:53:
This verse says that when God clothes our perishable, mortal bodies with a body that can never decay or die, the words of Scripture will come true: death is swallowed up and completely overcome, and the victory belongs to God. "Clothed with" is a picture: the perishable is dressed in the imperishable, like putting on new clothing.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. In this chapter he explains that Christ rose and that believers will also rise. Here he quotes the prophet Isaiah (25:8), and in the next verse he mocks death, which no longer has the last word.

For today: if you have lost someone dear or fear death, you can hold on to this hope. Pray with confidence and live without fear, serving God and others, because your labor in the Lord is not in vain.
exp.0:0:
Paul presents himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus, that is, a messenger sent with authority to carry his message. He says he was "called," meaning chosen, and that this happened "by the will of God," not by his own merit. He also mentions Sosthenes, whom he calls "our brother."

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth, a large and very diverse city. The verses that follow show that this is the opening greeting. Exactly who this Sosthenes was is not known for certain; some connect him with a man mentioned in Acts 18:17, but the Bible does not confirm this. Paul begins by affirming his authority before correcting several problems in the church.

God continues to call ordinary people to serve him, and this does not depend on our being perfect. We can serve with humility, remembering that our place comes from his will and grace. Furthermore, it is good to serve alongside other brothers and sisters, as Paul did.
exp.1:8:
It says that God has prepared things so great for those who love him that no one could see them, hear them, or imagine them by their own means. The word for "hear" here refers to taking in sound, and the phrase about what "no heart has imagined" means what the mind or imagination could never come up with alone. The word "rather" at the start of the sentence is the one that carries the contrast.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who boasted in human wisdom. He reminds them that the rulers of this world did not understand God's plan, and that is why they crucified Jesus. Paul introduces the quotation with the words "as it is written," probably drawing on Isaiah 64:4 and 65:17, though the quotation is not exact. In the verse that follows, he explains that God reveals these things through his Spirit.

For today: do not be content to measure your future only by what you see or understand. Ask the Spirit to teach you, and trust that God keeps something good for those who love him.
exp.8:13:
In the same way, the Lord has arranged that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel. In other words, they have the right to receive support from those who receive their teaching. The word "prescribed" means that he set it up this way.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and defends his right as an apostle to be supported. He gives examples from the priests of the temple, who ate from what was offered there. However, Paul makes clear that he did not use that right, so as not to put obstacles in the way of the gospel. Many understand that his words are similar to what Jesus said in Luke 10:7.

Today we can support with generosity and gratitude those who teach us the Word, and they can serve with humility, without seeking gain.
exp.14:30:
Paul says that he faces death every day. He states this strongly, and he speaks of the boasting he does about the believers in Corinth, who are the fruit of his work in Christ Jesus. "Brothers" is the way he addresses them, and his pride in them is real. He is not speaking of literally dying each day, but of living always exposed to danger and giving himself completely.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some of them denied the resurrection of the dead. He argues that if there is no resurrection, his daily sufferings for the gospel would make no sense. His risky life is proof that he truly believes in the hope of rising again.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith costs us anything. If we hope in the resurrection, we can serve, forgive, and obey God even when it costs us comfort, time, or reputation.
exp.0:25:
Paul asks the believers in Corinth to think about who they were when God called them. "Calling" here means God's call. He reminds them that not many of them were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, and not many were of noble birth.

Paul writes to a church that is divided and proud of its wisdom and of its favorite leaders. He has just said that the cross seems foolish to the world, but it is the power of God. Now he uses the Corinthians themselves as an example: God works through ordinary people. He does not say that none of them were wise or noble, but "not many."

For today: if you ever feel like you are of little worth, remember that your value does not depend on your education, your money, or your family name. God called you by his grace. Serve with humility and do not boast of what you have, because everything comes from him.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that God knows exactly what the people considered wise are thinking, and that their thoughts are "futile," meaning empty and without lasting value. "Again" shows that Paul is quoting Scripture once more, here Psalm 94:11.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were divided and boasted of following human leaders, such as Paul, Apollos, or Cephas. They valued eloquence and worldly wisdom greatly. Paul reminds them that before God this wisdom is not what matters most, and so he concludes: let no one boast in men.

Today we can examine what we take pride in: our studies, intelligence, opinions, or the leaders we admire. It is wise to learn with humility, to ask God for wisdom, and not to think ourselves superior to others or to use knowledge to divide.
exp.8:18:
Paul says that he is free and not bound to anyone, yet he chose to make himself a slave to everyone. His goal was to win as many people as possible to Christ. The word "slave" here means someone who serves others completely, and "win" means to bring people to believe the gospel.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. In this chapter he explains that, as an apostle, he had the right to receive financial support for his work, but he did not insist on it. He preferred to preach without charge so that nothing would get in the way of the gospel. By giving up his rights, he gives them an example to follow.

Today we can ask ourselves what rights or comforts we are willing to set aside out of love for others. Perhaps it is listening patiently to someone different from us, or serving without expecting recognition, so that others may see the love of Christ in our lives.
exp.3:3:
Paul says that, even though his conscience does not accuse him of anything, that does not prove he is right before God. The word "vindicate" here means shown to be in the right. In the end, the one who examines him and decides is the Lord, not Paul himself or other people.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which is divided by favoring some leaders over others. Some were criticizing Paul and Apollos. He reminds them that God's servants must be faithful, and that the final judgment belongs to the Lord, who knows even what is hidden in the heart.

For today: having a clear conscience is good, but it is not the last word. We can ask God to examine our heart, and avoid judging others harshly, trusting that He judges with perfect truth and also knows how to recognize what is good.
exp.8:19:
Paul says that he adapted himself to the Jews, living as a Jew, in order to win them to Christ. He also adapted himself to those who were "under the law," that is, those who tried to keep the law of Moses, even though he himself was not under that law. "Win" here means leading them to believe in Jesus.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. He has just explained that he gave up his rights, such as receiving payment for preaching, so as not to hinder the gospel. He made himself a servant to all out of love for people. He did not change the message, but his manner of approaching people, showing respect for the customs of each group.

For today: before speaking about Jesus, try to understand and respect the culture and history of the other person. You can yield on tastes and customs, without compromising the truth of the gospel.
exp.10:12:
Paul asks the Corinthians to judge for themselves: is it proper for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered? The word "proper" here does not mean sincere; it means what is right, worthy, and suitable. The "covering" refers to some kind of veil or covering on the head.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth to correct problems in their gatherings. He has just said that man and woman depend on one another in the Lord, and that everything comes from God. Scholars discuss what the custom of that city exactly was and how it should be applied today, so it is wise to be humble when interpreting it.

For today: when we worship, let us seek to have our conduct honor God and not cause stumbling to others, taking care with order, respect, and cultural sensitivity, without losing unity among brothers and sisters.
exp.13:0:
Earnestly pursue love, as someone chasing after something of great importance would. Eagerly desire the spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy, which here means speaking words from God that help others.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings had become disorderly. Some were showing off by speaking in tongues when no one could understand them. Following chapter 13, on love, Paul joins the two themes: the gifts must be used with love and for the benefit of everyone.

For today: before you serve or speak in your church, ask yourself whether what you are doing will help others understand, grow, and receive encouragement. Seek love first, and then use your gifts to strengthen others, not to draw attention to yourself.
exp.1:14:
The spiritual person, guided by God's Spirit, is able to judge the worth of all things. Yet no one without the Spirit can rightly examine that person.

Context: Paul writes to the Corinthians, who boasted of human wisdom and were divided. He explains to them that God's truths are understood only through the Spirit. The "natural man" is the one who depends only on his natural reasoning. Paul is not speaking of personal superiority, but of the mind of Christ that God gives to believers.

For today: Before deciding something important, ask the Spirit to guide you through the Bible and prayer. And if others do not understand your convictions of faith, respond with humility and not with pride.
exp.2:5:
Paul says that he planted the seed of the gospel in Corinth, and that Apollos watered it, meaning he continued caring for and teaching the believers. But it is God who actually makes the plant grow. "God made it grow" means that God is and continues to be the one who gives life and fruit.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided. Some said "I am with Paul" and others "I am with Apollos." Paul calls them "fleshly" because they fought over human leaders. He reminds them that he and Apollos are only servants through whom they came to believe, each with the task the Lord gave him.

For today: serve faithfully in what God has entrusted to you, without comparing yourself or boasting. And if you see fruit in others, do not fight over who deserves the credit. Thank God, because it is He who makes things grow.
exp.13:24:
When someone who does not believe comes into the meeting and hears God's word clearly, the secrets of his heart are brought into the open. Then he humbles himself, falls facedown, worships God, and declares that God is truly among the believers. "Falling facedown" means bowing to the ground. The one who does not believe is the outsider who has not yet come to faith, and the people who do not know these things are the ones who lack understanding.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly and many spoke in tongues with no one understanding them. He wants everything to serve the building up of others. He sets tongues spoken without interpretation, which confuse visitors, against prophecy, which is understood and reaches the heart.

For today: when we gather, let us aim to speak and serve in a way that everyone can understand. Let our words be clear, sincere, and full of the truth of God, so that whoever visits us may encounter Him.
exp.10:13:
Paul asks whether nature itself does not teach you that it is a disgrace for a man to have long hair. The word "disgrace" here refers to something unbecoming or dishonorable, not to lying or deceit. The verse describes a man letting his hair grow long.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, whose gatherings had become disorderly. He is speaking about how men and women should present themselves when praying and prophesying. He appeals to what they considered proper in their culture. Scholars debate exactly what "nature" means here: some think of the created order, others of social custom. There is also discussion about what long hair meant in that period.

For today: take care that the way you present yourself at church reflects respect for God and love for others, without making customs a cause for quarrel. What matters most is reverence and peace.
exp.13:1:
This verse says that the one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to people but to God, because no one understands him. Although in the Spirit he utters mysteries, meaning hidden things that God reveals, the listeners do not grasp what is being said.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some valued speaking in tongues very highly and used it in the meetings without anyone understanding. He does not forbid it, but he teaches them that in the congregation what matters most is what helps everyone, such as prophecy, which builds up, encourages, and comforts. Some scholars think these are real languages and others think it is a language of prayer; the text does not fully clarify this.

For today: when you serve in the church, ask yourself whether what you do or say helps others understand and grow in faith, because love seeks the good of others.
exp.10:5:
If a woman does not cover her head, she should have her hair cut off. And if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut or shaved off, she should cover her head.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorder in its gatherings. He speaks of a custom of that time about how men and women presented themselves when praying and prophesying. Scholars discuss exactly what the covering was (a veil or hair arranged a certain way) and how much of this was cultural. Paul uses the argument to defend order and respect.

For today: when we worship, let us take care that our manner and our appearance honor God and do not cause stumbling or division, always seeking love and order among brothers and sisters.
exp.12:11:
Today we see only a dim reflection, as in a mirror, but one day we will see face to face, that is, directly. Today we know only in part; then we will know fully, just as we are fully known by God. A "dim reflection" is an image that is unclear, and "love" is what this passage places above all else.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and boasted about its spiritual gifts. He reminds them that those gifts are partial and temporary, while love is what endures. Ancient mirrors were usually polished metal, and they gave an imperfect image. Interpreters debate when the complete state arrives, though many see it in the return of Christ.

For today: accept with humility that you do not understand everything. Faced with what you do not comprehend, trust God and treat others with love, instead of arguing as if you knew it all.
exp.6:17:
Paul asks whether a man was already circumcised when he was called by God. That would describe a Jew. In that case, Paul says, he should not try to undo his circumcision or hide it. He also asks whether a man was still uncircumcised when called, which would describe a Gentile. Such a man should not get circumcised. Paul's point is that a person should stay as he was when God called him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. Earlier in the chapter he has said that each person should live as the Lord assigned to him and called him. For Paul, being a Jew or a Gentile does not make anyone better before God. What matters is obeying God, as he says right after this verse.

For today: you do not need to change your background, your culture, or your situation to be valued before God. Serve the Lord faithfully where you are, and ask Him for wisdom if He opens another path for you.
exp.7:8:
Be careful, he says: your freedom must not become a stumbling block to those who are weak, that is, those weak in faith or in conscience. The word "careful" means to watch out and take care, a stumbling block is something that causes a person to fall, and the weak are believers whose conscience is easily troubled.

The apostle Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some were debating whether it was right to eat meat that had been offered to idols. Those who had knowledge understood that idols are nothing and ate without guilt. But others, who had formerly worshiped idols, felt defiled when they saw this. Paul asks that knowledge be used with love.

Today, even if something is not a sin for you, ask yourself whether it could hurt or confuse a weaker brother. Sometimes love means willingly giving up a right in order to protect another person's faith.
exp.5:14:
Paul asks whether they do not know that their bodies are members of Christ. Then he asks whether anyone would take what belongs to Christ and unite it with a prostitute. His answer is "Never!"

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city with a great deal of sexual immorality. Some people thought the body did not matter, because it would one day be gone, like food. Paul answers that the body does matter: it belongs to the Lord, and God will raise it, just as he raised Jesus.

For today: our body is not only our own, it belongs to Christ. Before deciding what to do with your body, your time, or your relationships, ask yourself: "Does this honor Christ, to whom I belong?"
exp.4:9:
What it says: Paul clarifies an earlier instruction. When he told them not to associate with the sexually immoral, he did not mean all the sexually immoral, the greedy, the swindlers, or the idolaters of this world. Those who practice sexual sin are the sexually immoral, and the greedy are those who want what belongs to others. Avoiding all such people would be impossible without leaving this world altogether.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a man living in serious sexual sin. They had misunderstood an earlier letter. Paul clarifies that his concern is the conduct of those who call themselves brothers, not that of unbelievers.

For today: We can treat neighbors and coworkers who do not believe with kindness, without isolating ourselves, and at the same time humbly guard purity and integrity within the church.
exp.7:1:
Paul says that the person who thinks he already knows something does not yet know as he ought to know. The phrase "thinks he knows" refers to assuming or believing oneself to be very wise. "Knowing" here means real understanding. True wisdom includes humility and the recognition that there is always more to learn.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some were debating whether it was right to eat meat that had been offered to idols. Those who considered themselves more knowledgeable looked down on the brothers and sisters whose conscience was weak. Paul reminds them that knowledge without love becomes pride, and that love is what builds others up.

For today: before correcting or arguing with someone about matters of faith, ask yourself whether you are doing it with humility and love. Knowing a great deal about the Bible is not enough if I treat others badly. Ask God that your knowledge may lead you to serve, not to boast.
exp.10:24:
It says that Jesus, after supper, took the cup and explained that this cup is the new covenant, that is, a new agreement between God and his people, sealed with his blood. He told his followers to keep doing this in remembrance of him, as often as they drink it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the Lord's Supper was being celebrated with disorder and selfishness. He reminds them of what he himself received and taught: what Jesus did the night he was betrayed. Christians understand in different ways how Christ is present in the Supper, but all agree that it remembers his sacrifice.

For today: when you take part in the Supper, do so with calm and gratitude, remembering that Christ gave his life for you. Beforehand, examine your heart and seek to be reconciled with anyone you have an unresolved offense against.
exp.15:3:
Paul says that if the offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem is advisable enough to be worthwhile, he will also go, and the men the church chooses can travel with him. Here "business" means a matter or assignment, not a commercial deal. "Worthy" means that it is fitting for it to be done.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and gives them instructions for the collection for Jerusalem. He had already asked them to set money aside each week. Here he leaves open the possibility of accompanying the delivery, without requiring it. Some think the amount collected would influence his decision, but the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when we handle church money or help for others, let us do it with order, with several responsible people involved, and with complete transparency, so that no one doubts our integrity.
exp.6:22:
You were bought at a price, so God has paid for you and made you his own. For that reason, do not let yourself become a slave to other people's opinions, fear, or demands. The word "slaves" here means people who are owned and controlled by others. The "price" points to what Christ did on the cross to set us free.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about how to live their faith in everyday life. Earlier he spoke about slaves: if they could become free, that was better, but their worth did not depend on their social standing. Some scholars believe he also warns against submitting to human pressures that pull people away from Christ.

For today: before deciding something, ask yourself whom you want to please. Seek to live for God with freedom, and not to be controlled by what others will say.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that when the church gathered for the meal, each person went ahead and ate his own food without sharing with the others. The result was unfair: some went hungry while others ate and drank so much that they became drunk. The "meal" here is the supper that went along with the Lord's Supper.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to correct divisions among them. The poorer members, who had less, were humiliated in front of those who had more. That is why Paul says that in this way they are not really eating the Lord's Supper, since they were forgetting the love and unity that it represents.

For today: before taking part in communion or in any gathering of the church, let us consider whether we are waiting for, caring for, and looking after our brothers and sisters who are in greatest need, instead of seeking only our own.
exp.2:20:
It says that no one should boast or take pride in following certain human leaders. The reason is that "all things are yours": believers do not belong to a leader, but the leaders and God's gifts are at the service of believers. The phrase "stop boasting in men" means to boast or to put one's trust in something.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided: some said they followed Paul, others Apollos, others Cephas (Peter). Earlier he had reminded them that human wisdom has no value before God. So he corrects them: the teachers are servants, not masters or rival teams. The verses that follow explain that all things belong to the believers, but they belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

Today we can thank the pastors and teachers who help us, without competing or boasting about whom we follow. If something in the church divides us over preferences for leaders, let us remember that our identity is in Christ.
exp.15:8:
Paul says that in Ephesus a great opportunity for effective work has opened up to him, a chance to preach the gospel with real results. But he also says that many oppose him. "Effective" here means that the work bears fruit and accomplishes something.

Paul writes this letter to the Corinthians from Ephesus. He explains why he will stay there until Pentecost: the work is moving forward, though there is opposition. He also tells them about his plans to visit them at a more relaxed pace, "if the Lord permits." Commentators see in this his humility before the plans of God.

For today: a good opportunity does not always come without difficulties. If God opens a door for you to serve, do not be discouraged by opposition. Pray, ask for wisdom, and continue with patience and love.
exp.8:12:
The explanation says that those who work in the temple eat of its food, and that those who serve at the altar share in its offerings. The verse describes this when it speaks of people who eat from the temple's food and take a portion of what is offered on the altar.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and defends his right to receive support from them for preaching the gospel. He relies on the example of the Jewish priests, who ate from the offerings made in the temple. However, he makes clear that he did not use that right, so that no one would think he preached for money and the gospel would not meet any obstacles.

For today: let us support generously those who serve full time in the church, and, if we serve, let us do so with a heart free from financial ambition.
exp.15:21:
If anyone does not love the Lord, the verse says, that person is under a curse, meaning cut off from God. The word for curse here refers to something set apart for judgment.

Paul writes this in his own hand, at the end of his letter to the Corinthians, a church marked by divisions, pride and disorder. Before saying goodbye, he reminds them of what matters most: love for the Lord.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our love for Jesus is real and not merely religious. That love shows itself in obeying him, in treating others well, and in living with hope, praying, "Come, Lord."
exp.1:4:
This verse says that Paul preached in a plain way so that the faith of the Corinthians would not depend on people's intelligence or arguments, but on God's power. The phrase "rest on" means to be built upon a foundation. "Men's wisdom" is human reasoning.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city where fine speaking and philosophy were greatly admired. There were divisions and pride among them. He recalls that he came to them weak and fearful, without brilliant speeches, but with the work of the Spirit. He then makes clear that there is indeed a wisdom of God, which is not of this world.

For today: examine what your faith rests on. Appreciate what you are taught, but trust in what God does, not in a preacher's talent or in your own arguments. Pray, asking that the Spirit sustain you.
exp.8:25:
Paul says that he runs with a clear purpose, knowing where he is going, and not like someone who runs without a goal. He also says that he fights with purpose, and not like someone who swings wildly without ever landing a blow. In plain terms, "running aimlessly" means running with no direction or defined goal, and "fighting like one beating the air" means swinging without ever hitting a target.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city that knew the athletic games well. He uses the image of the athlete to speak of discipline and of his commitment to the gospel. Shortly before, he explained that he gives up certain rights in order to win others. Then he adds that he keeps his body under control so that he does not disqualify himself after preaching to others.

For today: define what matters most in your life with God, such as prayer, serving, or growing in his Word, and practice it with consistency, not only when you feel like it.
exp.3:5:
Paul says that he has used his own case and that of Apollos as an example, for the good of the Corinthians. He wants them to learn from them not to go beyond what is written, and so that none of them will take pride in one man over another.

Paul writes to a divided church, where some were boasting that they followed Paul, Apollos, or others. Earlier he has said that only the Lord judges truly. Here he shows them that not even the apostles are grounds for pride, since they are servants.

Some understand "what is written" as the Scriptures in general; others understand it as earlier quotations from the letter itself.

Today: before you praise or criticize a pastor or teacher, ask yourself whether what you are saying rests on the Bible. Avoid competing between leaders, and remember that everything good comes from God.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that those who are entrusted with something that does not belong to them are asked for one thing only: that they be found faithful. "Stewards" are managers or caretakers, people who look after and distribute another's goods. "Is required" means "is demanded" or "is expected." "Found faithful" means that, when their work is examined, it proves trustworthy.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were dividing into groups and comparing their leaders. He presents himself, together with the other apostles, as a servant of Christ and a steward of the "mysteries of God," that is, the truths of the gospel. For this reason he says that the judgment of people matters less; the one who truly evaluates is the Lord.

For today: whatever you have, whether time, gifts, or responsibilities, is a charge from God. Seek to carry it out with honesty and perseverance, without looking for applause, trusting that He sees everything.
exp.1:15:
It says that no one can know the thoughts of the Lord well enough to instruct Him. But believers, through the Spirit, have "the mind of Christ," that is, a way of thinking and understanding that comes from Him. The question "who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct Him?" is meant to make the point: no one. It echoes Isaiah 40:13.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who boasted of human wisdom and divided themselves into groups. He explains that God's true wisdom is understood through the Spirit, not through intellectual pride. The "natural man" refers to a person who is guided only by what is natural, without the Spirit. Paul does not say that believers know everything, but that God has given them understanding.

For today: before deciding or arguing, ask God for His guidance and see how Jesus thought and acted. Study the Gospels with humility, willing for Him to correct your way of thinking.
exp.5:3:
Paul says that if believers have disputes about everyday matters, the things of this present life, they should ask people from the church to settle them. The phrase "those of no standing in the church" is understood in two ways: some think Paul speaks with irony, as if to say, "not even the most ordinary people in the church would do so poor a job," while others believe it refers to those whom the world does not value.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were taking one another to pagan courts. He tells them this is shameful, because if they will one day take part in judging the world, how can they fail to settle small matters among themselves?

Today, before going to court against another believer, seek the counsel of leaders or mature brothers and sisters in your church who can help you reconcile with humility and truth.
exp.6:32:
The explanation says that the married man is concerned with the affairs of this world, such as the home, work, and providing for the family, and looks for how he can please his wife. "But" means "but," and "concerned" means that he takes thought for these things. "This world" here is not something bad, but the normal affairs of this life.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage. He believes that the times are difficult and short, and he wants them to live without anxiety. He does not say that marriage is sinful, but that the married person has more responsibilities to attend to. He himself makes clear that he does not want to put a snare on them, but to help them serve the Lord without distractions.

For today: whatever your situation, review how you divide your time and your attention. Care for your family with love, but set aside space each day to be with God.
exp.11:10:
This verse says that all the gifts mentioned earlier (faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, tongues, and others) come from one and the same Spirit. He apportions them to each believer personally, as he determines. Where the verse says "who apportions them to each one," the Spirit gives to each person individually, according to his own decision.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over spiritual gifts. Some felt superior to others. Paul reminds them that every gift has the same source, the Spirit, and that the church is like a body with many members, each one necessary.

For today: instead of comparing yourself with others or envying their gifts, be thankful for the gift God has given you and use it to serve others, knowing that your place in the church is important.
exp.11:19:
The explanation says that, as things stand, the church has many parts, yet all of them together make up one body. The wording is handled as follows: the phrase "as it is" refers to the present reality, and the word "but" marks the contrast between many parts and one body. In other words: there is variety, and at the same time there is unity.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a church marked by divisions and by people who boasted of their spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the human body to show that God himself distributed the gifts and the place of each person. No one is unnecessary, and no one is worth more than another.

Today, instead of comparing yourself to others, thank God for the place he has given you and serve with your gift. Value also those who are different from you, because the church needs them just as it needs you.
exp.5:8:
This verse asks whether believers do not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God. Paul warns them not to be deceived, and gives a list of wicked behaviors: sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, and men who submit to or perform homosexual acts. The phrase "the sexually immoral" refers to those who engage in sexual behavior outside the boundaries God has set. The word "inherit" here means to receive as one's own.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had lawsuits between brothers and sisters and cheated one another. He reminds them that injustice is a serious matter. But he immediately tells them that some of them used to be like this, and that God washed, sanctified, and justified them through Jesus.

For today: do not use grace as an excuse to remain in what God calls wicked. Examine your life with humility, leave behind what distances you from God, and trust that his forgiveness and his Spirit give you a new beginning.
exp.6:36:
The explanation says that the man who has firmly settled in his heart, free from pressure and with full control over his will, who has resolved in his heart not to marry the young woman, does well. The sense of the word rendered "constraint" is pressure or urgency, and not marrying her is what the phrase "not to marry" means here. Some scholars believe the passage speaks of a man and his fiancée rather than a father; the text allows both readings.

Paul is answering the Corinthians about marriage and the single life. He advises them with their good in mind, not to lay a burden on them, but so that they may serve the Lord without distraction. He recognizes that marrying is not sin and that each person must decide with freedom.

Today we can make important decisions, such as marrying or remaining single, with calm, prayer and personal conviction, without yielding to family or social pressure, and always seeking to serve the Lord better.
exp.14:3:
The explanation says that Jesus was placed in a tomb and that God raised him from the dead on the third day. The references to "that he was buried" and "that he was raised" describe these two events directly, so no word needs special comment here. The phrase "according to the Scriptures" means that this agreed with what the sacred writings of the Old Testament had already announced.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. For that reason he reminds them of the essentials of the gospel that he himself received and taught them: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised. He then mentions witnesses who saw him alive, many of whom were still living at that time.

For today: our hope does not rest on an idea, but on a fact. If Christ was raised, we can face pain, failure, and even death with confidence. Today, thank God for that victory and place your fears back in his hands.
exp.13:9:
This verse says that there are many different languages in the world, and that none of them is without meaning. The phrase "different languages" is the wording your Bible uses, and it points to the many tongues people speak. The idea behind "without meaning" is that every language exists so that someone can make themselves understood to others.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where many spoke in tongues during the gatherings without anyone understanding them. He uses the example of the trumpet and of languages to show that a sound that is not understood helps no one. His goal is that the congregation be built up.

For today: before you speak or share something at church, at home, or at work, ask yourself whether the people around you are really understanding you. Use clear and simple words, because loving your neighbor also means making yourself understood.
exp.15:14:
Paul makes a request of the brothers in Corinth. He reminds them that Stephanas and his household were among the first to believe in Christ in Achaia (the region of Greece where Corinth was located). The word "firstfruits" refers to the first part of the harvest. He also says that they have devoted themselves completely to serving the believers, whom he calls "saints," that is, the people of God.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus to correct and encourage a church with divisions. The appeal in this verse is completed in the next one: that the readers respect and follow the example of those who serve with diligence. Paul does not say that Stephanas held an official office; he emphasizes his voluntary devotion.

For today: notice the people in your church who serve quietly, and thank them. Better still, be willing to serve alongside them.
exp.14:2:
Paul says that the first and most important thing he taught the Corinthians was what he himself had received: that Christ died for our sins, according to the Scriptures. The phrase "as of first importance" in the verse can be understood as "in the first place" or "as the most important thing."

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. To answer them, he reminds them of the basic gospel they had already received. Here he passes on a summary of the Christian faith that had been circulating since the earliest days. Scholars believe the "Scriptures" refer to the writings of the Old Testament, although he does not point to one exact passage.

For today: when your faith feels confused or weighed down by debates, return to what is essential. Christ died for your sins, and that is good news to receive with gratitude and to share with simplicity.
exp.7:4:
