Paul says that even if many people call various things "so-called gods," whether in heaven or on earth, and even if there are many such "gods" and "lords" according to what people believe, that does not change the truth. Food is what is eaten, and "knowledge" means understanding.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city full of temples. They were asking whether they could eat meat that had been offered to idols. Paul recognizes that idols are nothing compared to the one God, but then he asks for care toward brothers and sisters with a weak conscience. Some understand "so-called gods" as false spiritual powers; the text does not fully explain this.

Today there are many things that people worship: money, fame, pleasure. We can live without fear of them because only God is God, but also with love and respect for those who are still struggling in their faith.
exp.9:29:
If I eat with thankfulness, why am I denounced for the very thing I give thanks for? Paul asks this: if I take part in a meal and give thanks to God for it, why would someone condemn me for something I receive with gratitude? "Partake" here means I eat or take part in the meal. "Denounced" means criticized or spoken against, not necessarily insults aimed at God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians about meat that had been offered to idols. He teaches that, in itself, the food is good, because the earth belongs to the Lord. But he also asks us to care for the conscience of others. This question defends his freedom, although some believe it is a rhetorical question that he himself answers later: everything must be done for the glory of God.

For today: before using your freedom, ask yourself whether it gives thanks to God and whether it helps or confuses the one who watches you. Sometimes love means giving way.
exp.5:9:
This verse continues a list of unjust behaviors. It says that those who live in theft, greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse, or swindling will not inherit the kingdom of God. "Verbal abusers" are those who speak with insults and slander. "Thieves" are those who steal by force or take advantage of others. "The greedy" are those who always want more, without caring about the harm done to others.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, who had lawsuits and cheated one another among brothers and sisters. He warns them that a life of injustice contradicts the kingdom of God. But right away he reminds them that some of them had been like that, and that they had already been washed, made holy, and made righteous in Jesus. He does not speak to condemn without hope, but to call them to change.

Today we can examine our words, our money, and how we treat others. If there is something unjust in us, let us ask forgiveness, make right the harm done, and trust that Christ gives the power to change.
exp.4:7:
It says that the Christian life is like a continuous celebration, but not with the old bread, which here represents sin, malice (ill intent), and wickedness. We should celebrate it with unleavened bread, that is, bread without yeast, which symbolizes sincerity (a heart without duplicity) and truth. The celebration refers to living thankful for what Christ has done.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which tolerated a serious case of immorality and even boasted about it. He uses the image of the Jewish Passover, when all leaven was removed from the house. Since Christ is our Passover, sacrificed for us, Paul calls them to clear out what harms the whole community.

Today, we can ask ourselves: is there some hidden sin or false attitude that I am letting grow? Ask God for help to live with honesty, to recognize it and to change, grateful for the forgiveness of Christ.
exp.5:16:
It says that whoever unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit. The word "but" introduces the contrast with what came before. To "unite" with someone means to be bound closely to them. It is a real and deep union with Christ, through faith, that reaches the innermost part of the person.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, a city where sexual immorality was common. He has just said that joining oneself to a prostitute makes the two "one body." Now he contrasts this: the believer already belongs to Christ and is united with Him. For that reason he cannot take his body and give it over to something else as if it were his own.

For today: before deciding how to use your body, your time, or your relationships, remember that you are united with Christ. Ask yourself: "Does this honor the One with whom I am united?"
exp.2:7:
The explanation says that the one who plants and the one who waters are one in purpose and do not compete. Even so, God does not overlook anyone's effort: each one will be rewarded according to his labor. The phrase "according to his own labor" means "in keeping with the work he has done." A "reward" is the payment or prize that God gives.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were divided and gathered around leaders, some saying "I am of Paul" and others "I am of Apollos." Paul reminds them that he planted, Apollos watered, but only God makes things grow. Both are servants, not stars.

Today, serve in your church with humility, without comparing yourself or competing. Rejoice in what others contribute, and do your part faithfully, trusting that God sees your work and is the one who gives the fruit.
exp.4:6:
Believers are called to remove from their lives and from their church whatever contaminates them, which this passage calls "the old leaven." Leaven makes dough rise, and here it stands for sin that spreads. "A new unleavened batch" means a renewed people. "As you really are" means that, in Christ, they are already clean.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, correcting them because they were proudly putting up with a serious case of immorality in the church. He draws on the image of the Passover, when the Israelites removed leaven from their homes. His point is that tolerated sin can affect the whole community. He then says that Christ is our Passover lamb, and that he has been sacrificed for us.

For today: if Christ has given himself for us, we must not treat sin lightly. Ask God to show you some habit or attitude you should leave behind, and respond with humility and gratitude.
exp.13:8:
Paul says that if we speak in a tongue without using clear, understandable words, no one will be able to follow what is being said. It would be like speaking into the air. He has in mind a message whose meaning people can grasp, and speaking means actually saying the words out loud.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where several people used the gift of tongues in meetings with no one to interpret. Earlier he gave the example of the flute, the lyre (a stringed instrument), and the war trumpet: if they do not sound clearly, no one knows what is being played or when to get ready. His aim is that the church be built up.

For today: when you speak, teach, or pray in a group, use simple, clear words so that everyone can understand and be encouraged. Ask yourself: "Is what I am saying being understood?"
exp.6:26:
This verse says that a man who is committed to a wife should not seek to be released from her, and a man who is free of commitment should not look for a wife. "Committed" means joined in marriage, and "free of commitment" means having no spouse at all.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage and staying single. He makes clear that here he is giving his own judgment, not a direct command from the Lord. He speaks of "the present distress," a difficult situation that some understand as persecution or crisis in that time. Scholars interpret it in different ways. He does not forbid marriage, as the next verse shows.

For today: trust in your present situation and serve God there. If you are married, take care of your marriage. If you are single, do not live anxiously about getting married; make the most of this season with peace and devotion.
exp.13:38:
The explanation says that believers should eagerly desire and pursue the gift of prophesying, that is, speaking words from God that build up, encourage, and comfort. It also says that speaking in tongues should not be forbidden. The word "eager" means to strive for something and want it strongly.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was disorder in the meetings, because many wanted to speak at the same time and boasted about their gifts. In this chapter he teaches them that what matters most is that everything builds up the church. For this reason he values prophecy more, but he does not look down on tongues. Right after this, he asks that everything be done with decency and order.

For today: value the gifts of others even when they are different from yours. Seek to serve in a way that builds up everyone, and make sure that in your church everything is done with respect and love.
exp.13:16:
The explanation says that the person who prays or gives thanks to God in a tongue no one understands may be doing it well enough, and their thanksgiving can be sincere. But the one who listens receives no benefit. The phrase "You may be giving thanks well enough" means that the thanks given can be genuine, and "but the other one is not edified" means that the listener is not strengthened or encouraged in their faith.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the gatherings had become disorderly. Some were speaking in tongues without anyone interpreting, and the others were left without understanding. Paul does not despise that gift, since he practices it himself, but he insists that what matters in the congregation is that everyone be helped.

Today we can ask ourselves whether what we say, sing, or teach in the church helps others to understand and to grow. Speaking clearly and thinking about those who are listening to us is a way of showing love.
exp.9:1:
The verse says that all the people of Israel, when they came out of Egypt, were "baptized into Moses." That is, by following Moses under God's cloud and crossing the Red Sea, they were identified with him as their leader and joined to him. The word "sea" in the verse is the same as "the sea" in ordinary speech.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church that felt secure because it had been baptized and took part in the Lord's Supper. He reminds them that Israel also received great blessings and miracles, but many later fell into sin. Paul sees in the crossing of the sea a picture of Christian baptism, although scholars explain in various ways how closely the two resemble each other.

For today: do not trust your past religious experiences as if they guaranteed your future. Follow Christ every day with humility and obedience.
exp.10:0:
Paul invites the believers in Corinth to imitate his example, but with a clear condition: he himself imitates Christ. Paul's words here mean "imitate me," that is, copy his way of living. Christ is the final model.

Paul writes to a church with many problems of division and pride. Just before, in chapter 10, he taught them not to seek their own advantage but the advantage of many, so that they may be saved. Some scholars see this verse as the close of that teaching, and others as the beginning of what follows. There is debate about where the chapter should have begun.

For today: think about who imitates you, such as your children, companions, or brothers and sisters in the church. Try to live in such a way that, by imitating you, they come closer to Christ. And imitate those who truly follow Jesus.
exp.1:2:
Paul recalls how he arrived in Corinth: he came in weakness, with fear, and with much trembling. "Weakness" means a lack of strength, and "fear and trembling" describes deep anxiety, not an attitude of confidence or pride.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some admired eloquent speakers and human wisdom. He reminds them that he did not come with brilliant speeches, but proclaiming Christ crucified. The text does not say exactly why he felt that fear, so it is not wise to invent a cause. What is clear is that his weakness left room for God's power to work.

Today, you do not need to feel strong or speak perfectly to serve God. If you feel weak or afraid when sharing your faith, trust that God can work even through your frailty.
exp.13:12:
This verse says that whoever speaks in a tongue that others cannot understand should pray that they will be able to explain what was said. The word "tongue" refers to a language the listeners do not know, and the idea of explaining means making the meaning clear so that everyone can follow it.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some people often used the gift of tongues in their meetings, but without anyone understanding them. He reminds them that what matters most is building up the whole church. So if you speak in a tongue, you should also seek to make it understood, so that others are strengthened and not left confused.

Today, when you serve in the church, whether by speaking, singing, or teaching, try to be clear. Use simple words and ask God that what you share will help others understand and grow in their faith.
exp.0:28:
He says that God chose this way so that no one would feel proud in front of him. The verse is not using "flesh" in a special sense; it simply means human beings, with all their weakness. The word "boast" means to brag or to feel superior because of what one is or does. "His presence" refers to God himself.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a divided community where some bragged about their wisdom, their favorite leaders, or their social standing. He reminds them that God called ordinary people, without influence, to show that salvation does not come from human merit. Everything they have they receive by being united with Christ, who is their wisdom, righteousness, and redemption.

For today: when you feel pride in your achievements, studies, or successes, remember that everything is a gift. Give thanks to God and treat with humility and respect those who seem to have less.
exp.9:15:
Paul asks the Corinthians whether the cup we bless at the Lord's Supper is not a sharing in the blood of Christ, and whether the bread we break is not a sharing in his body. "Sharing" here means holding something together with others, having a part in it. The "cup of blessing" was the cup taken while giving thanks to God.

Paul writes to a church surrounded by pagan temples. Some Christians were eating at feasts connected with idols. He reminds them that the Supper unites believers with Christ and with one another, so they cannot also share the table of idolatry. How Christ is present in the Supper is understood differently among the various Christian traditions.

For today: when you take the Supper, do so with gratitude and reverence, remembering that you belong to Christ and to his people. Check whether there is anything in your life that competes with your loyalty to him, and let it go.
exp.8:7:
Paul asks two questions. He asks whether what he has just said is only human reasoning, an idea based on the logic of ordinary people. And he answers with another question: the law of God says the same thing too.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his right, and that of Barnabas, to receive support from the church for their work in the gospel. He uses everyday examples, such as the soldier, the vineyard worker, and the shepherd. Then he shows that Scripture teaches the same thing, by quoting the law of Moses about the ox that treads out the grain. Although he had that right, he later explains that he chose not to use it.

For today: it is right to value and support those who serve in the church, without taking advantage of them. And the one who serves may, out of love, give up what is rightfully theirs.
exp.14:22:
The verse says that the resurrection happens in turn, one group after another. First comes Christ, whom Paul calls "the firstfruits," meaning the first part of the harvest, which shows that the rest will follow. Then those who belong to Christ rise, the ones who are his through faith, and this will happen "then, at His coming," when Jesus returns.

Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, where some denied that the dead would be raised. He reminds them that just as death came through Adam, life comes through Christ. His resurrection is the guarantee of ours. The verses that follow speak of the end, when Christ will hand over the kingdom to the Father; Christians explain the details of that time in different ways.

For today: if Christ has already risen, death does not have the final word. That hope can bring comfort in grief and strength to live faithfully today.
exp.10:25:
It says that each time believers eat the bread and drink the cup of the Lord's Supper, they are proclaiming the Lord's death. They will keep doing this until He comes.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church with divisions. Some turned the supper into a time of disorder, and even of selfishness toward the poorest. Paul reminds them of what he himself received: Jesus instituted this supper in memory of His sacrifice. For that reason it should be observed with respect and unity.

For today: the next time you take part in the Supper, do not do it out of routine. Think about what Christ did for you, give thanks, and be reconciled with anyone you have something unresolved with. In this way your participation will be a sincere proclamation of His death and of His return.
exp.2:9:
Paul says that, by the grace God has given him, he acted as an expert builder. He laid the foundation, and someone else is building on it. He also warns that each one must be careful how he builds.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, which was divided by following different leaders. He founded that church by preaching Christ, and others, such as Apollos, continued the work. Here he reminds them that the workers serve God and should not become a cause of rivalry. The following verse makes clear that the foundation is Jesus Christ.

For today: if you teach, serve, or help others in the faith, take care that your work rests on Christ and is done with honesty and diligence. Ask yourself humbly: "Am I building with what truly lasts?"
exp.12:12:
This verse says that three things remain: faith, hope, and love. Love is the word used here for generous, selfless love (in Greek, agape). Of the three, the greatest is love.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions and boasted about spiritual gifts. Earlier he spoke of things that will come to an end, such as tongues and prophecy, and he compared our present knowledge to seeing in a blurry mirror. Interpreters debate when the partial will come to an end, but many see it in the return of Christ, when we will see face to face.

For today: before seeking to be right or to shine in something, ask yourself how you can love a specific person this week. Listen to them with patience, help them, or forgive them. That remains.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that believers have not received the spirit of the world, meaning that way of thinking and valuing things that turns away from God. We have received the Spirit who is from God, so that we may understand what God has freely given us through grace. Here, the word "understand" points to grasping and recognizing these gifts.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, a church that boasted of human wisdom and was divided into groups. Paul reminds them that the gospel is not understood through talent or philosophy, but because God himself reveals it through his Spirit. The verses that follow show that someone without the Spirit sees these things as foolishness.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God for his Spirit to help you understand and give thanks for what he has already given you, rather than relying only on your own intelligence or on what people think.
exp.6:10:
The passage says that a wife who has separated from her husband has two paths: to remain unmarried, or to be reconciled to him. It also says that a husband must not divorce his wife. "Separate" means to part from one another; "divorce" means to end the marriage; "unmarried" means single.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth and answering questions about marriage. Just before this verse, he recalls a teaching of the Lord Jesus: a wife should not separate from her husband. Then, for new situations, such as couples where one spouse does not believe, he gives his own counsel as an apostle. Some scholars think Paul is speaking to difficult circumstances, and Christians differ in how they apply this teaching in cases of abuse.

For today: if there is conflict in a marriage, first seek reconciliation, through honest conversation, humility, forgiveness, and the help of a counselor or pastor. If there is danger or violence, seek protection and wise support.
exp.2:4:
Paul asks what Apollos and Paul are. He answers that they are servants, or helpers, through whom the Corinthians came to believe. Each one did only the work the Lord assigned to him.

Paul is writing to the believers in Corinth, who were divided and boasted of following one leader or another. He corrects that attitude by showing that the leaders are not the center: they are servants. Apollos was another teacher who worked in that church after Paul.

Today we can give thanks to those who teach us the faith, but without putting them in the place of Christ. Let us avoid comparing pastors or groups, and instead serve with humility in the role God has given us.
exp.1:13:
The explanation says that the "natural man", that is, the person who lives only by his human nature and without God's Spirit, does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. They seem like foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are only understood with the help of the Spirit. The word "natural" refers to the human nature, and it does not mean "brutish" or without reason.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who boasted of human wisdom and were divided into groups. He reminds them that the message of the cross is not discovered through cleverness or eloquence, but God reveals it by his Spirit. Those who have received it have the mind of Christ.

For today: before reading the Bible, ask God humbly that his Spirit open your understanding. And with those who do not believe, be patient: do not look down on them, and pray that God will open their eyes.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that we should not pass final judgment on others before the appointed time, that is, before the Lord comes back. When He comes, He will bring to light what is now hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of people's hearts. Then each person will receive his praise from God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were criticizing their leaders and dividing into camps, one favoring Apollos and another favoring Paul himself. Paul says that he does not even judge himself, because only the Lord knows each life and each motive thoroughly.

Today, before you criticize someone for what they did, remember that you see only a part. Leave the final verdict in God's hands and treat others with humility.
exp.0:23:
He says that for those whom God has called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. What others see as weakness or foolishness, those who are called recognize as the greatest work of God.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and took pride in human wisdom. The Jews asked for miracles and the Greeks sought philosophy, so a crucified Messiah seemed to them scandalous or absurd. Paul reminds them that God's calling changes the way we see the cross.

For today: you do not need to impress anyone with your intelligence or your strength. Trust that Christ is sufficient, and in your decisions and problems, seek first his wisdom and his power, even when the world sees him as small.
exp.11:1:
You know that before you knew Christ, you were pagans, and you were influenced and led astray toward mute idols. Those idols could not speak, could not answer, and could do nothing at all. The verse describes being pulled along by these influences without really choosing them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city full of temples and pagan religions. He is about to correct problems with spiritual gifts. First he reminds them where they came from: the worship of idols that have no voice. This sets up the contrast with the Holy Spirit, who does speak and guide, and who leads people to confess Jesus as Lord.

For today: let us remember with gratitude where God brought us out of. It is also worth examining what carries us along without our noticing, such as fashions, pressures, or desires, and asking the Spirit to guide us toward Christ.
exp.8:11:
Paul asks: if other preachers have the right to receive support from the Corinthians, shouldn't he have it even more, since he founded that church? The word "right" here means the authority to receive support. But Paul did not exercise that right. He put up with anything rather than get in the way of the gospel of Christ, enduring lack and hardship so that nothing would stand in the path of the message.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he himself started. He defends his apostleship and explains that those who work in the gospel deserve support, just as the one who plows or threshes expects a share of the harvest. Even so, he gave up that right so that no one could think he preached out of self-interest or for money.

For today: sometimes using a right is not the wisest course. Ask yourself whether something that is lawful for you might hinder others in their faith, and whether it is worth setting aside for the sake of the gospel.
exp.0:1:
Paul writes to the church of God in Corinth. He tells them they are "sanctified in Christ Jesus," that is, set apart for God through Christ. They are also "called to be holy," meaning invited by God to live as his people. The greeting includes all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, because he is Lord of them and of Paul.

Paul and Sosthenes write to a church with many problems: divisions, pride, and disorder. Even so, Paul begins by reminding them of their identity in Christ before correcting them. Who Sosthenes was is not known for certain; some connect him with a man mentioned in Acts 18, but this is not certain.

Today, your worth before God does not depend on your perfection, but on the fact that Christ made you his. Remembering this helps you live with humility and feel united with other believers, even when they are far away or very different from you.
exp.14:32:
Do not be deceived. The bad company Paul has in mind is harmful companionship or conversation, and "good character" means upright conduct and a healthy inner life. In other words, bad influences can ruin a life that was going well.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and defending the resurrection. Some among them were saying there is no resurrection, and Paul sees that this belief leads people to live without restraint. The verse appears to be a familiar saying that Paul quotes, and he uses it as a warning. Then he calls them to wake up and stop sinning.

Today, think about whom you spend the most time with, what you listen to, and what you see every day. Seek out friendships and conversations that strengthen your faith, and set kind but firm limits on whatever pulls you away from God.
exp.14:6:
It says that the risen Jesus appeared to James, and then to all the apostles. The word "appeared" here means he truly let himself be seen. Here "James" is probably the brother of the Lord, the leader of the church in Jerusalem, though the text does not make this clear. The phrase "all the apostles" seems to refer to a wider group than the twelve, but it is not known exactly who they were.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, some of whom doubted the resurrection of the dead. For that reason he presents a list of witnesses who saw Christ alive. Many of them were still living, so anyone could ask them. Paul places himself at the end of the list, as the last witness.

For today: our faith does not rest on a vague idea, but on the testimony of real people. We can believe with confidence and share what Christ has done in us, with humility and simplicity.
exp.8:14:
Paul says that he has never used the right he had to receive support for preaching the gospel. He is not writing this to ask the Corinthians to give him that support now. He would rather die than let anyone nullify his boast, meaning the reason for pride and joy he finds in preaching without charge. To nullify it would be to leave that boast empty of value or to cancel it.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and earlier he argued that those who work for the gospel have the right to make their living from their service. Here he makes clear that, although that right is real, he chose not to use it, so that no one could think he preached for money or that the message would be hindered. Some scholars think he was also responding to criticism in Corinth about the way he supported himself.

For today: sometimes it is good to give up something that is rightfully ours out of love for the gospel and for others. Ask yourself what right you could let go of in order to serve better, without boasting or demanding recognition.
exp.9:26:
If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you decide to go, this verse says you may eat whatever is served to you without raising questions about it. An unbeliever is simply someone who does not follow Christ. To "eat what is set before you" means to eat what your host serves you. Raising questions of conscience would mean stopping to investigate where the food came from, out of worry that eating it might offend God.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, a city where much of the meat sold in the markets came from pagan temples. Some believers were asking whether eating such meat was a sin. Paul answers that the earth and everything in it belongs to the Lord, so the food itself is not the problem.

For today, we can accept the hospitality of people who do not believe with freedom and gratitude. But we should always be careful that our freedom does not cause others to stumble or damage our witness.
exp.7:7:
The explanation says that food does not change our relationship with God. The verse itself, in the Berean Standard Bible, states that food does not bring us closer to God. Being "commended" or accepted before God is what the verse speaks of, so I can say it that way. If we eat, we gain nothing before God; and if we do not eat, we lose nothing either. The food itself does not bring us closer to Him or push us away from Him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were doubts about eating meat that had been offered to idols. Some believers, with a sensitive conscience, still felt troubled when they ate it. Paul acknowledges that there is one God and that idols are nothing, but he teaches that knowledge must be accompanied by love toward those who are weaker in the faith.

For today: there are things that, in themselves, do not make us better or worse before God. Before using my freedom, I can ask whether it helps or causes a brother to stumble. Love sometimes means giving up something that is permitted.
exp.8:26:
Paul says he deals firmly with his own body. The word for "discipline" means to train with discipline, and the phrase about making his body his slave means he puts it under control, so that it does not rule over him. The word for "disqualified" refers to being rejected after the test. His concern is that after preaching to others, he himself would not be approved.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, and he uses the image of athletes in the Greek games, which they knew well. He has just been speaking about giving up his rights for the sake of the gospel. Interpreters debate what exactly being disqualified means: some think of losing salvation, others of losing approval or reward in service. The text does not fully settle it.

For today: choose one concrete habit, such as rest, phone use, or daily prayer, and set limits on it consistently, so that your desires do not direct your life and your witness is consistent.
exp.14:57:
Here is what the verse says: because of what Christ has already accomplished, believers should stand firm and not be moved from their faith. The phrase "always excel in the work of the Lord" means giving more and more in service to the Lord. The phrase "not in vain" means useless or without result. Nothing done for God is lost.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had doubts and divisions, and some denied the resurrection of the dead. After explaining that Christ rose and that believers will also rise, and after saying that God gives us victory over death, he closes with this call. Because the resurrection is real, Christian work has eternal value.

For today: when you grow tired of serving, of praying, or of doing good without seeing results, remember that God sees and does not forget. Stay faithful today in one concrete task, such as helping someone or serving in your church.
exp.2:2:
It says that the Corinthians are still living by their human impulses and not by the Spirit. The proof is the jealousy and the divisions among them. "Worldly" means guided by human nature without the influence of God, and "walking in the way of man" means behaving like any ordinary person in the world. "Dissension" refers to arguments and conflicts.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had split into groups: some said they belonged to Paul and others to Apollos. He calls them "babes in Christ" because their conduct showed little maturity. He had given them milk, basic teachings, and not solid food.

For today: if there is rivalry in your church or family, ask yourself whether you are defending a person or a faction instead of Christ. Seek peace and serve with humility.
exp.8:24:
Anyone who competes in the games trains with strict discipline. Athletes give up many things to prepare. Saying they train with strict discipline means they control themselves and set aside whatever gets in the way. They do it for a crown that is perishable, a prize of leaves or branches that wilts. We do it for a crown that is imperishable, one that never fades and never comes to an end.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a city known for its athletic games. He uses that picture to encourage them to live with discipline and not to take their faith lightly. He himself says he pushes hard, because he serves the gospel and wants to finish well.

For today: think of one thing that distracts you or holds you back in your life with God, such as your phone, a bad temper, or laziness. Give it up this week and use that time to pray or read the Bible.
exp.6:25:
Paul says that, because of the present crisis, it is good for a person to remain as they are. The word "crisis" points to a time of pressure and urgency pressing in on a person. "To remain as he is" means staying in the state one is already in, especially being unmarried. It is his own judgment, not a command.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage. Earlier he makes clear that he has no command from the Lord about virgins, but only his own opinion. Scholars debate what the crisis refers to: perhaps the hardships of that time, or the shortness of the time that remains. He himself says that marriage is not a sin.

For today: before deciding about marriage or any major change, ask what will allow you to serve God better in your situation. Seek counsel calmly and without pressure.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that if a Christian woman is married to a man who does not believe, and he is willing to keep living with her, she must not divorce him. The word "unbelieving" here does not mean being unfaithful in the marriage, but having no faith in Christ. "Willing" means that he is ready and accepts it.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage. Some believers may have thought that staying married to an unbeliever made them unclean. Paul makes clear that this is not so: one person's faith can bring blessing to the home, and God desires peace in the family. He himself says that he gives this advice "I, not the Lord," meaning that there is no direct word from Jesus about this case.

Today, if your spouse does not share your faith but wants to stay with you, try to live with love, respect, and patience. Your daily example can speak louder than your words.
exp.14:18:
Paul says that if our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all other people. The word "pitied" here does not speak of wickedness but of deserving pity, like someone who has staked everything on something that never comes true.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some were saying there is no resurrection of the dead. He answers that if Christ was not raised, the Christian faith is empty, forgiveness would not be real, and believers who have died would have no hope. The verses that follow affirm that Christ was in fact raised, and that his resurrection is the guarantee of ours.

For today: when faith costs you sacrifice or misunderstanding, remember that your hope does not end in this life. Live with patience, generosity, and faithfulness, trusting that Christ has risen and that your hope rests in him.
exp.14:16:
Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, then believing in him is of no use. The word "futile" means empty, without value or result. The phrase "you are still in your sins" means that they would remain under the guilt of sin, without true forgiveness.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. Some among them were saying that the dead do not rise. Paul shows them that denying this leads to denying the resurrection of Christ as well, and then the whole gospel falls apart. For him, the resurrection is the center of the faith, not a detail.

For today: our hope does not rest on feeling good or on being good people, but on a fact in which God acted. When you doubt or feel guilty, remember that Christ lives, and that in him there is real forgiveness and firm hope.
exp.14:36:
It says that when someone sows, they do not put the fully grown plant into the ground, but only a seed, a simple grain without its final form. It may be of wheat or of some other seed. "Perhaps" here means "for example." "Is going to sprout" means "that is going to come up."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the body. He answers the one who asks how the dead are raised and with what body. He uses the seed as an example: what is buried is very different from what later comes up. Many understand that in this way he prepares the idea of a risen body that is different, yet with continuity.

For today: when you face losses or painful endings, remember that God can bring life from what you see only as a buried seed. Trust in his power and wait with hope.
exp.9:7:
Paul says we must not give in to sexual immorality, as some of the Israelites did in the desert, and in one day twenty-three thousand of them died as a result. The term refers to any sexual relationship outside God's design.

The apostle Paul is writing to Christians in Corinth, a city known for its atmosphere of vice. He reminds them of what happened to Israel so that they might learn from that nation's mistakes. The episode appears to be the one recorded in Numbers 25, where the death toll is given as twenty-four thousand; Paul gives twenty-three thousand, and scholars offer several explanations for the difference, with no definitive answer.

Today, the warning invites us to guard our purity without trusting in our own strength. We can avoid situations, images, or relationships that weaken us, and seek support from fellow believers, remembering that God cares for those who obey him.
exp.4:0:
Paul says that there is sexual immorality reported as a fact among the church in Corinth, of a kind so serious that even pagans would not tolerate it. A man was living with his father's wife, that is, his stepmother. "Sexual immorality" here refers to sexual sin in general. "Pagans" are people outside the faith, in this case non-Jews.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he founded. News of this case had reached him, and what troubles him most is that the church was not responding. The verses that follow say they were puffed up, that is, proud, instead of grieving. Paul asks them to act with seriousness. The Bible does not clarify the details of the relationship, and that does not change the gravity of the matter.

For today: let us not take sin lightly or tolerate it out of pride or out of unwillingness to cause discomfort. If a brother is in serious error, let us act with humility, prayer, and love, seeking his restoration.
exp.14:5:
It says that the risen Jesus appeared to more than five hundred believers at the same time. Paul adds that, when he writes, most of them are still living, though some have already died. The word "appeared" means that he was truly seen. The "brothers" are the followers of Jesus.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. To answer them, he lists those who saw Christ alive. By mentioning that most of the witnesses were still living, he invites his readers to ask them directly. This event is not told in the Gospels, so we know of it only from this text.

For today: our faith rests on a fact that was proclaimed publicly, and not on a private idea. When you have doubts, do not be ashamed to ask and to study. Read the accounts of the resurrection calmly, and ask God to strengthen your trust in Christ.
exp.13:31:
They say that those who receive and pass on a message from God must keep control of themselves. The word "spirits" here refers to the gift or prompting of prophecy in each person, and the phrase "are subject" means that they submit, or allow themselves to be put in order. The prophet is not swept along by a force he cannot stop; he can wait for his turn and be silent.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the meetings were disorderly and several people spoke at the same time. He wants the messages to build up everyone. Some understand that "prophets" refers to the others who weigh what is said; others, that each prophet controls himself. Both ideas point to order.

For today: before you speak or serve in the church, ask yourself whether you are doing it with respect, waiting your turn, and whether what you say helps others grow. Self-control is also a fruit of the Spirit.
exp.3:10:
It says that Paul and the other apostles, up to that very moment, were hungry and thirsty, did not have enough clothing, were treated brutally, and had no permanent home. The verse itself explains the terms: "we are hungry and thirsty" describes going without food and drink, "poorly clothed" describes not having adequate clothing, and "homeless" refers to people without a stable place to live.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who felt proud, rich, and superior to others. With an almost ironic tone, he shows them the contrast: while they boasted of their position, the apostles lived in suffering for serving Christ. He wants to correct their pride and remind them that the way of Jesus includes humility and self-giving.

For today: let us not measure the value of a Christian life by comfort or success. Let us honor those who serve with sacrifice and, if we are called to suffer for doing good, let us keep trusting God with humility.
exp.7:9:
Paul says that if someone with knowledge, that is, with understanding and maturity in the faith, is seen eating in the temple of an idol, a weaker believer (one whose conscience is fragile and unsure) might be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols. "Encouraged" here means pushed or drawn to do it, even though his conscience tells him it is wrong.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who lived surrounded by pagan temples. Some believed that idols are nothing and ate that meat without any problem. Paul agrees with the principle, but warns them that their freedom can cause other believers who do not see it that way to stumble.

Today, before using a freedom that God permits, ask yourself how it will affect someone whose faith is more fragile. Sometimes loving a brother is worth more than exercising my right.
exp.14:56:
The explanation says that we give thanks to God because He gives us the victory, and that this victory comes through Jesus Christ, our Lord. The word "but" marks a turn from what came before. The victory is not something we win for ourselves; it is a gift.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, and he has been speaking about the resurrection. He has just said that death loses its power, and that sin is its "sting", that is, what does the harm, like the bite of an insect. He also mentions that the law showed sin without being able to remove it. So Paul ends with praise: Christ accomplished what we could not.

Today, when you feel defeated by your guilt or by the fear of death, begin by giving thanks. Rest in what Christ has already done, and from there keep going forward with courage.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that love does not take pleasure when someone does something unfair or wrong. The word "rejoices" in this verse means "is glad" or "takes delight." Instead, love rejoices when the truth wins out and comes to light.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, pride, and a great deal of attention to spiritual gifts. In this chapter he shows them that without love, every gift loses its value. He describes what true love is like, with simple examples from everyday conduct.

For today: think about whether you have ever taken pleasure in gossip, mockery, or someone else's downfall, even silently. Ask God to help you delight in what is honest and just, and to speak the truth with respect and kindness.
exp.8:22:
Paul says that he does everything, including adapting himself to different kinds of people, for the sake of the gospel. "So that I may share in its blessings" means that he wants to receive the good that the gospel brings, not only to proclaim it to others. The "weak" are those who are weak in faith or in conscience.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. In this chapter he explains that he gave up some of his rights so as not to hinder anyone. He adapted himself to Jews, to Gentiles, and to the weak, without changing the message or abandoning the law of Christ. Right after this, he moves on to the image of the race, which speaks of discipline.

For today: think of someone close to you who thinks differently from you. Ask yourself what you might give up, or how you could listen to them with more patience, so that they may see the love of Christ, without compromising the truth.
exp.15:18:
The explanation says that the churches in the province of Asia send greetings to the believers in Corinth. Aquila and Prisca also greet them warmly "in the Lord," that is, as brothers and sisters united to Christ. The church that meets at their house greets them along with them. "The churches in the province of Asia send you greetings" means they are sending their greetings to you.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus, in Asia, near the end of it. Aquila and Prisca had lived for a time in Corinth and knew that church well. In those days believers often met in homes. These greetings remind the Corinthians that they are not alone, but connected with other churches.

For today: the Christian faith is not lived in isolation. We can encourage others with a message, a call, or a visit. And if we have a home, we can open it simply so that others may gather, pray, and encourage one another.
exp.14:14:
It says that if the dead do not rise, the apostles would be exposed as false witnesses about God. They had declared that God raised Christ from the dead. But if the dead are not raised, then God did not raise Him, and their testimony would be untrue.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. He shows them the consequence: denying our resurrection also means denying Christ's. Paul and the other apostles had preached that Christ rose, and many witnesses had seen him alive (verses 3 to 8).

For today: our hope does not rest on a lovely idea, but on a fact in which God fulfilled what he promised. When you doubt or suffer, remember that Christ rose, and that gives firmness to your faith and your hope for the future.
exp.15:5:
Paul tells the Corinthians that he may stay with them for a while, perhaps even spending the winter there. In this way they could help him continue his journey, supporting him on to his next destination. The word "winter" here means spending the winter season, and the phrase "help me on my journey" means accompanying him or providing what he needs for the road.

Paul writes this letter from Ephesus, and he is planning his trip. First he will pass through Macedonia, and then he will come to Corinth. He does not want to make just a quick visit, but to stay a good while, if the Lord permits. Even so, he leaves his plans in God's hands.

For today: make your plans with good sense, but with humility. Place your projects before the Lord and keep your heart open to Him adjusting them. We can also support generously those who serve God on their way.
exp.8:15:
Paul says that preaching the gospel gives him no reason to boast. For him it is not an option but a duty that God has placed on him. The word "boast" here means to take pride in something. "Obligated" means he is bound to do it. And "Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel" expresses a strong warning: it would be serious if he stopped.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. He has just explained that he had the right to receive financial support for his work, but he did not use that right so that he would not hinder the message. Here he makes clear that his motive is not to seek praise. His calling comes from God, and that is why he feels responsible to carry it out.

For today: when you serve God, examine your motives. Do what He has entrusted to you faithfully and humbly, without seeking applause, remembering that it is a gift of grace to be able to share the good news of Jesus.
exp.6:16:
Paul says that each person should live the life the Lord has assigned to them and to which God has called them. He adds that this is the teaching he gives in all the churches.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and Christian life. Earlier he spoke of marriages where one partner believes and the other does not. Then he mentions circumcision, that is, Jews and non-Jews. His point is that being a Christian does not require changing one's social or family situation to please God.

Today, you do not have to wait to change your job, marital status, or circumstances in order to serve God. You can live your faith faithfully where you are, with love and peace, knowing that the Lord is with you.
exp.5:17:
Paul tells us to flee from sexual immorality, meaning any sexual relationship outside of marriage. He does not say simply to avoid it but to run far away from it. He says that every other sin a person can commit is outside the body, but the one who sins sexually sins against his own body. Interpreters explain that phrase in several ways, but they all agree that this sin touches the person in a very intimate way.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who lived in a city full of sexual immorality. He reminds them that their bodies belong to the Lord and are united to Him. Therefore they must not join themselves to anything that dishonors Christ. The next verse says that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.

For today: when temptation comes, don't test your strength; get away quickly. End the conversation, turn off the screen, or change where you are, remembering that your body belongs to God.
exp.8:10:
Paul asks: if we have sown spiritual seed among you, through the teaching of the gospel, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you? "Reap" means to gather a harvest, and a material harvest here means support for living, such as food or other help.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his right as an apostle to receive support from the church. He uses examples like the ox that treads out the grain and the one who plows in hope of a harvest. However, he soon makes clear that he did not use that right, so as not to hinder the gospel.

For today: if we receive spiritual teaching from someone, it is right to support those who serve in the church with generosity. And those who serve can do so with humility, without demanding, thinking first of the good of the gospel.
exp.14:0:
Paul tells the brothers in Corinth that he wants to remind them of the gospel, the good news about Jesus, which he had already preached to them. In this verse, "remind" points to what Paul is bringing back to their attention, the message they already knew. They had received this message, and they stand firm in it, meaning they remain steady in that faith.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing a letter to the church in Corinth. Earlier in the letter he has addressed several problems in the community, such as divisions and disorder. Now he begins to speak about the resurrection, a subject on which some had doubts. So he returns to the basics: the central message they themselves had believed.

For today: even when we have many debates and worries, it is good to return often to the center of our faith, which is Christ, his death, and his resurrection. Read this slowly this week and thank God for that message.
exp.11:29:
Paul asks three questions, and the answer he expects to each is "no." Not everyone in the church has gifts of healing, not everyone speaks in tongues (other languages or spiritual speech), and not everyone interprets what is said in tongues. "Teachers" are those who instruct, and "works of power" probably refers to miracles.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over the most showy gifts. He reminds them that the church is a body with many members, and that God distributes gifts as he wishes. For that reason, no one should feel superior or inferior. Then he leads them to "the more excellent way": love, from chapter 13.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or envy their gifts. Discover how God has equipped you to serve, use it with humility, and always accompany it with love.
exp.9:3:
Paul says that all the Israelites in the desert drank the same spiritual drink, that is, one given by God in a supernatural way. That water came from a rock, and Paul states that the rock was Christ. The phrase "accompanied them" can be understood as meaning that the provision of water went with them, or that Christ himself was present with them. Some believe Paul is drawing on a Jewish tradition about a rock that moved; that is not certain.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, believers who felt secure because they had been baptized and took part in the Lord's Supper. He reminds them that Israel also received great blessings, but many fell into sin. It is a warning.

Today we can remember that receiving God's blessings is not enough if we stop obeying him. Seek Christ as your daily source, and do not trust in your spiritual past.
exp.10:32:
When the believers come together for the church meal and the Lord's Supper, they are to wait for one another. The phrase "when you come together to eat" means that they gather to eat, and the word "wait" means they hold off until everyone has arrived. It is an invitation not to begin alone or in a hurry, but to share together.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions. According to the verses before it, some were eating and drinking without considering the others, so while some went hungry, others had too much. For this reason Paul corrects that unequal treatment and calls for personal self-examination. Some think the waiting also included the poor who arrived late, although the text does not spell this out.

Today, before we serve ourselves, eat, or take part in the church, we can look at who is missing, who is alone, or who needs a place. Waiting and making room is a concrete way of showing love.
exp.9:17:
Paul asks the Corinthians to consider the people of Israel as a nation, in their ordinary, everyday identity. He points out that those who ate the sacrificed portions were joined to the altar and to what it stood for. "Fellow partakers" means they shared in something together.

Paul is writing to a church where some believers were attending feasts held in pagan temples. First he speaks of the Lord's Supper, where believers share in fellowship with Christ. Then he uses the example of Israel to show that eating at an altar creates a real bond. That is why one cannot be joined to Christ and to idols at the same time.

For today: examine what things bind you spiritually. If something competes with your loyalty to Christ, step away from it and seek fellowship with Him and with His people.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that the rulers of that time did not understand God's hidden wisdom. If they had understood it, they would not have crucified Jesus, whom it calls "the Lord of glory." The word "age" in the verse refers to the present era, and "rulers" means the leaders or authorities.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where some took pride in human wisdom. He reminds them that God's plan, centered on the cross, seemed foolishness to the world. Interpreters debate whether "rulers" refers only to human leaders such as Pilate and the Jewish leaders, or also to spiritual powers; the text allows both readings.

For today: do not measure what God does only by what seems logical or successful. Ask him for humility to receive his wisdom, even when it does not fit the ideas that are in fashion.
exp.6:23:
He says that each one should remain in the situation they were in when God called them, whether they are brothers or sisters. "Called" refers to the moment someone comes to faith in Christ. "Remain" means to stay where they are. The phrase "in the situation" points to the circumstances of life a person is living when God calls them, and the verse teaches that they can live that situation in God's presence.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. Earlier he speaks of slaves and free people: before Christ, all belong to Him. Paul does not say that one can never change one's situation, but that faith does not depend on it. Some interpret that he also advises calm because of the pressing circumstances.

Today, your work, your family, or your situation can be places where you serve God faithfully. Live each day aware that He is present with you.
exp.12:2:
Paul says that even if I give away everything I own to feed the poor, and even if I surrender my body and exult in it, but have no love, I gain nothing. The word "love" here refers to the kind of love that seeks the good of the other person. "All I possess" means everything I own or have.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions, pride, and rivalry over spiritual gifts. This verse follows a list of impressive things: speaking in tongues, prophesying, having great faith. Paul shows that even the greatest sacrifices are empty without love.

Today, before you serve or help others, ask yourself: am I doing it out of love for the other person, or so that people will see me? Ask God to purify your motives.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that a person cannot take part in the Lord's supper and, at the same time, in feasts tied to demons. "Sharing" means that one takes part in, joins, or has fellowship with something. The "cup" and the "table" speak of fellowship and of loyalty.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city full of pagan temples. Some believers were eating at feasts where meat was offered to idols. Paul makes clear that the idol itself is nothing, but that behind that worship stand spiritual forces opposed to God. For this reason he asks them not to mix the two.

For today: examine whether there is anything in your life that competes with your loyalty to Christ, such as a habit, a friendship, or a practice that pulls you away from God. Ask him to give you a faithful and undivided heart.
exp.14:10:
It says that Paul and the other apostles, though they are different people, proclaim the same message, and that the Corinthians believed it. The words "whether, then, it was I or they" mean "whether it was I or whether it was they." "This is what we preach" means that they announced the good news, and "this is what you believed" refers to the faith of the Corinthians.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He has just mentioned that Christ rose and appeared to many witnesses, and he speaks with humility about his own calling. Here he emphasizes that his message is not a personal idea, but the same one the other apostles preached. He does this because some in Corinth doubted the resurrection of the dead, and he reminds them of the foundation of their faith.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith rests on the central message of the gospel: Christ died and rose again. Even though there are different teachers and styles, let us always return to what is essential and stand firm in it.
exp.0:30:
It says that if anyone wants to feel proud or boast, let them do it for what God has done, not for what they themselves have accomplished. "To boast" means to show off or take pride in something. The phrase "as it is written" shows that Paul is quoting Scripture, probably an idea found in Jeremiah 9:23-24.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church full of divisions and of people proud of their wisdom and of their favorite leaders. He reminds them that their new life comes from God through Christ, who is for them wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption. No one has reason to boast before God.

Today we can practice humility: when something goes well for us, let us give thanks to God out loud. And when we see the success of others, let us rejoice without comparing ourselves, remembering that everything good is a gift from Him.
exp.5:13:
It says that by his own power God raised the Lord Jesus from the dead, and that he will raise us up as well. The verse speaks of God's power at work in the resurrection of Jesus and in the resurrection of believers.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, a city where sexual immorality was common. Some people thought the body did not matter, because it would one day be destroyed, like food. Paul answers that the body is not disposable: it belongs to the Lord, and God will raise it. That is why what we do with our bodies truly matters.

Your body has eternal value to God. Today you can honor it by taking care with what you do, what you look at, and who you join yourself to, remembering that you belong to Christ and that your hope is the resurrection.
exp.3:7:
He says the Corinthians feel completely satisfied and rich, as if they had already become kings, and they seem to manage this without needing the apostles. "Already you have all you want" means they feel they lack nothing. Paul's wish, "How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!", is a wish that they would truly reign, so that he could reign alongside them. It is irony, not sincere praise.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was pride and division, with groups boasting of their favorite teachers. The Corinthians acted as if they already lived in the fullness of God's kingdom, without going through suffering. Paul uses this ironic tone to shake them, and in the verses that follow he contrasts their pride with the humble, suffering life of the apostles.

For today: when you feel you have already arrived or that you have more than enough spiritually, remember that everything you have received comes from God. Ask for humility and value those who serve with simplicity.
exp.10:9:
Paul says that a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, and he adds that this is "because of the angels." Some read this as a call to wear a covering on the head during worship.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, where the meetings had become disorderly. He is addressing customs for how men and women prayed and prophesied in public. The phrase "because of the angels" is difficult: some think the angels watch over the order of the church, while others think it refers to a background we do not fully know. Scholars do not agree on its meaning.

For today, although customs change, we can make sure that the way we worship shows respect for God. We can also remember, as the next verse says, that man and woman need each other "in the Lord."
exp.9:24:
It says that believers may eat any meat sold in the meat market without raising questions out of matters of conscience. The idea is not to complicate things by investigating where the meat came from.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where much of the meat sold in the market came from sacrifices made in pagan temples. The believers were debating whether eating it was a sin. Paul answers that the earth and everything in it belongs to the Lord (Psalm 24:1), so the food itself is not defiled. But in the nearby context he also asks them to care for the weaker brother and to seek the good of others.

For today: do not make a heavy burden out of what is secondary. Enjoy with gratitude what God gives, but exercise your freedom in love, thinking about how your decisions affect the faith and conscience of those around you.
exp.7:10:
The passage says that a person with a lot of understanding can cause a weaker brother in the faith to be destroyed. It makes this more serious by reminding us that Christ died for that brother. The weak one is someone whose faith or conscience is fragile. Interpreters debate whether being destroyed means a final loss or a serious harm to his faith.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were arguing about whether it was right to eat meat offered to idols. Those who were more informed knew that idols are nothing and ate without guilt. But some believers, newly come out of paganism, were troubled when they saw this. Paul asks them not to use their freedom without thinking of others.

For today: before doing something you consider permissible, ask yourself how it will affect someone whose faith is more fragile. Loving that brother is worth more than defending your right.
exp.14:55:
It says that what makes death so painful is sin, like the sting of a scorpion that pierces and wounds. And sin has power because the law, by showing what God requires, exposes our guilt. The word "power" means strength or force.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to affirm the resurrection. He has just quoted the question: "Where, O death, is your sting?" Here he explains why death seemed so fearsome: it confronted us with sin and the law. Right after this, he thanks God because Jesus Christ gives us the victory.

For today: if guilt weighs on you or you fear death, bring that to Christ. He bore your sin, so you can live with peace, forgiven and steadfast in serving God.
exp.13:25:
Paul asks what a church meeting should look like. When the brothers and sisters come together, each person may bring something to share: a song, a teaching, a message in a tongue, a revelation, or an explanation of a tongue. "You" here means all of you together. What matters is that everything be done to build up the church, that is, to strengthen and help grow the faith of everyone present.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, whose meetings were disorderly. Many wanted to show off their spiritual gifts and did not think about the others. That is why, before and after this verse, Paul speaks about outsiders being able to understand what is said and about bringing order to the use of tongues.

For today: before you take part in your church, whether by singing, teaching, or praying, ask yourself, "Will this help others grow in faith?" Use your gifts to serve, not to stand out.
exp.10:26:
It says that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner, that is, in a way that does not match what the meal means, will be guilty: they become responsible for sinning against the body and blood of Christ.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the Lord's Supper had become disorderly. According to the earlier verses of this chapter, there were divisions, and some were eating without waiting for or sharing with others. He reminds them that this meal proclaims the death of Jesus. Scholars agree that the problem was attitude, not that anyone had to be perfect.

For today: before taking part in the Lord's Supper, take a moment to examine your heart. Ask for forgiveness, be reconciled with anyone you have offended, and remember with gratitude what Christ did for you.
exp.12:0:
Here the explanation says that even if someone speaks the languages of men and even those of angels, without love they only make noise. The word "love" here means the kind of love that gives without expecting anything in return. A "ringing gong" is a metal disk that sounds loudly, and a "clanging cymbal" is a cymbal that makes only an empty clash.

The apostle Paul is speaking, writing to the church in Corinth. That community highly valued spiritual gifts, such as speaking in tongues, but there were divisions and pride. Paul reminds them that gifts without love lose their worth. Some think "tongues of angels" is an exaggerated way of speaking; others take it to refer to a spiritual language. This cannot be stated with certainty.

Before seeking to stand out for what you know or do in the church, ask yourself whether you are doing it with love. Today, treat someone with patience and kindness, even if no one notices.
exp.9:9:
Paul tells us not to complain against God, as some of the Israelites in the desert did. They paid for it with their lives: the Berean Standard Bible says they were killed by the destroying angel. Complaining here means more than an honest word of pain. It describes grumbling born of rebellion and distrust.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who were tempted by idol worship and immoral living. He reminds them of what happened to Israel after they left Egypt. He probably has in mind episodes such as the one in Numbers 16, where the people complained against Moses and Aaron, though the text does not say which one exactly. He uses these events as a warning.

Today we can examine our own complaints. There are moments of pain when we can cry out to God with sincerity, as the Psalms do. But rebellious complaining arises from not trusting his care. When it arises, it is good to stop and give thanks for something concrete.
exp.10:4:
He says that a woman who prays or prophesies in the congregation with her head uncovered dishonors her head. That word "head" can refer to herself or to the man, and scholars debate which sense is dominant. "It is just as if her head were shaved" means that for Paul, going uncovered was as shameful as having the head shaved. Here it is taken for granted that women also pray and prophesy in public.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had disorders in its meetings. He responds to matters of decorum according to the customs of that city. Scholars discuss whether the covering was a veil or the hair itself, and what it meant exactly in that culture. That is not known with certainty.

For today: in worship, let us seek to have our conduct honor God and not scandalize others, and distinguish between the principle of order and respect and the customs of an era.
exp.14:41:
Paul says that the resurrection is like a sowing. A body is "sown" when it is buried, and it is perishable, that is, subject to decay, breakdown, and death. But what is raised is imperishable, that is, it will rise without any power to decay or to die ever again.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted the resurrection of the dead. Before this verse he spoke of the variety of bodies and glories, such as the sun, the moon, and the stars, to show that God can give bodies of different kinds. With the image of the seed, which seems to die and then gives life, he explains that the risen body will be different and better.

For today: if God promises a life that never ends, we can face pain, sickness, and grief with hope, and live serving him without fear of losing everything.
exp.10:23:
He says that on the night Jesus was betrayed, he gave thanks for the bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples. He told them that the bread stood for his body, given for them, and asked them to do this in remembrance of him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had problems: at their shared meals some ate too much while others, the poor, were left ashamed. Paul reminds them of what he received from the Lord about the supper, to correct their disorder. Christians understand in different ways how Christ is present in the supper, but all agree that it is an act of remembrance.

For today: when you take part in the Lord's supper, do so with gratitude and attention, and treat the other believers with respect and kindness, especially those in greatest need.
exp.1:10:
Paul says that no one knows the thoughts inside a person except that person's own spirit. In the same way, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. The word "knows" here means "has come to know" or "understands," which points to real insight into something hidden.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who took pride in human wisdom. He reminds them that the message of the cross cannot be worked out by one's own intelligence. God himself makes it known through his Spirit, and believers have received it.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God to help you understand it through his Spirit. Do not rely only on your own intelligence or your opinions. Pray with humility before reading, and listen patiently to what God wants to show you.
exp.6:38:
A married woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives. If her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord. The phrase "bound to her husband" means that marriage is a commitment that holds as long as both are alive.

The apostle Paul speaks here, answering questions that the Christians in Corinth had sent him about marriage and singleness. Earlier, he had already taught that marriage is lasting. Here he clarifies the situation of widows. The condition "as long as he belongs to the Lord" is commonly understood to mean marrying a fellow believer, though some also interpret it as marrying with an attitude of obedience to God.

For today: if you are thinking about getting married, do not look only at affection; look for someone who loves God and with whom you can grow in faith. And pray before you decide.
exp.10:22:
Paul says that he received from the Lord what he had already passed on to the Corinthians: that the Lord Jesus, on the night he was betrayed, took bread. The Berean Standard Bible uses "passed on" for what he taught them, and the event described is the night Jesus was betrayed, when he was handed over to his enemies.

Paul is writing to a divided church. Some were eating and drinking too much during the gathering, while others went hungry and felt humiliated. That is why he reminds them where the Lord's Supper comes from. Scholars discuss how he "received" this from the Lord: it may have come through direct revelation or through tradition handed down, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: when we take part in the Lord's Supper, let us do so with gratitude and reverence, thinking of Christ and of our brothers and sisters. Before we eat together, let us ask ourselves whether we are caring for those in greatest need.
exp.6:35:
The verse says that if someone thinks he is acting inappropriately toward his betrothed, and the young woman is past her youth and they ought to marry, he may do as he wishes. He is not sinning; they should get married. The key idea is that marriage is permitted and not a sin.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. He advises them to live without distractions for the Lord, but makes clear that he does not want to place a burden on them: marrying is not a sin.

For today: let us not turn our own preferences into a law for others. We can decide with prayer and freedom, without guilt or pressure, seeking to serve the Lord wholeheartedly at every stage of life.
exp.6:19:
Each person should remain in the situation they were in when God called them to faith. Here "calling" does not mean a job or profession. It refers to God's call and to the circumstances a person was in when they received it. The word "remain" in the verse means to stay in that same situation.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. Some believed that, once they trusted in Christ, they had to change their status: be circumcised or stop being circumcised, or alter their social condition. Paul answers that what matters is obeying God, not changing one's outward position. Even so, he adds that if a servant has the chance to become free, it is good to pursue it.

Today we can serve God faithfully where we are: at work, in the family, or at school. There is no need to change place to please him; we can live with honesty and love right there.
exp.15:13:
This verse says that everything we do, great or small, must be done in love. The word love here means the generous care that seeks the good of others. Everything we do includes our words, our work, our decisions and our service.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had divisions, pride and arguments. At the end of his letter, he gives brief commands: watch, stand firm and be brave. Then he sets this limit: firmness and courage must go together with love. In this way he returns to what he taught in chapter 13.

Today, before you respond in an argument or make a decision, ask yourself: "Am I doing this in love?" You can be right and still speak harshly. Today, try to make your tone, your patience and your actions reflect the love of Christ.
exp.5:15:
This verse asks whether you do not know that the one who unites himself with a prostitute becomes one with her in body. Paul supports this with a quotation: "The two will become one flesh." A prostitute is someone who sells sex, and to unite oneself with someone means to join with them intimately. For Paul, sexual union is not something fleeting or unimportant.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city with much sexual immorality. Some believers thought that what they did with their bodies did not affect their spiritual life. Paul reminds them that their bodies belong to Christ and will be raised, so they matter greatly to God.

For today: take care of your body and your relationships as something that belongs to Christ. Before deciding on matters of sexuality, ask yourself whether it honors God and respects the other person. If you have failed, God offers forgiveness and a new beginning.
exp.5:1:
Paul asks whether believers do not know that the saints, that is, those who belong to God, will take part in judging the world. If you are to judge the world, he says, then surely you are competent to judge trivial cases. Here "competent" means capable and fit for the task.
