Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some brothers and sisters were taking one another to court before judges who did not believe. He is troubled by this and reminds them of their calling. How and when the saints will judge the world is understood in several ways, but Paul takes it as certain.

For today: when you have a conflict with another believer, first seek to resolve it with humility, through dialogue, and with the help of mature brothers and sisters in the church, before making it public or taking it to lawsuits.
exp.6:7:
Paul tells the unmarried and the widows that it is good for them to remain unmarried, as he is. The phrase "it is good" means that it is something advantageous and beneficial. The words "to remain unmarried" mean staying single.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage and singleness. He makes clear that he is giving advice, not a command. He recognizes that each person has their own gift from God: some for singleness and others for marriage. He then adds that whoever cannot control themselves should marry. Many believe he also had in mind the difficulties of that time, although this is understood in different ways.

For today: do not see your marital status, whether married or single, as being of lesser value. Ask God how to serve him faithfully where you are, and do not let anyone pressure you in making your decision.
exp.13:3:
The verse says that the one who speaks in a tongue builds up only himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church. The word "edifies" means to build up, to strengthen, or to help someone grow spiritually. Here, "prophesies" means speaking a message from God that people can understand.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where spiritual gifts were highly prized. He does not look down on speaking in tongues, but he addresses the confusion it caused: if no one understands what is being said, the congregation gets no benefit. For this reason he insists that every gift be used for the good of everyone.

For today: before you speak or serve in your church, ask yourself whether what you do helps others grow, and aim to communicate in a way that is clear and easy to understand.
exp.4:3:
When the church comes together in the name of our Lord Jesus, Paul says he will be with them in spirit, even though he is far away. The phrase "when you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus" points to the church gathering in his name, and the word "power" points to the strength and authority of the Lord Jesus. So the decision the church makes is carried out under the authority of Jesus, not by human opinion.

Paul writes from Ephesus, as is commonly understood, to the church in Corinth. There was a serious case of sexual immorality among them, and the church was doing nothing about it; they were even proud of it. Paul asks them to act together as a community. How exactly to understand being "handed over to Satan" is interpreted in several ways, but the stated purpose is that the person would ultimately be saved.

For today: when the church faces a serious sin, it should act with humility, unity and prayer, seeking the restoration of the person and not punishment or pride.
exp.11:21:
Paul says that the parts of the body that seem weaker are actually indispensable, meaning we need them more than we realize. The word "weaker" here means fragile or having little outward appearance of strength. The word "indispensable" means that the body cannot do without them.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there was division and pride over spiritual gifts. Some believed they were more important than others. Paul uses the image of the human body to show that the church is one body with many parts, and that all depend on one another.

For today: value those who go unnoticed in your church or family, such as the person who prays in silence, helps without being seen, or is going through a time of weakness. Today, seek out one of those people and thank them with specific words.
exp.6:29:
Paul says that those who weep should live as if they did not weep, those who are joyful as if they were not, and those who make a purchase as if they had nothing. These are three examples of not fixing the heart on what is passing away.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and the Christian life. Earlier in the chapter he said that "the time is short," and then that the present form of this world is passing away. Many understand him to be speaking of the urgency of living for God, perhaps also because of the hardships of that time. He does not say that sorrows, joys, or possessions do not matter, but that they should not rule over us.

Today we can enjoy what is good and grieve what is sad, but without placing our hope in them. Ask yourself: what is holding me too tightly today? Surrender it to God in prayer.
exp.2:6:
It says that the one who plants and the one who waters are not what matters most. The one who truly matters is God, because only He makes the seed grow. "Servants" are those who serve others, and "co-workers" are those who labor together.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where the people were divided and boasted of following one leader or another, Paul or Apollos. He reminds them that both are only servants. Paul began the work in Corinth, Apollos continued it, and God gave the growth. Each one will receive his reward according to his labor.

Today we can serve with enthusiasm, whether by teaching, praying, or helping, without competing or seeking applause. We do our part faithfully and trust that God is the one who transforms hearts. In this way we also avoid admiring a leader too much.
exp.8:5:
Paul says that he and Barnabas also have the right to stop working for a living and to be supported by the church. "Right" here means entitlement or authority. "Working for a living" refers to earning one's income through one's own trade, so that one can give oneself fully to the ministry. It is a rhetorical question: the expected answer is that they do have that right.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his ministry as an apostle. He has already noted that other apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Peter (Cephas) receive support. Paul and Barnabas, by contrast, chose to work for their own living. He does not claim the right in order to demand it, but to show that he gave it up willingly out of love for the gospel.

For today: value and generously support those who serve in ministry. And if you have some right, consider whether it is sometimes wise to set it aside in order to help others believe.
exp.4:1:
They say the Corinthians were proud, full of themselves, instead of grieved over the serious sin that was among them. Paul expected them to remove from their fellowship the man who had done this.

Paul, the apostle, writes to the church in Corinth. He had learned that a man was living with his father's wife, something that not even the pagans accepted. What concerns him most is the church's attitude, which was not reacting. It is not known for certain why they were proud; some think they boasted of their freedom or their wisdom.

For today: when we see serious sin in our community, let us not ignore it or present it as tolerance. We must respond with sorrow, humility, and a desire to restore, seeking the good of the person and of the church.
exp.1:1:
He says that when Paul was in Corinth, he resolved to put forward no other subject as the most important, but Jesus Christ, and in particular Jesus Christ crucified. The word "resolved" means "decided" or "made up his mind."

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a city that valued eloquence and human wisdom very highly. Some in the church were divided and boasted about their favorite leaders. Paul reminds them that when he visited them, he did not come with impressive speeches. He focused on the message of the cross, which seemed to many like weakness, but which God uses with power.

For today: before you speak about faith with someone, or teach others, ask yourself whether Christ and his work on the cross are the center, or whether you are trying to impress. Returning to Jesus keeps your faith simple and firm.
exp.6:1:
It says that, because there is so much sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. The word "but" connects this to the previous verse, and the phrase "because there is so much" points to the cause: the widespread temptation around them. The verse presents marriage as a good and protected place for sexual life.

Paul is answering a letter from the Corinthians. Some believed the most spiritual course was to avoid all sexual relationships, and he accepts that remaining unmarried can be good (v. 1). But Corinth was a city with a great deal of immorality, and Paul speaks with realism. He emphasizes that husband and wife belong to each other, with equal duties toward one another.

For today: care for your marriage with faithfulness, respect, and honest conversation. If you are married, seek to serve your spouse, not only to receive. If you are single, trust that God also gives you strength and wisdom to live in purity.
exp.11:26:
Paul tells the believers in Corinth that together they form the body of Christ, and that each one of them is a member, a part of that body. Each person is a distinct piece of the whole, not the whole body by themselves.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride over spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the body to teach them that everyone is necessary, that God gives different gifts to different people, and that no one should look down on another or think himself superior.

For today: this week, look for a brother or sister in your church and ask how they are doing. If they are struggling, come alongside them; if they are experiencing some joy, celebrate it with them. In this way you show that you belong to the same body.
exp.13:11:
Paul says that the Corinthians are very eager for spiritual gifts, that is, the abilities that the Holy Spirit gives. But he tells them to strive to excel in those gifts that build up the church, that is, that strengthen and help the whole church grow. "You" refers to the Corinthians, and "strive" means "work hard at."

Paul is writing to a church that is very enthusiastic about the gifts, but somewhat disorderly. Some were speaking in tongues that no one understood, and that did not help the others. Earlier, he compared this to languages: if you do not understand what someone is saying, that person becomes a stranger to you. For this reason he insists that what matters is that everyone understands and is helped.

For today: before you use your gifts or abilities in the church, ask yourself: "Does this help others know and love God better?" Serve with clarity, humility, and a concern for the good of everyone.
exp.9:8:
He says we should not test Christ, that is, not wear out his patience or doubt his care, as some Israelites did in the desert. Here "test" means to try or to challenge, and the verse says they were killed by snakes.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who lived surrounded by many temptations and felt secure in themselves. He reminds them of what happened to Israel after leaving Egypt (Numbers 21), when the people spoke against God and against Moses. Paul sees in Christ the God who accompanied his people, and he uses that story as a warning.

For today: do not live testing God with your disobedience, thinking that his forgiveness permits everything. Give thanks for his mercy and trust in him with humility.
exp.6:33:
The explanation says that the unmarried woman or virgin can devote herself fully to the work of the Lord, so as to be holy in both body and spirit. By contrast, the married woman is concerned with the affairs of this world, that is, with everyday life and the home, and with how to please her husband. The word "concerned" in the verse means focused on or attentive to something.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had asked him questions about marriage. He wants them to live without anxiety. He clarifies that he does not intend to put a burden on them or restrict them; he only seeks that they serve the Lord without distraction. Paul does not say that getting married is a sin.

For today: whatever your situation, single or married, ask yourself how you can serve the Lord with your time. If you are married, caring for your family is also serving God; do it with love and without losing your devotion.
exp.10:8:
It says that man was not created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man. The phrase "was created for" simply means "was created." Paul is pointing back to the account in Genesis 2, where God forms the woman as a helper for the man.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to correct disorder in their meetings, and here he speaks about wearing a veil or covering on the head when praying or prophesying. He uses Genesis to support his point. Some believe he teaches an order of authority; others believe he speaks of customs of that time. But in verse 11 he clarifies: neither is man without woman, nor woman without man, in the Lord. They need each other.

For today: value people of the other sex as necessary companions, not as inferiors. Treat everyone with respect and gratitude, seeking to serve the Lord together.
exp.6:8:
He says that whoever cannot control themselves and lives in constant struggle would do well to marry. "Self-control" is the word in this verse that matches the idea of mastering oneself, especially in sexual matters. The phrase "to burn with passion" is usually understood as burning with desire, though some scholars think it refers to a wider anguish over not being able to live unmarried.

Here the apostle Paul is answering questions the Corinthians had written to him about marriage and singleness. He had said that singleness is good, but he clarifies that each person receives a different gift from God: some to remain single and others to marry. Marrying is not something lesser.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or pressure yourself. Ask God sincerely which path is yours, whether singleness or marriage, and live it with honesty, self-control, and gratitude.
exp.6:6:
Paul says he wishes everyone were as he is, that is, single and free to serve the Lord. But he recognizes that each person has their own gift from God, their particular ability or calling: some for marriage and others for singleness.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and sexual life. He has just spoken about life as a couple and makes clear that he gives advice, not a command. Many think that when he says "I wish that all men were as I am" he is referring to being unmarried, though some believe he is also speaking of his self-control.

For today: do not compare your path with that of others, and do not feel lesser for being married or single. Ask God how he wants you to serve him in your present situation, and live it with gratitude.
exp.8:20:
Paul speaks of those "without the law," that is, the Gentiles, who had not received the law of Moses. He says he approached them as one of them, without imposing Jewish customs on them. He clarifies that he was not outside God's law, since he was under the law of Christ, which many understand as the command of love and the teachings of Jesus. His aim was to win those people over to Christ.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a varied city full of differences. He explains that, though free, he chose to serve everyone so that the gospel would reach more people. He adapted his customs, but never his faithfulness to God.

For today: approach people with respect, understanding their world and their customs, without making them feel they must change everything in order to listen to you. Always take care that your love for Christ and your obedience to Him are never bargained away.
exp.0:19:
Paul asks three questions: "Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the philosopher of this age?" The word "philosopher" refers to someone who examines ideas and argues about them with great cleverness; "age" here means this present world. The statement that God has made foolish the wisdom of the world means that God has exposed human wisdom as foolishness.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, divided by pride and by admiration for certain teachers. He has just quoted Isaiah (29:14) to show that God does not depend on human intelligence. His point is that no wise person, whether Jew or Greek, reached God through their own reasoning; God chose to save through the message of the cross.

Today we can study and value knowledge, but without boasting in it. Before we debate or compete with arguments, let us remember that no one draws near to God by being cleverer, but by humility and faith in Christ.
exp.4:2:
Paul says that although he was not physically with the Corinthians, he was present with them in spirit. Because of this, he had already pronounced judgment, as if he were there, on the man who did this. Here, "judged" means that he had already reached a decision about the case.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was tolerating a serious case of sexual immorality: a man was living with his father's wife. Instead of grieving, the Corinthians were proud. Paul asks them to act with firmness. Interpreters explain the phrase "handed over to Satan" in different ways, but many understand it as removing the man from the community, in the hope that he would repent.

Today, the church and every believer must take sin seriously, without pride or indifference. Correcting with humility, prayer, and a desire to restore is a demonstration of love.
exp.1:0:
Paul reminds the brothers in Corinth that when he came to them, he did not come with eloquence or wisdom. "Eloquence" here refers to showy, polished speech meant to impress. "Declaring to you the testimony about God" means proclaiming to them what God did and revealed in Jesus.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city that greatly admired eloquence and wisdom. There were divisions among the believers, and some boasted of brilliant leaders. Paul reminds them that his first visit was simple, so that their faith would rest on God and not on human abilities.

For today: when you speak about Jesus to others, you do not need impressive words. Be simple, honest, and faithful to the message; God works through him.
exp.14:27:
It says that when Christ has defeated everything, including death, the Son himself will be placed under the authority of the Father, who gave him that rule. "Subjected" here means brought under authority. The verse uses the phrase "when all things have been subjected," which marks the point at which that work is finished. The final goal is that God be all in all, meaning that God reigns fully and his presence fills everything.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some denied the resurrection of the dead. He explains that Christ's resurrection begins the final victory over death. That the Son will be made subject to the Father does not mean he is lesser in worth; Christians have understood it in different ways. The theme is the order and purpose of the work of redemption.

For today: the story ends with God at the center and with death defeated. That hope helps us live with peace, serve without fear, and put God first in every area of life.
exp.0:9:
Paul asks the believers in Corinth, with great warmth and in the name of Jesus, to agree with one another. "That all of you agree together" means they should not split apart over opinions that set them against each other. "Divisions" means splits or disagreements. "United in mind and conviction" describes being well fitted together, like pieces that fit, with one mindset and one purpose.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Corinth. He has just reminded them that God is faithful and called them into fellowship with his Son. Then he learns, from people of Chloe's household, that they were splitting into groups, each following the leader they preferred: Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ.

For today: if there is division in your church or family, do not take the side of one person or one faction. First look for what unites, which is Christ, and speak with humility and respect.
exp.14:19:
He says that Christ truly rose, and that His resurrection is the beginning of a greater one. The "firstfruits" are the first part of a harvest, and they announce that the rest will follow. "Have fallen asleep" is a gentle way of speaking of those who died, as one who expects to wake up.

The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom some denied the resurrection of the dead. Earlier he has said that if Christ has not been raised, faith is empty. Here he answers firmly: "But Christ has indeed been raised," that is, things are not that way, Christ has risen. Then he compares Him with Adam: by one man came death, and by another comes life.

Today, this truth gives us hope in the face of pain and death. If you have lost a loved one who trusted in Christ, you can rest in the knowledge that the grave does not have the last word. Live with that firm hope.
exp.5:19:
You were bought at a price, so honor God with your body. The word "bought" means "were bought," and "glorify" means "honor" or "give glory to." Paul is saying that God has paid for you, and so your body now belongs to him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city known for much sexual immorality. He reminds them that their body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and that they no longer belong to themselves. The "price" refers to what Christ gave for them; Paul does not spell out the payment here, but in other passages he connects it with Christ's blood and his cross.

For today: before you make a decision about what you see, say, eat, or do with your body, ask yourself whether it honors God, who loved you and made you his own.
exp.11:6:
Paul says that God gives each believer a visible sign of the work of the Holy Spirit, and that he gives it for the common good. The word "Now" marks a turn in his thought, and "manifestation" means that something of the Spirit becomes noticeable in the life of each person.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and gave too much importance to the most striking gifts. Earlier he has said that there are different kinds of gifts, service, and works, but one Spirit, one Lord, and one God. Afterward he will list several specific gifts.

For today: do not look down on what God has given you, nor envy what others have. Ask yourself how you can use your gift, whether great or simple, to help and encourage others in your church and in your community.
exp.4:4:
It says that this person is to be "handed over to Satan," that is, removed from the fellowship of the church and left in the world where Satan holds sway. The phrase "destruction of the flesh" can mean the suffering or ruin of his sinful desires, or even physical harm; scholars understand it in different ways. The goal is that his spirit may be saved "on the Day of the Lord," when Christ returns.

Paul writes to the Corinthians because a man was living in serious sexual sin, and the church was doing nothing about it, even taking pride in it. Paul asks them to act together, with the authority of Jesus. Then he reminds them that a little yeast leavens the whole batch.

Today we can learn that true love does not ignore sin. Correcting with humility, seeking the restoration of the person and not his punishment, protects the community and can lead to repentance.
exp.8:8:
Paul quotes a command from the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 25:4): "Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." The ox that treads out the grain must not be kept from eating, so it could eat as it worked. Then Paul asks, "Is it about oxen that God is concerned?", a question that invites us to look beyond the animal.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and defends his right, as an apostle, to receive support from the church. Earlier he gave examples from the soldier, the vinedresser, and the shepherd. Here he supports his argument with Scripture. Although God does care for animals, Paul explains right away that the principle also applies to those who serve in spiritual work.

For today: value and support with generosity those who teach you the Word and serve your church. Whoever works for the good of others deserves to be cared for.
exp.0:16:
Paul says that Christ did not send him mainly to baptize, but to preach the gospel. He does this without "words of wisdom," that is, without polished speeches meant to impress. The verse warns that if the message were delivered with clever rhetoric, the cross of Christ would be emptied of its power.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was split into groups that followed different leaders. He is glad that he baptized only a few people, so that no one could claim he had gathered a following for himself. He does not downplay baptism; he simply makes clear that his central task was to preach the message of the cross, which the world sees as foolishness.

For today: when you share your faith, do not seek to show off or win admiration. Speak simply and sincerely about what Christ has done for us, and trust that God gives power to that message.
exp.14:48:
It says that we have all carried the likeness of Adam, the first man, who was made from the dust of the earth. But one day we will also carry the likeness of Christ, the man from heaven. "Carrying the likeness" means bearing a resemblance. "Earthly" describes a man made of earth; "heavenly" describes one who comes from heaven.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to answer doubts about the resurrection. He compares Adam, who left us a weak and mortal body, with the risen Christ, who will give us a transformed body. The verses that follow explain that our present body cannot enter the kingdom of God as it is, and that we will be changed. Christians understand the details of that change in different ways, but they all share the same hope.

Today, this promise gives us encouragement in the face of sickness, weariness, and death. It also invites us to resemble Christ now: choose one of his qualities, such as forgiveness or patience, and practice it today.
exp.14:54:
Here Paul asks a question as if mocking death. The "sting" is the venomous jab, like that of a scorpion or a wasp. The "victory" belongs to death in the sense of the power and triumph it seems to hold, and the question is: where has that victory gone? In the same way, the question about the sting asks where its harm has gone.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who doubted the resurrection. After explaining that Christ rose and that believers will also be transformed, he uses words that echo the prophet Hosea (13:14) and Isaiah (25:8). The verses that follow say that the sting of death is sin, and that God gives us the victory through Jesus Christ.

For today: when the fear of death or the grief over a loved one weighs on you, remember that for the one who trusts in Christ, death does not have the last word. You can weep with hope.
exp.3:9:
Paul contrasts himself and the other apostles with the Corinthians. He says that they are seen as foolish and weak for Christ, while the Corinthians think of themselves as wise and strong in Christ. "Honored" means respected and held in good standing, while "dishonored" means looked down on and treated as having no worth in the eyes of the world. It is ironic language.

Paul writes to a proud church, divided by following different leaders and boasting of its wisdom. With irony, he shows them that they feel like kings, while the apostles go hungry, are struck, and face contempt for serving Christ. He does not seek to humiliate them for its own sake, but to correct them as a father would, so that they will give up their arrogance.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek applause and a good image, or faithfulness to Christ. Serving Jesus sometimes means being looked down on or thought foolish. Let us ask him for humility, so that we measure our faith not by success, but by love and obedience.
exp.10:19:
Paul tells the Christians in Corinth that, although they gather together as a church, what they eat cannot be called the Lord's Supper. "When you come together" means that they meet in the same place. With these words, Paul points out that their gathering does not match what Jesus established.

Paul writes because there are divisions among them. According to the verses that follow, each person was eating his own meal without waiting for the others. As a result, one went hungry while another became drunk. The poor were left feeling ashamed. Scholars generally agree that this happened during the ordinary meal that accompanied the Supper, although the exact details are debated.

For today: before taking part in the Lord's Supper, let us examine how we treat our fellow believers. Sharing the table with Christ calls us to wait for one another, to serve, and to care for the most needy in the community.
exp.9:31:
The passage says that we should live in such a way that we do not become a stumbling block to anyone. It mentions three groups: the Jews, the Greeks, and the church of God. "Do not become a stumbling block" means "do not put something in someone's way that makes them fall or lose their footing in faith."

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who had doubts about eating meat offered to idols. He tells them that, although they have freedom, they must use that freedom with care and love. At the end, in the following verse, Paul sets himself as an example: he seeks the good of many so that they may be saved, not his own benefit.

Today, before doing something that is permitted, we can ask ourselves: "Will this help others draw near to God, or will it make them stumble?" Choosing with love, even giving up something of our own, can be a powerful witness.
exp.10:18:
Paul says that divisions among them are unavoidable, and that they serve to show who has genuine faith. The word translated "differences" here comes from a Greek word meaning groups or factions that separate, rather than false doctrines. And "there must be" means the divisions are unavoidable, not that God desires them.

Paul is writing to the church at Corinth, correcting their behavior at their gatherings. He has already mentioned the divisions, and he will soon rebuke how the wealthy ate without waiting for the poor at the Lord's Supper. Commentators explain this verse in different ways, but they all agree that divisions expose the character of the people involved.

Today: when tensions arise in your church or family, do not be scandalized. Use them to examine your own heart, and seek to act with humility and love toward those who are weaker.
exp.5:4:
Paul says that what he is about to say is meant to make the Corinthians feel ashamed. He asks them with irony: is it really true that there is no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between your brothers? The word "arbitrate" here means to settle a dispute.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with many problems. Some believers were taking one another to court before judges who did not believe in Christ. Paul reminds them that Christians will one day take part in judging the world, so they ought to be able to settle everyday matters among themselves.

Today, when there is a conflict with another believer, let us first seek the counsel of mature and prudent brothers and sisters in the church. Resolving differences with humility and in private protects the witness of the community and cares for the relationship.
exp.14:50:
Paul says he is about to reveal a "mystery," meaning something that was not clearly understood before. "Sleep" refers to death. So he explains that not all believers will die before Christ returns, but all will be "changed," transformed to receive a new body.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, who had doubts about the resurrection. He has just explained that our present body, weak and mortal, cannot enter the kingdom of God as it is. That is why we need to be changed, whether we have died or are still alive at that moment.

Today, this promise gives us hope in the face of sickness, aging, and death. We can live with peace and confidence, knowing that God has prepared a new body for those who trust in Christ.
exp.11:23:
It says that the parts of the body that look good and seem worthy do not need special attention. "Presentable" here means proper and becoming. Instead, God has composed the body so that the parts that lacked honor are given greater honor and care. In this way, no one is forgotten.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided and valued showy gifts more, such as speaking in tongues. He uses the picture of the body to show that every believer is necessary. Some understand the parts that are "less presentable" to mean the private parts we cover with clothing, but the central point is mutual care.

For today: notice who in your church goes unnoticed, such as someone older, sick, or shy. Look for that person this week, greet them, and give them a place. In this way you reflect God's care.
exp.14:13:
Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, then what he and the other apostles proclaim is worthless, and so is the faith of the Corinthians. Here "worthless" means empty, without value or result. The "preaching" is the message they were proclaiming.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul shows them the consequence: if the dead are not raised, then Christ was not raised either. And if Christ was not raised, the whole gospel falls apart. For him, the resurrection is not a detail but the center of the Christian message.

For today: our faith does not rest only on beautiful ideas or good advice, but on a fact: Christ lives. When you doubt or feel weary, return to this foundation and ask God to strengthen your trust in the risen Jesus.
exp.12:10:
Paul says that as a child he talked like a child, thought like a child, and reasoned like a child, but when he became an adult he set aside those childish ways. A mature person is what the verse means by becoming an adult. The verb is simply "was" in ordinary modern usage.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church that greatly valued spiritual gifts such as prophecy and speaking in tongues, yet lived divided and proud. In this chapter he explains that love is more important than any gift. He uses the picture of the child and the adult to say that the gifts we have now are partial, and that what is "perfect" will bring complete knowledge. Believers have understood what "that which is perfect" refers to in different ways, and it is often thought to mean the return of Christ.

Today we can ask whether, in some area of our lives, we still react with immaturity: pride, arguments, or selfishness. Growing in faith shows less in how much we know and more in how we love others with patience and humility.
exp.6:3:
In marriage, the wife does not have authority over her own body, because her husband has a claim on it; and the same is true the other way around: the husband does not have authority over his own body, because it also belongs to his wife. The verse says the wife "does not have authority over her own body," so the word "authority" here means control. What matters is that the right is mutual and equal.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had asked him questions about marriage and sexual life. Corinth was a city with a great deal of immorality. Paul teaches that marriage is a healthy place for intimacy, based on mutual service rather than demand.

For today: instead of thinking about what I deserve, ask yourself how you can care for and honor your spouse. Speak to each other with respect and affection about your needs, without imposing or manipulating.
exp.2:22:
It says that believers belong to Christ, and that Christ belongs to God. The word "you" here means the believers themselves. It is a short phrase that closes a list: everything Paul has mentioned belongs to you, but you belong to Christ. Christians understand that "Christ belongs to God" speaks of Christ's relationship with the Father; interpreters explain in various ways how to understand that order, but the general sense is an order of belonging and love.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was divided, since some said they followed Paul, others Apollos, and others Peter (Cephas). He corrects them: do not boast in human leaders, because those leaders are a gift to them, not their owners.

For today: stop comparing yourself with or competing against others over their leaders or followers. Rest in this: you belong to Christ, and that gives you security. Value those who teach you as a gift from God, but follow Christ.
exp.14:34:
Here Paul presents the questions someone might ask: "How are the dead raised?" and "With what kind of body will they come?" The words "But someone will ask" mean that a person will raise these questions. They are either sincere or mocking doubts about what the resurrection will be like.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, where some denied the resurrection of the dead (verse 12). Earlier he had warned them against bad influences and a lack of knowledge of God. Now he answers with an image from the field: a seed that dies and produces a different plant. The exact details of how the resurrected body will be are not fully explained.

For today: when you have doubts about the faith, bring them to God and to his Word with humility, without mockery. And trust that God, who gives life to the seed, can fulfill his promise.
exp.13:14:
Paul says that he will pray and sing in two ways: with his spirit and also with his mind. In other words, he does not want his prayer to be only an inner feeling, but also something his mind can grasp. The phrase "What then shall I do?" means "So what am I to conclude?" "Spirit" here is usually understood as the spirit of the person praying, moved by God, although some interpret it in other ways.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where speaking in tongues was very common in the meetings, but often without anyone explaining what was said. He does not forbid that gift, but he insists that what is done in the community must build up everyone. For this reason he asks for order and understanding.

For today: when you pray or sing, try to understand what you are saying. Think about the words of the songs and about your words to God, so that your heart and your mind worship together.
exp.13:33:
Paul says that women are to be silent in the church meetings. They are not permitted to speak, but they must be in submission, as the law says. "Churches" here means the gatherings of believers. "Submission" means placing themselves under order and authority.

Paul writes to a church in Corinth that had a great deal of disorder in its worship. The whole chapter is about putting the gifts and prophecies in order so that there may be peace. It is not clear which "law" he means; some think of the Old Testament, others of custom. Christians understand this verse in different ways: as a general rule, or as an instruction for a specific problem, such as the questions that interrupted the meeting. Paul himself allows women to pray and prophesy in 1 Corinthians 11:5.

For today: let us seek to make our meetings orderly and peaceful, and let us study this passage with humility, comparing it with the rest of the Bible.
exp.0:18:
Paul quotes a line from Scripture to say that God will overturn the plans of those who trust only in their own wisdom. The word the verse uses here means to bring to nothing or to frustrate. The words translated as "wise" and "intelligent" refer to people who are very clever or well educated. God does not say that knowledge is bad, but that human wisdom cannot save.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was divided and admired certain teachers for their eloquence. He reminds them that the message of the cross seems like foolishness to the world, but it is the power of God. This quotation comes from Isaiah 29:14, where God was speaking to a people who prided themselves on being wise.

Today we can study and learn with gratitude, but without thinking we are self-sufficient. Before trusting only in our own ideas, we can pray with humility and ask God to teach us to depend on Christ.
exp.10:6:
Paul says that a man should not cover his head when praying or prophesying, because he is the image and glory of God. By contrast, the woman is the glory of man. Here "man" means male, and "created" means made by God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to correct the order in their gatherings. He refers to the customs of covering the head in that culture, and it is not entirely clear what exact practice he had in mind. His argument recalls Genesis, but scholars disagree about what it means for the woman to be the glory of man: some see order, and others see mutual honor. Later in this same chapter, Paul clarifies that both depend on one another in the Lord.

For today: seek to worship in a way that honors God and does not cause others to stumble. Treat people with respect, recognizing that all of us reflect the glory of God.
exp.0:6:
He says that the believers in Corinth did not lack any spiritual gift, meaning that God had given them the abilities they needed through his grace. Meanwhile, they eagerly waited for the revelation of Jesus Christ, which means his appearing or return, when he will be made fully known to all. "Revelation" here means that they were looking forward to the Lord being made known in his coming.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a community with many gifts but also with divisions and disorder, as he will point out later in the letter. Before correcting them, he acknowledges the good that God has done in them. He reminds them that their final hope is placed in Christ, and not in their own abilities.

For today: give thanks for the gifts God has given you and use them to serve others with humility. At the same time, live with your eyes fixed on the return of Jesus, trusting that he will sustain you.
exp.14:26:
This verse says that God has put everything under the feet of Christ, quoting Psalm 8:6. But it makes an important clarification: when it says "everything" has been put under him, this clearly does not include the One who put everything under him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend the resurrection. He explains that Christ reigns until he defeats every enemy, and that the last enemy will be death. Here he makes clear that Christ reigns with the authority of the Father, and that in the end everything will be fulfilled in harmony between the two. How the relationship between the Son and the Father is understood here has been widely discussed, but the central point is the triumph over death.

Today we can rest in the fact that Christ has the last word. In the face of fear, grief, or injustice, we can pray with hope, knowing that death will not win.
exp.7:12:
Paul says he is willing to stop eating meat forever if doing so would keep another believer from stumbling. Causing someone to stumble means that something leads them to fall away in their faith or to act against their own conscience. The word "offend" here does not mean spreading gossip or causing a quarrel, but being a stumbling block in someone's path. The "weak" person is the believer whose conscience is still weak and who does not yet have a clear understanding.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. There, people debated whether it was right to eat meat that had been offered to idols, which was then sold in the marketplace. Paul acknowledges that idols are nothing, but some newly converted brothers and sisters still felt that eating such meat was worshiping idols. He asks that knowledge be used with love, not with pride.

Today: before using your freedom in something doubtful, ask yourself whether it could cause someone close to you to stumble. Sometimes love means giving up a right for the good of another.
exp.11:20:
It says that no member of the body can look down on another. The eye cannot say to the hand, "I do not need you," nor can the head say to the feet, "I do not need you." Each part, though different from the others, is important for the body to work well.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where there were divisions and pride, especially over spiritual gifts. Some people felt superior to others. Paul uses the image of the body to explain that the church is one body with many members, and that all depend on one another.

Today we might ask ourselves: whom in my church or family have I looked down on? This week, thank someone whose service often goes unnoticed and tell them that you need them.
exp.13:35:
Paul asks the Corinthians two pointed questions. He asks whether the word of God started with them, or whether it reached only them. The word "Did" here works like "Did it really...?" and expects the answer no.

Paul is writing to a church whose gatherings were very disorderly. With these questions he reminds them that they are not the center, nor the only authority, of Christian life. There are other churches, and all of them should follow the same order. The verses before this one about women are much debated: some read them as a general rule, others as instruction for a specific problem in Corinth. There is no single agreed view.

For today: before we assume that our own way of doing things is the only right way, let us be humble and listen to the Bible and to the church of every age.
exp.13:37:
Paul says that whoever ignores what he has written will himself be ignored. The Berean Standard Bible reads "ignores," and the sense is that a person who will not take this seriously will not be recognized or accepted by God and the church. The alternative manuscript wording, "does not recognize it, he will not be recognized," has the same basic meaning, and scholars debate which reading is original.

Paul corrects the Corinthians for the disorder in their meetings. He reminds them that they are not the source of God's word, nor the only ones who have received it. Whoever considers himself a prophet or spiritual must accept these instructions as commands from the Lord. Paul does not argue further with the one who stubbornly refuses.

For today: if we claim to be spiritual, we should show it with humility, letting ourselves be corrected by Scripture and serving with order in the church, without imposing our experiences on others.
exp.11:24:
God arranged the body so that there is no division or quarreling among its parts. Instead, each member should truly care for the others. "Division" means disagreement, a split, or a lack of unity. "Mutual concern for one another" means that each person looks out for the well-being of the rest.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was marked by divisions and pride, especially about spiritual gifts. He uses the image of the human body: the parts that seem less important are given greater honor, because every part is necessary. The church is the body of Christ, and God ordered it this way so that there would be unity and mutual concern.

Today we can look out for someone in our church or family who seems to go unnoticed. This week, call them, listen to them, or help them with something specific, and in that way we practice this mutual concern.
exp.6:5:
Paul makes clear that what he has just said is not a command from God, but a concession. A concession is a allowance or permission to do something, not a binding order.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had asked him questions about marriage. He is referring to what came before: that spouses may separate for a short time, by mutual agreement, to pray. Interpreters differ a little: some believe "this" points only to that temporary pause; others, to the whole of the earlier advice. In either case, Paul offers wise guidance, not a law.

Today we can distinguish between what the Bible commands and what it leaves to our freedom. In marriage, couples should decide together, with respect and mutual agreement, how to give time to prayer, without imposing it on one another.
exp.3:2:
Paul says that it matters very little to him whether he is judged by the Corinthians or by any human court. In the Berean Standard Bible's wording, he cares very little if he is judged by them or by any human court, and he adds that he does not even judge himself. So the point is that he does not treat his own opinion of himself as the final word either.

Paul is writing to a divided church, where some were comparing and criticizing their leaders. He has just said that ministers are stewards of the mysteries of God, and that a steward is required to be faithful. That is why the final judge is neither the Corinthians nor Paul, but the Lord, who will judge in his time.

For today: serve God faithfully without living on the lookout for applause or criticism. Listen to advice with humility, but leave the final verdict in the hands of the Lord, who sees the heart.
exp.3:6:
Paul asks three questions to show that no one has reason to boast. The first question, "who makes you so superior?", asks what sets you apart from others. Then the second question, "what do you have that you did not receive?", points out that everything you have was given to you. If you received it as a gift, there is no sense in boasting as though you had gotten it on your own.

Paul is writing to the Christians of Corinth, who were divided and took pride in their favorite leaders, such as himself and Apollos. He asks them not to compare themselves with one another or think of themselves as superior. Then, with irony, he confronts them about their air of greatness, while the apostles were suffering.

For today: when you feel pride in your talents, your work, or your faith, remember that everything is a gift from God. That leads us to be thankful, to serve with humility, and to stop comparing ourselves with others.
exp.14:47:
Paul's point in this verse is that we take on the character of the one we belong to. Those who are of the earth reflect the earthly man, Adam, who was made from dust, and all of his descendants. Those who are of heaven reflect the heavenly man, Christ, and belong to him. Here "earthly" means of the earth and "heavenly" means of heaven.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to explain what the resurrection will be like. Some doubted that the dead would rise with a body. He compares Adam with Christ: from the first we inherit a frail and mortal body, and from the second we will receive a glorious and imperishable body, as the following verses say.

Today we can remember that our final identity does not depend on our present frailty. If you belong to Christ, your future is his. Live with hope, and let his character shape you from now on, even in your weaknesses.
exp.11:4:
This verse says that in the church there are different ways of serving, but they all come from the same Lord. The word "ministries" points to the different kinds of service done for the benefit of others. In other words, God does not give out just one kind of service, but many.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, who were divided and placed too much importance on certain spiritual gifts. Earlier he spoke of the Spirit, now he speaks of the Lord Jesus, and next he will speak of God the Father. Many see here a glimpse of the Trinity, although Paul does not explain the subject in detail. His point is that variety should not divide, because the source is one.

Today, do not compare your service with that of others. Whether it is teaching, visiting the sick, praying, or helping with practical needs, do your part as service to the Lord, and value what others do.
exp.11:5:
There are different ways God's work is carried out and its effects produced, but behind every one of them stands the same God. The phrase "works all things in all people" means that God is the one who gives the power and makes things happen in each believer.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was divided and gave too much importance to certain spiritual gifts. Here he refers to the Spirit, the Lord, and God. Many see in this a reflection of the Trinity. His purpose is to show that variety is no reason for rivalry, because the source is one.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or look down on your own contribution. Serve with what God has given you, recognizing that the power comes from him, and value the brothers and sisters who serve in ways different from yours.

sum.3: Paul asks that people see him as a servant of Christ, and that what matters most is being faithful, since only the Lord truly judges. He calls the Corinthians to set aside their pride, reminding them that they have received everything they have. He presents himself as a father who corrects them out of love. He announces that he will come to them soon, and that the Corinthians must decide whether they would prefer to see him come with a rod or in gentleness.
sum.1: Paul recalls that when he went to Corinth, he did not use fancy words or human wisdom. Instead, he proclaimed Jesus Christ crucified, relying on the power of the Spirit, so that the faith of his hearers would rest on the power of God. He explains that God reveals his hidden wisdom through the Spirit, and that a person who is not spiritual does not understand it, but believers have the mind of Christ.
sum.4: Paul rebukes the church in Corinth for tolerating, and even taking pride in, a serious sexual sin among them, and he tells them to remove the person who committed it from the community. He reminds them that a little yeast works through the whole batch of dough, and that Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed, so they should live with sincerity and truth. They are not to judge the outside world, but to guard purity within the church.
sum.5: Paul rebukes the believers in Corinth for taking their lawsuits before judges who do not believe, and he tells them it is better to endure injustice than to harm a fellow believer. He also warns that those who live in sin will not inherit the kingdom of God, even though they have already been washed and made right with God in Christ. He asks them to flee sexual immorality, because their body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and belongs to God.
sum.13: Paul teaches that when the church gathers, everything should be done in love and for the building up of the church. For this reason he values prophecy more highly than speaking in tongues without interpretation, since prophecy is something everyone can understand. He calls for order and peace in worship. He concludes by saying that people should seek to prophesy, not forbid speaking in tongues, and that everything should be done properly and decently.
sum.0: Paul greets the church in Corinth and thanks God for the gifts he has given them in Christ. He urges them to put an end to their divisions, since each of them was claiming to follow a different leader. He teaches them that the cross seems like foolishness to the world, but it is the power and wisdom of God, so no one should boast except in the Lord.
sum.15: Paul asks that each Sunday they set aside an offering to help the saints in Jerusalem, and he tells them about his plans to visit them. He encourages them to stay alert, stand firm in the faith, and do everything with love, and he asks them to show respect to Timothy and to those who serve, such as Stephanas. He ends with greetings and a blessing of grace.
sum.12: Paul teaches that without love, the greatest gifts, such as speaking in tongues, prophesying, having faith, or giving everything to the poor, are worth nothing. He describes what love is like: patient, kind, without envy or pride, and that it never fails. Gifts will come to an end, but faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love.
sum.10: Paul corrects two problems in the church at Corinth: how people pray and prophesy during their gatherings, with instructions about covering the head, and abuses at the Lord's Supper, where some ate without waiting for others. He reminds them that the Supper proclaims the death of Christ and calls for self-examination, waiting for one another, and treating each other with respect.
sum.2: Paul rebukes the Corinthians for following human leaders and quarreling with one another, since this shows they are still immature. The leaders are only servants of God, who gives the growth, and each person's work will be tested. The Corinthians are God's temple, and everything belongs to them because they belong to Christ.
sum.14: Paul recalls the gospel: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, and many saw him. He explains that if there is no resurrection, faith is empty, but Christ has been raised as the firstfruits. Believers will be transformed with imperishable bodies, death will be defeated, and for this reason we must stand firm in the Lord.
sum.6: Paul answers questions from the Corinthians about marriage and staying single. He advises faithfulness and mutual devotion within marriage, that spouses should not separate, and that each person should remain in the situation they were called to. He prefers singleness because the time is short and because it allows a person to serve the Lord without distractions, but he permits marriage without sin.
sum.7: Paul explains that although Christians know that idols are nothing and that there is only one God, knowledge without love only puffs a person up with pride. Some believers who are weak still feel confused about food that has been offered to idols. For that reason, love leads us not to use our freedom in a way that causes a brother or sister to fall.
sum.9: Paul recalls how Israel fell into idolatry, sexual immorality, and grumbling in the wilderness, and he warns us not to trust too much in our own strength. God is faithful and provides a way out when we are tempted. He calls us to flee from idolatry and to live in freedom, seeking the good of others and the glory of God.
sum.8: Paul defends his status as a true apostle and says he would have the right to be supported by his ministry, but he gave up that right so that he would not place any obstacle in the way of the gospel. He became all things to all people so that he might win some. He compares the Christian life to a race that requires discipline and self-control.
sum.11: Paul teaches that there are many different spiritual gifts, but all of them come from the same Spirit, Lord, and God, and they are given for the good of everyone. The church is like a body with many parts: all of them are different, all of them are necessary, and they should care for one another. At the end, he invites people to seek the best gifts and announces a more excellent way.
